We're coming near the end of our time together,and I want to share a story with you about someone who I think I would give an A to on their answer to this question,what is success.

So I was sitting in a Wharton conference room attending a seminar on happiness and relative income throughout the world,and someone had done a countrywide study across different national boundaries,Nigeria,Bhutan,India,America,Denmark,Germany,and doing correlational studies between overall happiness,

the kind you measure by thinking,you ask yourself,overall,how happy are you,and wealth in that country and income.

It's a pretty complicated social science study.

And I was in there with about 15 faculty from across the university.

And before the seminar started,and there was a presenter who was getting ready to show his data,the door opened.

And this older gentleman walked in who obviously looked to me as if he had been working on the campus on some construction project and had heard that there was a seminar being offered on happiness.

And we have a tradition here at the University of Pennsylvania that the members of the public are welcome to attend any seminar that is available.

And so seeing members of the public come in is not a crazy thing.

It's always some,we always sort of wonder,you know,what it is that this person might take away or what they might say when they got there.

We're not sure since they're not part of our tribe,the academic tribe,what to make of them.

But here comes this gentleman.

And he ended up sitting down at the end of the table next to me.

And I could see from his hands,because his hands were on the table and resting on the table,that they were definitely working man's hands.

They were sort of calloused,and he was wearing like a flannel shirt and blue jeans and sort of a rough-hewn face.

And so,you know,I just turned my attention back to the presentation.

And the scholar who was giving the research paper,you know,talked about the data here and the wealth levels there and the answers to the questionnaires and how happiness and wealth may or may not be correlated.

And then he concluded and he asked for questions.

And someone asked a question about the,you know,regression analysis that was used on this data set.

And there was some discussion.

And then this guy sitting next to me raised his hand.

Now,you know,as I said,when a member of the public shows up at one of these seminars and actually speaks,the rest of the faculty kind of hold their breath because it's hard to know exactly what they might be saying or where.

they're coming from.

So there was this sort of holding of the breath as this guy raised his hand and the presenter said,yes,sir.

And he said something I'll never forget.

He said,you know,I'm just a member of the public and I don't really understand a lot of what it is you're talking about here.

But it does seem to me you're talking about happiness and money.

And he said,as far as I can understand it,happiness and money have really nothing whatsoever to do with each other.

He said,as far as I know,happiness is just three things.

Good health,meaningful work,and love.

If you have those three things,you're happy.

Now,at this point,there was this dead silence in the seminar room because nobody knew what to say.

And the presenter said,well,thank you,sir.

And there was a pause.

And then someone else said,what about that data in the Denmark sample that you were studying?

And someone else made a comment.

And then the conversation just rolled over this guy's comment like a wave on the beach that just sort of flattens all the sand and covers it back up so that you didn't even know there was a sandcastle there.

And this guy waited for a few minutes and the discussion drifted off.

And then he just sort of quietly got up and walked out the door.

And I thought to myself,Wharton has just been visited by a wise angel.

God has sent an angel to reveal to us the secret of life.

And nobody listened.

But I remembered it.

And I give this guy a lot of credit because,you know,he said it was hisory of happiness,but in many ways it was a theory about success because it combined the inner life,good health,love,with the outer life,meaningful work,and had it in a package.

It was very easy to understand.

And it was quite clear that this guy had learned this through some very,very important life lessons that had taught him the truth of it.

Now,I don't know if he's right for you.

I think you can have good health and bad health.

And sometimes you have no control over that.

And just because your health turns bad doesn't mean that you're not happy or can't be successful.

And you can have love in your life,and it can disappear.

You can lose a loved one.

And that's not anything you control either.

And just because the love in your life has changed in its amount or quality doesn't mean that you can't be happy ever again or successful.

He was the first one who used the phrase meaningful work for me.

And we just finished talking about that.

So I took his phrase and explored it in the context of this research on jobs and careers and calling.

So he taught me something very important about how to think about work.

But even if your work isn't exactly the most meaningful work in the world,it still could be that you're doing something that you're good at and that allows you to support your family.

And the real passion and interest and excitement in your life comes from the coaching that you do on the weekends for your kids'soccer team or from a hobby that you have studying reenactments of the Civil War or you're a gardener and love to work in the public garden down the street.

So even meaningful work is not a final test of whether you're successful or not.

But I give this guy credit because he thought it through.

And he had his own values,he had his own conclusions,he had his own aspirations,and he could articulate them in a really simple way that I credited him a great deal as being a truly wise person.

And that's why I call him the wise angel.

And so that's my final challenge to you in your journey towards success.

And that is this.

See if you can come up with your own definition of what this word success means.

What are the components?

What are the elements?

What are the goals and aspirations that you package together to make into the journey that you want to take the way you want to travel on that journey?

And if you can do that,and bear in mind,it may not be the same today or 25 years from now.

Life happens.

We change our definitions of what we think success means.

But it's a well-worthy effort to put that down as a task to summarize for yourself your own theory of success and how you plan to achieve it.

That is,by the way,the final paper that I always assign my students at the end of our success course.

What is my personal theory of success and how do I plan to achieve it?

And we recognize that this paper is just a snapshot of a moment in time when the students have given it some thought,they articulate their thoughts,and my goal for them is not to commit them to some path.

It's really to give them a photo of their thinking at a given point in time.

And then 10 years down the road,I feel I've succeeded if that paper for them is something they can reread and reread with interest and profit and think to themselves,hmm,that's what I was thinking at that stage of my life aboutWhat success meant and how I would achieve it,and I now see the nuances that I didn't see then,or I now see that I may have actually drifted from the path and I should go back to the path that I had sketched out for myself.

And I need to remind myself of that better self that wrote that paper.

There are all kinds of ways that these little moments where you actually crystallize some thinking can be useful much later in life.

1-04-01.06_结论

现在，我想为本次课程做个总结，为我们共同的学习画上一个句号。

这个想法源于课程本身。

它来自最后一天的最后一次课，以及我们在课堂上做的一件事情。

我们整个学期一起学习了十四周，你们完成了各种各样的练习，还阅读了大量来自不同文献的高深读物，这些我们就不在这里一一细说了。

但在最后一堂课上，我要求每位同学带来自己最喜欢的一句话，这句话可以来自他们读过的某本书、看过的某本最喜欢的书、一首诗、一部戏剧、一部音乐剧或一首歌。然后在课堂上，把这句话读给大家听，并谈谈为什么它对自己很重要，这句话又体现了他们成功理论的哪个方面。

他们想从这句话中带走什么样的象征，而它又代表了成功的什么意义？

所以，在课程结束之际，我想分享三句话，但我也想请你们思考一下，如果是你，你会把哪句话带到这最后一堂课，并与你的家人、朋友分享，把它当作一面旗帜，在你的人生中，为你所信奉的成功理论指引方向。

我想，当你把它与我们之前所做的许多其他练习结合起来思考时，你会发现它意义非凡。

对于“六种人生”练习，你们会有自己的答案，这是我们最初几节课和练习中一起做过的。

你们会有自己总结出的“四颗钻石”，它们代表着你的兴趣、能力和经历，这些元素共同构成了你独一无二的人生故事。

你们会对有意义的工作的各个方面，对幸福和成就感的哪些方面对你最重要，以及你如何理解和珍视它们，形成自己的认识。

然后，你们会找到一个可以用来指导自己的比喻，它就像一种象征、一个意象、一幅图画，帮助你思考成功究竟是什么——它可能是一棵树、一个指南针、一汪池塘、一架梯子，或是一场赛跑。

所有这些加在一起，就像是为自己编写了一本小小的成功之书。你可以写下属于你自己的成功之书，一本只属于你的书，而不是那些号称适用于所有人的“成功法则”。

我想，如果你能做到这一点，那么用一句意味深长的话来说，我们共同的努力或许就可以称得上是“成功”了。

接下来，是我想要送给你们的三句话。

第一句与成就有关。

这是我非常喜欢的一句话。

我十分欣赏一本中国的智慧之书，叫做《易经》。

在大多数书店都能找到它，也可以在网上订购。

它基本上是一本包含六十四章节的书。你投掷石块或钱币，它们会以某种方式排列，然后指引你去阅读其中某一章。

你阅读之后，它就能帮助你解答投掷钱币时所提出的问题。

在其中一个章节里，我认为下面这句话与如何真正聚焦于我们讨论过的“成就”部分有很大关系。

这句话是：只有当你有勇气直面事物本来的样子，不带任何自欺或幻想时，事件本身才会生发出光芒，借此，通往成功的道路才会被辨认出来。

我认为这句话非常重要，因为它告诉你，你取得成就的能力并非外在于你的事物。

你取得成就的能力，是早已潜在于你体内，或是已经发展出来的东西。

你需要做的，是直面你的天赋、你的技能，认清它们的真实面貌，不带任何自欺或幻想。

专注于那些你擅长的事情，别再梦想着那些你或许想成为NBA球星之类的事，那种机会实在渺茫。

所以，专注于你真正做得好的事情，并将它们组合起来，形成你独特的价值主张。

一旦你能清晰地认识自己能做什么，并把你的各种能力整合起来，那么你人生成功中关于“成就”的那一部分，就会加速实现。

它会呈爆发式增长。

因为那时你提供的是一种独特的价值主张，一旦找到合适的环境，它就会像火箭一样腾飞。

所以，要清晰地、有勇气地看清事物的本来面目。

这就是我认为这句话非常有力的原因。

我要分享的第二句话关乎幸福。

一位罗马哲学家曾说过：你幸福所需的一切，都很简单。

这是一个非常容易被忽视的真理。

在我们追求幸福的过程中，我们想要更多、更多样化、更多体验、更奇特、更多选择、更多的一切。

而关于幸福——无论是瞬间的幸福、整体的幸福，还是深沉的幸福——的真相是，它们都只是人类体验的一部分。

而且，你很可能体验过的最深沉的幸福，往往是偶然发生的。

也许你会在佛罗里达州出差时，在一家酒店里度过一个不眠之夜。

你辗转反侧，担心着家人，因为你没能和他们在一起。

你担心着第二天要做的演示。

你的思绪无法平静。

最后，你放弃了，向无法入睡的事实投降。

你走出房间，来到海滩。

就在你沿着海滩漫步的时候，恰逢破晓，太阳将它的圆盘边缘刚刚推过海平面。

天空骤然从黑暗变为绚丽的粉红色，一只紫色的鸟儿飞过。

你看到一条鱼在岸边跃起，你被那一刻的景象完全俘获，对自己在自然万物中的位置感到一种彻底的敬畏。

你被自己生命与周围所有生命之间那种深刻的联结所震撼，一时失语。

而那一刻并不复杂。

那只是你身处当下，感受着生命正在发生的时刻。

我认为，你越是能让自己敞开心扉，去拥抱幸福的简单，你越是能让自己的感知节奏与周围生命的韵律同步，你就越有可能更多地体验到这种成功的非常重要的面向，那种内心的喜悦和深沉的幸福感。

最后这一句话，既无关成就，也无关幸福。

最后一句话关乎的是如何思考成就、幸福和成功——这正是我们整个课程一直在探讨的核心。

它来自柏拉图。

柏拉图的老师，当然是苏格拉底。

柏拉图撰写了对话录，开创了西方哲学的先河。

在描述苏格拉底生平的最后的几本书中，你知道，他是雅典的一位哲学家。

他是个相当不受欢迎的人。

事实上，他因为污染雅典年轻人的思想，以及通过让未成年人思考过多而败坏他们，而受到审判——后者是城邦的长老们所反对的。

他以几票之差败诉，被判处死刑，不得不饮下毒堇汁，基本上是为了做一个有思想的人而献出了生命。

我们之所以记住苏格拉底，是因为他将自己的思想赋予了贯穿其一生的意义。

在他生命的最后日子里，他说过一句话，我认为这也是我在教学中努力去体现的，也是我们刚刚学完的这门课程试图呈现的。

它是一个过程，一种聚焦。

苏格拉底是这样说的：未经审视的人生不值得过。

我认为，他的意思是，如果你度过一生，却不去审视你所继承的文化价值观，不去审视塑造了你的家庭影响，不去审视那些迫使你顺从的社会力量或社会压力——它们如何塑造了你，让你带着不同的想法置身于不同的境地——只是过一种未经审视的生活，本质上是一种自动化的生活，并非基于你自己的思考，而仅仅是吸收了你恰好生于其中的、周遭所有纷繁复杂的思想。

我不确定这样的人生是否真的值得一过。

我们在这里讨论的一切，都在引导你走向自我审视，将其作为真正的方法，去发现你真正的成就能力，发现你真正的成功价值观，发现幸福对你而言究竟意味着什么。

而所有这些问题的答案，都无法在电视里、电脑上或书本中找到。

它们都将在你的内心中被找到。

我认为，这就是苏格拉底的意思。

这也是为什么，在我心目中，它一直是最能诠释成功的名言之一。

我想用它来作为我们最后一堂课的结束语，把它作为礼物送给你们。

我也希望你们能与自己的朋友、同事和家人分享属于你们自己的那句箴言。

那么，我们到了课程的终点。

非常高兴能和大家一起度过这段时光。

我感觉就像在我的办公室里接待了你们一样，就是那间我的学生们来找我答疑的办公室，他们和我分享他们必须面对的棘手问题、冲突和选择。

而我们只是把它聊开。

当然，我处理问题的方式，不是试图通过给他们建议来回答他们提出的问题，而是反过来问他们自己，觉得答案可能是什么。

令人惊讶的是，很多时候，如果有人只是问问你是怎么想的，另一面是什么，你有没有考虑过这个，他们往往就能通过这样的谈话，为自己做出完全正确的选择。

我希望这门课程能够帮助你们，为自己做出完全正确的选择。

能与你们分享这些，是我的荣幸。

我期待着随着课程的推进，听到大家不同的经历和故事，期待在课程学员和我们沃顿商学院课程制作团队之间，建立起持续的反馈循环。

感谢你们加入我的课程。

祝你们好运，愿你们收获一切成功。

英文原文

I have a wrap-up that I want to offer you now,a conclusion to our work together.

And it comes from the course.

It comes from the final day in the final class and something that we do in the class.

So we worked for 14 weeks throughout the semester with all the different exercises that you've doneand a lot more sort of esoteric readings from this and that literature that we haven't bothered you with.

But in the final class,what I ask everybody to do is bring their one favorite quote,that is from a source that they've read or a favorite book that they've seen or a poem or a play or a musical or a song and bring that final quote that embodies something about their theory of success and read it to the rest of the class and talk about why it's important to them.

What is the emblem that they want to take with them from that quote and why does it signify something about success?

So I'm going to share three quotes to bring our class to an end,but I want you to think of what quote you would bring to the final class and share that with your family,with your friends,as a sort of banner that you would march under as far as your theory of success is concerned.

And I think you'll find that meaningful when you put it together with a lot of the other work we've done.

You'll have your own answers to the Six Lives exercise,which we did in the first set of exercises and sessions that we worked on.

You'll have your own four diamonds that we assembled that are your interests and your capabilities and your experiences that all come together that are your unique story.

You'll have your own sense of what aspects of meaningful work,what aspects of happiness and achievement mean the most to you and how you understand them and value them.

And then you'll have a metaphor that you can bring to bear that is kind of an emblem and an image and a picture that helps you think about what success is,whether it's a tree or a compass or a pond or a ladder or a race.

So all these together kind of can make up a little success book for yourself and write your own success book that's just your success book,not the how to succeed book that is supposed to work for everyone.

And I think if you do that,our work together has maybe,to use a pregnant word,been successful.

So here are the three quotes I want to give you.

The first one relates to achievement.

It's one of my favorites.

I'm a big fan of a Chinese book of wisdom,which is called the I Ching.

You can Find it in most bookstores,and you can order it online.

It's basically a book of 64 chapters,and you throw stones or coins,they arrange themselves in a certain way,and then it directs your attention to one of the 64 chapters.

You read it,and then that helps you answer a question that you ask when you threw the coins.

And in one of the chapters,the following quote I think has a lot to do with how you actually zero in on that achievement part that we talked about.

And this is the quote:It is only when we have the courage to face things exactly as they are,without any self-deception or illusion,that a light will develop out of events by which the path to success may be recognized.

I think this is a really important quote because it tells you that your achievement skills are not things that are outside yourself.

Your achievement skills are things that are already latent or developed inside yourself.

Your problem is to face your aptitudes,your skills exactly as they are,without any self-deception or illusion.

And focus on those things that you do well and stop dreaming about the things that you may want to be an NBA star,but the chances of that are pretty remote.

So focus on the things you actually do well in the combination that gives you a unique value proposition.

And once you're able to get that clarity on what you do and put together the set of things that you do,the achievement part of your success in life will just accelerate.

It will explode.

Because that's when you're offering a unique value proposition,which when it finds the right context,just takes off like a rocket.

So clarity and courage to see things exactly as they are.

It's the reason I think this quote is really powerful.

My second quote concerns happiness.

A Roman philosopher once said,Everything you need to be happy is simple.

This is a truth that's really easy to lose sight of.

In our quest for happiness,we want more,more variety,more experience,more exotic,more choices,more of everything.

And the truth about happiness,momentary happiness,overall happiness,deep happiness,is that they are just a part of the human experience.

And it's very likely that the deepest happiness you'll ever feel will be accidental.

You'll spend a night,sleepless night in a hotel in Florida on a business trip.

You'll be tossing and turning,worried about your family and the fact that you're not with them.

You'll be worried about the presentation you'll be making the next day.

Your mind is restless.

Finally,you give up,surrender to the fact that you can't sleep.

Walk outside out to the beach.

It just happens that as you're walking down the beach,the dawn breaks,the sun just tips its little disc edge over the edge of the sea.

The sky suddenly goes from dark to a gorgeous pink and purple bird flies by.

You see a fish jump just off the shore,and you're just captured by a moment of complete awe at your place in the nature of things.

And you're struck dumb with the profound connection that you have between your life and the life all around you.

And that's not complicated.

That's just being in that present moment where life is happening.

And I think the more you can open yourself to the simplicity of happiness,the more you can get to the pace of your perceptions and the rhythms of the life around you,the more likely you are to experience more of this very,very important aspect of success,that inner sense of joy and deep happiness.

And then the final quote is not about achievement,and it's not about happiness.

The final quote is about how to think about achievement and happiness and success,which is what we've been working on for this entire course.

And it comes from Plato.

Plato's teacher,of course,was named Socrates.

And Plato wrote the dialogues and the beginnings of Western philosophy.

And in the last few books that describe Socrates'life,you know,he was a philosopher in Athens.

He was a pretty unpopular guy.

He was actually put on trial for contaminating the ideas of the youth of Athens and for corrupting the minors by making them think too much,which was something that the elders of the city objected to.

And he lost his trial by a few votes and was sentenced to death and had to drink the hemlock and died basically for the cause of being a thoughtful person.

The reason we remember Socrates is.

because he took his ideas and gave them the meaning of his entire life.

And one of the things he said in the last days of his life was something that I think I try to embody in my teaching,that the course that we've just gone through tries to represent.

It's a process and a focus.

And what Socrates said is this,the unexamined life is not worth living.

What he means,I think,is that if you go through life not examining the cultural values that you were endowed with,not examining the family influences that have shaped you,not examining the social forces of conformity or social pressures that have shaped you and put you in different places with different thoughts,

just an unexamined life,essentially an automatic life,not based on your own thoughts,but just on the assimilation of all of the swirling thoughts that you happen to have been born into.

I'm not sure that's really worth the effort.

And everything that we've talked about here has pointed you towards self-examination as the actual method by which you can discover your true achievement capabilities,discover your true success values,discover what happiness actually means to you.

And all the answers to those things are not found on a television,in a computer,or in a book.

They're all going to be found in your heart.

And that is what I think Socrates meant.

That's why this is one of my favorite quotes of all time for success.

And it's the one that I want to conclude with as my gift to you in our final class.

And I hope that you'll be sharing some of yours with your friends,colleagues,and family.

So we've gotten to the end.

It's been great to be with you.

I felt like I've visited with you here in the office,the very same office where my students come for office hours,where they share with me difficult problems and conflicts and choices that they have to make.

And we just talk it out.

Of course,my way of approaching that is not to try to answer the questions that they ask by giving them advice,but by asking them what they think the answers might be.

And it's amazing how often if someone will just ask you what you think and what's the other side of that and have you considered this,how often they talk themselves into getting the choice exactly right for themselves.

And I hope that this course will help you get your choices exactly right for yourself.

It's been a pleasure to share this with you.

I look forward to hearing different adventures as our course goes out and we get feedback loops that go on between the people who take it and here at Wharton,those of us who make these courses.

Thank you for joining me.

Good luck,and I hope you have every success.

大家好，我是玛丽·施魏策尔，宾夕法尼亚大学沃顿商学院的教授。

我教授谈判学与高级谈判课程，我的研究兴趣集中在信任、欺骗和情绪领域。

我是《亦敌亦友》一书的合著者，并且对我们这门课程将要探讨的话题很感兴趣。

更广泛地说，我对人际沟通以及动机也感兴趣。

我们会探讨目标设定，有时它能引领我们走向正轨，但有时也会让我们陷入麻烦。

感谢你的加入，让我们开始吧。

2-01-01.02_合作与竞争的一线之隔

合作与竞争之间的界限惊人地模糊。

举个例子，想想感恩节期间会发生什么。

在美国，我们有真正开启假日购物季的黑色星期五促销活动，有时你会看到大量人群，蜂拥到商店，期待一场大甩卖。

所以在这些商店外面，就有一群人在涌向一家商店。

人们经常以打架斗殴收场。

有一个特别可悲的例子，发生在2008年纽约州北部，当时黑色星期五真的有了一个不同的含义。

有一群人聚集在一家商店外面。

他们literally高喊着，把门拆下来，把门拆下来，急切地想冲进这家商店。

而员工们则组成了一道人链，试图挡住购物者。

当顾客们冲进这家商店时，他们literally把门从铰链上扯了下来，最终导致杰伊·迪特玛被踩踏致死。

当时，许多员工最后都爬到自动售货机上去躲避。

多人受伤，还有一人因此丧生。

这里具有讽刺意味的是，感恩节这个节日本是在庆祝合作。

我们想到的是早期美国定居者和美洲原住民之间历史上的合作。

在这里，我们庆祝这个家庭与合作的时刻。

然而我们却把这些促销活动，以及常常由此引发的、造成大量冲突的疯狂抢购潮，与之并列在一起。

而2008年的这个事件，以及我之前给你们看的那张早期照片，并非孤立事件。

我们经常能看到这种所谓的节日精神。

比如这个《赫芬顿邮报》的标题：枪击、刺伤和斗殴。

还有其他一些情况，你知道，人们实际上会互相偷窃，试图抢到最划算的商品。

所以我想思考的是，我们如何应对这种紧张关系。

是什么促使我们从合作转向竞争，或者从竞争转向合作？

在这个感恩节的例子中，我们有合作性的聚餐，然后又有竞争性的节日促销抢购。

但我认为，一个更能体现从竞争转向合作的戏剧性例子，是美国和日本之间的关系。

众所周知，二战期间的冲突非常激烈。

这是一张1920年燃烧弹轰炸的照片。

1941年，我们陷入了激烈的冲突。

除了投下两颗原子弹外，美国还燃烧弹轰炸了日本的67座城市，这一切在1945年达到顶峰，日本最终投降。

所以美国和日本之间的冲突，其激烈程度无以复加。

然而就在这场冲突结束后，立刻出现了转向合作的重大转变。

麦克阿瑟将军在日本接管后，立即转向合作，规定任何美国人殴打日本人都是非法的，甚至规定美国人吃日本食物也是非法的，因为当时日本食物严重短缺。

在当地的美国人只能吃美国配给的口粮。

接着，我们向前发展。

我们最终进行了合作，重建工厂，你可以看到这种合作贯穿整个二十世纪五十年代，并在1960年签署的这份合作宣言中达到顶峰。

而今天，你很难找到比日本民众更亲美的公民了。

所以我们看到了这种从竞争到合作的显著转变。

这种情况不仅发生在全球舞台上，不仅发生在购物商场里，也发生在我们最亲密的关系中。想想养育子女这件事。

养育子女，除了你的伴侣，你不可能与其他人有更亲密的合作了，想想抚养一个孩子需要付出多少合作。

然而，即使是在养育孩子这件事上，也存在着竞争。

你会和配偶竞争谁去睡觉，谁去给孩子换尿布或喂奶。

即使是在我们合作最紧密的关系中，也存在着竞争。

所以关键在于，我们在合作与竞争之间转换，即使在我们最紧密的关系中，我们也常常在平衡合作与竞争。

再想想兄弟姐妹之间的关系。

谈到兄弟姐妹，我们常想到的是手足之情。

但同时，我们也会想到同胞争宠。

这里有一个手足之情的例子。

我们在人类身上看到了这一点，但事实证明，地松鼠教会了我们一些关于兄弟姐妹的重要事情。

地松鼠实际上非常无私。

当捕食者靠近时，比如说头顶有只鸟或其他大型动物，地松鼠会发出尖叫声来警告其他松鼠赶紧躲开。

而通过尖叫，它们会把注意力引向自己。

这使它们，这会让它们置身于危险之中。

这会让它们容易受到攻击。

学者们研究了地松鼠尖叫的音量。

结果发现，当捕食者靠近它们的亲属时，它们叫得最响。

所以我们看到，即使在地松鼠之间也存在手足之情。

我们与兄弟姐妹之间存在着这种不可思议的关系。

然而，同胞争宠也可能极其激烈。

他们是我们最亲密的朋友，但有时也是我们最接近的对手，因为我们会竞争诸如父母的关注和投入之类的东西。

对于双胞胎来说，这种竞争开始得特别早。

甚至在子宫里，双胞胎就开始争夺资源了。

更广泛地说，我们考虑的是工作中的协作。

我们需要与工作中的同事协作，以完成共同的目标。

但同时，我们也在竞争一些东西，比如认可、晋升和加薪。

所以无论是在家里还是在工作中，我们都在既合作又竞争，我们需要弄清楚如何处理这种紧张关系，并把握好这个平衡。

所以关键在于，我们无时无刻不在竞争与合作，而且常常是在同一段关系中同时进行。

英文原文

The line between cooperation and competition is surprisingly thin.

As an example,think about what happens in Thanksgiving.

We have Black Friday sales here in the United States that really trigger the holiday season,and sometimes you see huge crowds,mob stores in anticipation of a great sale.

So outside of these stores,here's one mob that was mobbing a store.

People often end up in fist fights.

One particularly sad occasion when Black Friday really took on a different term was in 2008 in upstate New York.

There was a crowd of people that had gathered outside of a store.

They were literally chanting,tear the doors down,tear the doors down,eager to get into this store.

Well,the employees had formed a human chain trying to hold the shoppers back.

And as the customers stormed into this store,they literally took the doors off the hinges and they ended up trampling Jay Dittmar to death.

Now,many of the employees end up scampering up onto vending machines trying to get out of the way.

People were injured and in one case,killed.

Now,what's ironic here is that the Thanksgiving holiday celebrates cooperation.

We think about the historic cooperation between the early American settlers and the Native American Indians.

And here we celebrate this time of family and cooperation.

And yet we juxtapose this with these sales and often a big mad rush that creates a lot of conflict.

And this occasion in 2008 and that early photo that I showed you before is not an isolated incident.

We routinely see this idea of holiday spirit.

Here,this Huffington Post headline,shootings,stabbings,and brawls.

And then here,in other cases,you know,people actually stealing from each other,trying to get the best deals.

So what I want to think about is how we navigate this tension.

What pushes us from cooperation to competition or from competition to cooperation?

And this Thanksgiving example,we have the cooperative meal and then this competitive dash for these holiday sales.

But I think a more dramatic example of a shift from competition to cooperation is represented in the relationship between the United States and Japan.

As we all know,the conflict in World War II was intense.

Here,this is a photo of firebombing in 1920.

1941,we had intense conflict.

The United States firebombed 67 Japanese cities,in addition to dropping two atomic bombs,culminating in 1945,and the Japanese ultimately surrendered.

So the conflict between the United States and Japan could not have been more intense.

And yet immediately after that conflict,there was a pivot to cooperation.

And General Mac Arthur,when they took over in Japan,shifted immediately to cooperation,made it illegal for any American to strike a Japanese person,even made it illegal for Americans to eat Japanese food because there was such a food shortage on Japan.

Americans who were there could only eat the American rations.

Now,we moved forward.

We ended up cooperating,rebuilding factories,and here you see this cooperation through the 1950s,culminating in this declaration of cooperation signed in 1960.

And today,you'd be hard pressed to find citizens that are more pro-U.S.than those in Japan.

So we see this remarkable shift from competition to cooperation.

Now,this happens not just on the global stage,not just in terms of shopping malls,but it happens in our most intimate relationships.We think about parenting.

Parenting,you can't be more intimately cooperative with someone other than your partner and think about the cooperation that goes into raising a child.

And yet,even with raising a child,there's competition.

There's competition with your spouse of who's going to sleep,who's going to change or feed the baby.

And we have competition even within our most intensely cooperative relationships.

So the idea is that we shift between cooperation and competition,and we often balance cooperation and competition even in our most intense relationships.

Now,think about siblings.

So with siblings,we often think about sibling love.

But at the same time,we think about sibling rivalry.

Now,here's one example of sibling love.

We think about it with humans,but it turns out the ground squirrel teaches us something really important about siblings.

Ground squirrels are actually incredibly altruistic.

When a predator is nearby,say a bird overhead or another large animal,ground squirrels will screech to warn others to get out of the way.

Now,by screeching,they're drawing attention to themselves.

It makes them,it puts them at risk.

It makes them vulnerable to some attack.

Scholars have looked at the volume with which ground squirrels screech.

And it turns out they screech loudest when a predator is near their city.

So we see sibling love even among ground squirrels.

And so we have this incredible relationship with our siblings.

And yet,sibling rivalry can be incredibly intense.

These are our closest friends and also sometimes our closest rivals as we compete for things like parental attention and investment.

For twins,it starts particularly early.

Even in the womb,twins start competing for resources.

Now,more generally,we think about collaborating at work.

We need to collaborate with our colleagues at work to accomplish joint goals.

But then we're also competing for things like recognition,promotion,and raises.

So both at home and at work,we're both cooperating and competing,and we need to figure out how to manage this tension and navigate this balance.

So the idea is that we're competing and cooperating all the time,and often within the same relationships at the same time.

2-01-01.03_合作与竞争的三项原则

我想探讨一下导致我们在合作与竞争之间切换的三个原则。

它们让我们从朋友变为对手，然后再变回来。

所以我们要思考一下这三个原则的相互作用。

第一个原则是稀缺性。

我们环境中的资源可能是稀缺的，也可能是充裕的，而这正是驱使我们从朋友变为对手的原因。

想想稀缺性，这正是感恩节例子中发生的情况。

感恩节的家宴上，资源非常丰富，我们庆祝的是一个合作性的事件。

但当我们走向市场时，那些有限的打折商品，比如低价电视和其他东西，这些稀缺资源又驱使我们激烈竞争。

我们不仅从人类身上看到稀缺性会导致合作与竞争的转换，在对动物的研究中也观察到同样的现象。

一项对格列维斑马的研究发现，斑马的行为方式会根据其环境中可用水量的多少而变化。

当水源充足时，它们形成一种类型的群体。

当水源稀缺时，它们形成的群体则截然不同。

也就是说，它们的社会关系会随着这种宝贵水源的稀缺程度而发生巨大变化。

第二个原则是我们的社会性。

我们天生是社会性动物。

我们渴望陪伴。

事实上，最严厉的惩罚形式之一就是单独监禁。

在单独监禁中，仅几天后，人的心智就开始衰退。

人们会出现幻觉、暴怒发作、不适感和冷漠。

在被单独监禁后，我们既极度渴望与人接触，同时也变得不适应与人相处。

人类心智需要社会联系。

第三个原则是动态不稳定性。

我们周围的世界是随机的，它在变化，是不稳定的。

就像股票市场一样，我们周围的一切都在变化，我们需要在合作与竞争之间快速调整和转换。

所以，在这个不稳定且动态变化的世界里，当我们获取新信息时，我们努力收集新信息，这既促使我们合作，也促使我们竞争。

而正是这三个原则——稀缺性、社会性和动态不稳定性的相互作用，导致我们在合作与竞争之间来回转换。

有时我们会同时进行两者，我们需要找到自己作为竞争者和合作者之间的平衡点。

英文原文

I want to think about three principles that cause us to shift between cooperation and competition.

They transform us from friends to foes and back again.

So we think about the interplay of these three principles.

The first principle is scarcity.

The resources in our environment can either be scarce or plentiful,and that's what drives us from friend to foe.

We think about scarcity,and this is exactly what happened in Thanksgiving.

So Thanksgiving,with this feast,we have abundant resources,and we're celebrating a cooperative event.

But then we go out into the marketplace,and these scarce deals cause us to compete fiercely for these scarce resources of low-priced TVs and other things.

Now,we see scarcity not just in humans shifting us between cooperation and competition,but in studies of animals,we see the same thing.

A study of Grevi zebras found that the zebras actually behave differently as a function of how much water was available in their environment.

When water was abundant,they formed one type of collectives.

And when water was scarce,they formed a very different kind of collective.

That is,their social relationships shifted dramatically as a function of how scarce this very precious water resource was.

Now,the second principle is how social we are.

We're inherently social beings.

We crave companionship.

In fact,one of the worst forms of punishment is solitary confinement.

After just a few days,the human mind begins to decay in solitary confinement.

People experience hallucinations,spasms of anger,malaise,and apathy.

We both crave human contact after being in solitary confinement,and we're also unfit for it.

The human mind needs to be socially connected.

The third principle is dynamic instability.

The world around us is stochastic,it changes,it's unstable.

Just like the stock market,things are shifting all around us,and we need to quickly change and pivot between cooperation and competition.

So this unstable and dynamic world,as we learn new information,we try to gather new information,it causes us to both cooperate and compete.

And it's really the interplay between these three principles,scarcity,the sociability,and dynamic instability that cause us to pivot back and forth between cooperation and competition.

And sometimes we're engaging in both at the same time,and we need to find our balance as both competitors and collaborators.

2-01-01.04_比较的机制

接下来我想讨论的是比较。

我想剖析一下我们进行比较的机制，并论证它们是我们生活中一种非常基本的力量。

它们帮助我们理解一些有趣的谜题。

比如这一个。

为什么出生时就分开的双胞胎常常如此相似？

以汤姆·彼得森和史蒂夫·田积为例。

他们是出生时就分离的双胞胎。

两人在完全不同的家庭长大，信仰不同的宗教，接受不同的教育，然而当他们团聚时，他们惊讶于彼此是如此相似。

一人拥有并经营一家健美健身房，是个十足的健身迷。

另一人也拥有并经营一家健美健身房，并且完全热衷于健身。

当他们团聚时，他们说，哦，我们从第一次见面就很投缘，因为我们太像了。

我想思考一下这个问题。

也就是说，为什么出生时分开的双胞胎最终会如此相似？

这里有第二个谜题。

为什么准爸爸们会在没有生物学原因的情况下体重增加？

通过理解比较过程，我们可以洞察这些谜题。

那么，第一个关键观点来了。

我们所做的比较帮助我们理解所处的世界。

它们帮助我们判断自己是否度过了一个愉快的假期，薪水是否理想，是否需要翻新厨房，是否需要买辆新车。

正是比较帮助我们理解生活中所有这些不同的结果。

关于比较，还有其他一些关键观点。

首先，比较是不可避免的。

我们所有人都会进行比较。

有些人可能比其他人更频繁地查看脸书，但我们所有人都会不由自主地进行这些比较，它们帮助我们理解事物，同时也驱使我们感觉更好、激励我们，或者让我们感觉更糟。

它们起作用的部分原因在于，我们进行的比较有时是向上看，与那些比我们做得更好的人，那些拥有更漂亮公寓、更漂亮汽车的人比较；有时是向下看，与那些可能不如我们成就高的人比较。

向上比较可以激励我们。

它们也能让我们痛苦。

向下比较可以让我们感到满足和满意，但激励作用较小。

关于比较的另一个关键观点是，我们可以在自己内部进行，也可以与他人进行比较。

所以我们所做的比较通常是针对别人。

可能是我们的邻居，可能是我们的姐夫或妹夫，也可能是隔壁工位的人。

但我们也可以进行内部比较，比如思考自己以前做得怎么样，或者比较一下自己本可以做到什么程度。

所以这些是相对于自己的内部比较，或者是相对于他人的比较。

比较在什么时候最强烈？

事实证明，有三个维度会影响比较的强弱。

第一个维度是相似性。

说到相似性，我们会想到像兄弟姐妹这样的关系。

最亲密的兄弟姐妹就是双胞胎，他们之间有着极强的相似性。

所以我们越相似，这些比较就越重要。

而且这不限于兄弟姐妹。

也可能是非常亲密的朋友，那些我们认为与自己相似、属于同一群体的人。

我们可能曾一起入学，同在一个班级。

相似性非常重要。

事实上，相似性有助于我们理解像肥胖蔓延这样的现象。

所以，准爸爸们体重增加的一个原因，尽管没有生物学上的原因，是因为他们正在与身边最亲近的人进行比较。

夫妻之间在进行比较，而这种比较会影响动机。

从这些图表中可以看出，首先，某些类型的比较影响最大。那些是我们双方都视对方为朋友的比较，这些是最深厚的友谊关系。

以及我们与同性别他人进行的比较。

所以，一个人与我们越相似，这种比较的影响就越大。

事实上，我们看到这种社交网络有助于解释肥胖如何通过友谊、通过社交网络传播，我们进行的比较让我们受到潜移默化的影响。

所以，当我看到周围所有人都在伸手拿甜甜圈时，我会想，嗯，我不应该吃更多甜甜圈，但如果其他人都在这么做，或者如果那种行为在我看来没什么，我比较范围内的所有人都在影响我自己对什么可以接受、什么不可接受的判断。

基于类似的原因，聚会可能会让人压力很大，因为在聚会上，我们回到过去，进行着激烈的比较。

可能是高中同学聚会，也可能是家庭聚会。

在那里，我们会见到那些我们很可能会与之进行比较的人。

这些人与我们来自同一群体或相似的家庭结构。

他们或许起点相似，而现在，由于相似性，我们就要进行这些比较了。

第二个维度是接近性。

想想那些最激烈的rivalry，比如焦油脚跟队和蓝魔队，北卡大学和杜克大学。

这里我们看的就是rivalry。

这是两所相距仅九英里的学校。

都拥有非常强大的篮球队，而这种激烈的rivalry在一定程度上是由接近性助长的。

接近性不仅限于大学之间，也适用于像邻居这样的关系。

在这段引自波拉特的台词中，我们看到了这种强烈的邻里间比较，他们来回攀比家里有什么，直到他说，哦，大成功，当他终于得到邻居没有的东西时。

所以，前两个因素是：相似性和接近性。

第三个让比较变得尤为激烈的因素是自我相关性。

所谓自我相关性，是指我们关心的事物。

所以，如果我非常在意职业发展，那么谁得到了晋升就与我相关。

当我的邻居赢得烘焙比赛，而我不认为自己是个烘焙高手时，这就缺乏自我相关性，因此这种比较就不那么激烈。

因此，最激烈的比较发生在那些相似的人之间，比如兄弟、邻座同事、邻居、我的姐夫妹夫；接近的人，即物理空间上与我非常接近的人；以及自我相关的领域，即我真正关心的方面。

所以，如果我是一名音乐家，我会在意赢得那场音乐比赛，但如果不是，我就没那么在意。

社会比较具有这些特征，并且它们会影响几种不同的行为。

我们已经提到了其中一些。

首先是我们如何与他人合作。

当我们获知某些信息时，它会改变我们与他人合作或竞争的方式。

例如，我们可能发现别人比我们挣得多，这可能会让合作变得更困难。

或者我们可能发现别人有着与我们截然不同的背景，这可能会让合作变得更容易，并缓和原本可能发生的激烈比较。

所以，比较可以促使我们合作或竞争，但也可能导致我们完全退缩。

有时候，比较会让人非常不愉快，以至于我们想要脱离这种处境，因为我们觉得这种比较太令人反感了。

英文原文

What I want to talk about next are comparisons.

And I want to break down the mechanics of the comparisons that we make and argue that they're a very fundamental force in our lives.

They help us understand some interesting puzzles.

Here's one.

Why are twins separated at birth often so similar?

Take Tom Peterson and Steve Tazumi.

They were twins separated at birth.

The two grew up in completely different households,different religions,different schooling,and yet when they got together,they were shocked at how similar they were.

One owned a bodybuilding gym and was a complete fitness addict.

The other owned a bodybuilding gym and was totally into fitness.

And when they got together,they said,oh,we connected from the first time we met because we're so much alike.

I want to think about that question.

That is,why might twins separate at birth end up being so similar?

Here's a second puzzle.

Why do expectant fathers gain weight when there's no biological reason for them to gain weight?

By understanding the comparison process,we could gain insight into these puzzles.

Now,here's the first key idea.

The comparisons we make help us make sense of our world.

They help us understand if we went on a good vacation,if we're making a good salary,if I need to redo my kitchen,if I need to buy a new car.

It's comparisons that help us make meaning out of all of these different outcomes we have in our lives.

Now,here are some other key ideas about comparisons.

First,they're inevitable.

All of us make comparisons.

Now,some of us are drawn to check Facebook more often than others,but all of us are drawn to make these comparisons,and they help us make sense of things,but they also drive us to feel better or motivate us or to feel worse.

Now,part of how they work are we make comparisons that are sometimes going up,people who have done better than we have,people who have nicer apartments,nicer cars,or comparisons where we look down,people who might not have accomplished as much as us.

Upward comparisons can inspire us.

They can also make us miserable.

Downward comparisons can make us feel content and satisfied,but are less motivating.

Another key idea about comparisons is that we can make them within ourselves and with other people.

So often the comparisons we make are to somebody else.

So it could be our neighbor,it could be our brother-in-law,it could be the person in the cubicle next to me.

But we can also make internal comparisons where I think about how I did before or the comparison of what I could have done.

So these internal comparisons relative to me or comparisons relative to others.

When are comparisons most intense?

It turns out there are three dimensions that make comparisons more or less impactful.

The first dimension is similarity.

By similarity,we're thinking about things like siblings.

And the closest sibling is a twin,where we have very intense similarity.

So the more similar we are,the more these comparisons matter.

And it's not just siblings.

It could be very close friends,people that we find ourselves similar to in the same cohort.

We might have started in the same class together.

Similarity is really important.

And in fact,the similarity helps us understand things like the spread of obesity.

So one reason why expectant fathers gain weight,even though there's no biological reason for them to do so,is they're comparing themselves to people right next to them.

And so the husbands and wives are comparing themselves,and that comparison impacts motivation.

We can see from these graphs here,first,there's some kinds of comparisons that matter most.Those are comparisons where it's actually both of us see ourselves as friends,so those are going to be the strongest friendships.

And where we're comparing ourselves to the same sex others.

So the more similar the person,the more impactful that comparison is.

And in fact,we see this network that helps explain the spread of obesity through friendships,through the network,the comparisons that we're making,we find ourselves motivated.

So when I see everybody else around me reaching for a donut,I figure,well,I don't think I should eat more donuts,but if everybody else is doing it,or if that sort of look looks fine to me,everybody else in my comparison set is influencing my own assessment of what is or isn't acceptable.

Now,for similar reasons,reunions can be quite stressful because at reunions we're going back and we're engaging in intense comparisons.

So it could be a high school reunion,it could be a family reunion.

There,we're going to see people with whom we're likely to make comparisons.

These are people from our same cohort or the same family structure.

They started perhaps in similar circumstances,and now we're going to make these comparisons because of similarity.

The second dimension is proximity.

So you think about some of the most intense rivalries,like the Tarheels and Blue Devils,UNC and Duke.

Here we're looking at rivalries.

These are two schools separated by just nine miles.

With very strong basketball teams,and that intense rivalry is in part fueled by proximity.

Now,proximity is also not just between universities,but it's things like neighbors.

So,here in this quote from Borat,we see this intense neighbor comparison,where we're thinking about going back and forth who has what in their homes until he says,oh,great success when he finally gets something that his neighbor can't have.

So,here we have the first two:similarity and proximity.

The third thing that makes comparisons particularly intense is self-relevance.

By self-relevance,I mean something that we care about.

So,if I really care about advancing my career,who gets that promotion is self-relevant.

When my neighbor wins a baking competition and I don't consider myself much of a baker,that lacks self-relevance,and as a result,that comparison isn't very intense.

So,the most intense comparisons are people who are similar,like brothers,cubicle makes,neighbors,my brother-in-law,proximity,people who are very close to me physically,and then self-relevance,a domain that I really care about.

So,if I'm a musician,I care about winning that musical competition,but if I'm not,then I care less.

Social comparisons have these characteristics,and they influence a few different behaviors.

We've already alluded to some of those so far.

The first is how we collaborate with other people.

So,as we learn information,it can change the way we collaborate or compete with others.

So,we might find that somebody else is making more money than we are,that might make collaboration harder.

Or we might find that somebody else has a very different background than we do,and that might make collaboration easier and mitigate the intense comparisons we might otherwise have made.

So,comparisons can make us collaborate or compete,but they can also lead us to retreat altogether.

So,sometimes comparisons can be so unpleasant,we want to exit the situation because we find it so invidious.

2-01-01.05_向上比较的痛苦

我们探讨了比较如何能激励人，但它们也可能带来一些不良后果。

在这里，我们要思考一下比较中不好的一面。

我想引用弗朗斯·德瓦尔的一些研究，他实际研究了卷尾猴，一些非常聪明的猴子，对不公平现象的反应。

他教这些猴子用石头当钱，他把石头交给它们。

实验人员会出来，摊开手，拿到一块石头，然后给猴子一些奖励，比如一片黄瓜。

结果发现，这些猴子可以整天不停地做这种交易。

它们喜欢黄瓜，也很乐意交出石头。

也就是说，直到它们看到旁边的邻居，隔壁笼子里的猴子，得到了比黄瓜更好的东西，比如一颗葡萄。

这里我会播放他一项研究中的视频，视频里两只卷尾猴并排交出石头。

一只得到黄瓜，另一只得到葡萄。

我们来看看会发生什么。

关于这段视频，我想强调三点。

第一是那只得到黄瓜的卷尾猴，它有多么专注地盯着隔壁笼子里的情况，盯着它的邻居得到葡萄。

第二，我想关注这只卷尾猴有多么沮丧。

然后第三，这种状况如何驱使这只卷尾猴退出交易。

也就是说，它甚至不想再做这种交易了，扔掉黄瓜，拒绝参与，此时石头在它眼里已不再值得换取黄瓜。

这一切都是相对的。

也就是说，正是因为别的卷尾猴得到了更好的待遇，这个原本看起来不错的交易，现在变得无法接受了。

而且这不只是猴子的问题。

我想论证的是，我们天生就会进行这些比较，而这些比较也确实影响着我们。

所以，以斯科特·克雷布特里为例，他曾在一家科技公司工作，对自己的工作非常满意，感到很有动力。

受到工作的激励，直到公司不得不去人才市场招人。

他们招募了一位非常厉害的新员工。

这位新员工入职时的薪资，几乎和他花了多年时间才达到的水平一样。

突然间，他的工作变得令人烦躁，他为此感到非常沮丧。

他太沮丧了，最终竟然辞职了。

他加入了一家不同的公司，在那里成为了首席幸福官。

所以就像那些卷尾猴一样，斯科特·克雷布特里，当他意识到别人得到了似乎比他更好的待遇，一个更年轻的人拿着和他几乎一样的薪水，他最终选择了辞职离开，试图在别处寻找幸福。

这种情况不仅发生在个人身上，也会发生在群体中。

例如，多年前美国航空公司面临非常严峻的财务困境。

他们濒临破产。

他们与工会，飞行员工会、空乘人员、行李搬运工、机械师，进行了艰苦的谈判，并让他们同意了大幅的让步。

因此，工会共同同意了十八亿美元的让步。

与此同时，美国航空公司的高管们本可以离开美国航空，去其他更稳定的公司，所以他们试图留住这些高管。

为了留住他们，公司向他们提供留任奖金。

问题来了：他们提供了四千一百万美元的留任奖金。

美国证券交易委员会的文件提交截止日期到了，这个信息就公开了。

于是，就在工会同意大幅让步之后，他们得知高管团队最终将获得这些留任奖金。

你可以想象，就像那些卷尾猴一样，他们变得非常愤怒。

所以，让步原本是可以接受的，直到他们发现别人拿到了奖金。

他们做的第一件事就是解雇了他们的谈判代表，撤回了这些让步，不得不回到谈判桌前重新尝试谈判。

所以，问题来了：一块石头值一根黄瓜吗？

十八亿美元的让步合理吗？

我拿的薪水公平吗？

对于所有这些问题，答案是：嗯，这得看情况。

而我们的答案源于比较。

现在，我们把目光转向英国，想一想两兄弟，戴维·米利班德和埃德·米利班德。

他们是两兄弟。

他们一起长大，并且都是英国议会的议员。

当戈登·布朗辞去工党领袖职务时，他们都想角逐领袖之位。

哥哥戴维首先宣布他将竞选领袖，身后有十五位议员支持。

他宣布了自己的候选人资格，当时他似乎是最被看好的人选。

除了戴维和埃德之外，还有其他几位候选人也参与了角逐，但这两位是主要的竞争者。

随着投票的进行，戴维略微占优。

第一轮，戴维领先埃德。第二轮，还是如此。

第三轮，依然如此，但差距变得更小了。

要获胜，你需要绝对多数。

你需要超过百分之五十的选票。

第四轮就发生了这种情况，只剩他们两人对决，突然间，埃德获胜了。

关于这一点，有两件事值得注意。

一是胜利的差距非常小，另一种结果可能发生的反事实情景非常突出。

二是他们是兄弟，对戴维来说更糟的是，获胜的是弟弟。

结果，他们的关系最终破裂了，戴维谈到，这种永无休止、令人反感的比较让职业生涯变得无法继续。

他不仅离开了议会，实际上他离开了英国，去纽约的一家非营利组织工作。

所以在这里，这种比较快把他逼疯了。

基于类似的原因，我们可以想一想双胞胎的情况。

你可能会想，什么是人工双胞胎？

人工双胞胎就是收养一个年龄与亲生儿子或女儿相仿的孩子。

这样做的好处是你有了一个现成的玩伴。

可以实现规模经济。

可以一起拼车上学。

上同一所学校。

可以一起送去踢足球。

这可能很棒。

然而，收养专家萨姆·威尔·乔伊纳后来指出，人工双胞胎会造成破坏性的社会比较。

也就是说，这样做的话，总有一个双胞胎，其中一方，会领先于另一方，并且可能存在发育上的差异，而这种持续不断的比较会使人工双胞胎的关系变得非常有害。

因此，许多收养机构不仅提供咨询，而且几乎禁止收养人工双胞胎。

现在，我们来想想另一件事。

我们来想想表现更好但感觉更糟的情况。

这怎么可能发生呢？

同样，还是需要通过比较来解开这个谜题。

想想阿贝尔·基维亚特。

一九一二年奥运会银牌得主。

在那届奥运会上，首次使用终点摄影来判断谁获胜了，他以十分之一秒的差距屈居第二。

那是一九一二年。

这是他在一九九零年接受的一次采访。

差不多八十年后，他谈到自己醒来时会想，当时到底发生了什么？

他郁郁寡欢，强烈的反事实思维挥之不去：要是他跑得再快一点点，他就能拿第一了。

事实证明，这种强烈感受并非阿贝尔独有，实际上非常普遍，你会发现银牌得主经常表达不满。

有几篇学术文章研究了这种现象，甚至将其称为银牌脸，指的是那些看起来极其沮丧的银牌得主，非常不开心，而相比之下，你会看到铜牌得主最终看起来比银牌得主快乐得多。

所以在这项研究中，几乎所有的金牌得主都在微笑，但铜牌得主微笑的频率略低一些。

但在这些研究中，没有一位银牌得主在微笑。

如果你分析一下这些比较，银牌得主，比如阿贝尔，会将自己与金牌得主进行比较。

金牌显然好太多了。

当你把银牌和铜牌比较时，它们其实差不多。

但对于铜牌得主来说，如果银牌只是略好一点，这不算太强烈的上行比较。

但要是和第四名比，那可是天壤之别。

第四名就只是个运动员，而不是奖牌得主了。所以铜牌得主非常庆幸自己逃脱了另一种命运。

因此，我们在这些奖牌得主身上看到了这种表现更好但感觉更糟的现象，银牌得主往往极其痛苦。

所以，这里我们可以吸取一个重要教训：比较可以驱使我们前进，可以激励我们，但它们也能让我们痛苦不堪。

So,we've thought about how comparisons can be motivating,but they can also have some adverse consequences as well.

And here,we want to think about some of the bad in comparisons.

I want to draw on some of the work by Franz de Waal,where what he did is he actually studied how ketchup and monkeys,very clever monkeys,reacted to unfairness.

He taught these monkeys to use stones for money,where he gave them stones.

Experiment would come out,open up their hands,and receive a stone,and then hand the monkey some reward,like a slice of cucumber.

It turns out these monkeys would engage in this transaction all day long.

They love cucumbers,and they're happy to hand over the stones.

That is,until they see a neighbor,a monkey in a cage next to them,getting something better than a cucumber,like a grape.

And here I'll show you a video from one of his studies where two catchment monkeys side by side are handing over stones.

One's getting a cucumber,the other one's getting a grape.

We can see what happens.

I want to highlight three things about this video.

The first is how intensely focused the one catchment monkey is,the one who's getting the cucumbers,is in looking at what's happening in the cage next door to his neighbor getting the grape.

The second is,I want to focus on how upset this catchment monkey is.

And then,third,how this drives this catchment monkey to exit.

That is,to not even want to engage in this transaction,throwing the cucumber and not wanting to participate,where the stone now no longer becomes worth a cucumber.

And it's all relative.

That is,it's because some other catchment monkey is getting a better deal that this original deal that seemed fine is no longer okay.

And it's not just monkeys.

I want to argue that we're hardwired to make these comparisons,and these comparisons really influence us.

Inspired by it until they had to go out to the market.

And all of a sudden,his work became irritating and he got upset about it.

He was so upset,he actually ended up quitting.

He joined a different firm where he became the chief happiness officer.

Now,it's not just individuals,it happens to groups too.

And here,American Airlines years ago were facing very tough financial straits.

They were on the verge of bankruptcy.

Now,at the same time,the executives at American Airlines could have left American Airlines for other more stable companies,and they tried to retain those executives.

Are$1.8 billion in concessions reasonable?

Now,let's go to the United Kingdom and I want to think about two brothers,David and Ed Miliband.

Now,what happens is they end up,you know,their relationship ends up fracturing,and David talks about the permanent,invidious comparison made professional life impossible.

He not only leaves parliament,he actually leaves the United Kingdom,he leaves to work in a nonprofit in New York.

So here,this comparison is driving him crazy.

Now,for similar reasons,we can think about twins.

Now,one idea is you think,well,what's an artificial twin?

An artificial twin is adopting someone that's similar in age to a biological son or daughter.

Now,what would be great about it is you have a built-in playmate.

That is,by doing this,there's always going to be some twin,one of those twins,that's going to be out ahead of the other,and there could be developmental differences,and that constant comparison is going to make artificial twins really toxic.
