2-01-01.06_比较与动机

我想探讨一下比较带来的某些结果。

在这里，我想重点讨论比较实际上如何能够带来非常好的结果。

我想聚焦于比较与动机之间的联系。

那么，接下来要说的就是关于比较的一个非常有益且具有建设性的方面。

我先从一个关于杜克大学与密歇根大学比赛的故事讲起。

杜克大学在半场结束时落后一分。

你可以想象一下那个更衣室里发生了什么。

你可以想象一下教练可能对他们说的激励性讲话。

杜克大学在下半场开始发力，气势如虹。

他们彻底爆发了。

原本一场比分紧咬、非常激烈的比赛变成了一边倒的结局。

事实证明，这种情况并非杜克对密歇根这场比赛的独有现象。

事实证明，如果我们查看一万八千场美国职业篮球联赛比赛，乔纳·伯杰和丹尼斯·波普就做过这样的研究，他们分析了一万八千多场比赛，发现了一个不连续的现象：那些半场结束时落后一分的球队，实际上更有可能赢得比赛。

也就是说，通常情况下，如果一支球队领先很多，他们很可能会赢下比赛。

所以，如果你在半场领先，通常有助于预测谁将成为比赛的最终赢家，但有一个例外，那就是如果你只落后一点点。

因为当你只落后一点点时，你会被那种比较所激励，这种比较会给你动力，它会提升你的努力程度，所以半场落后一分的球队实际上更有可能获胜。

我们发现，这种现象不仅仅存在于体育领域。

我们在全球舞台上也能看到这一点。

想想太空竞赛。

现在，如果我们回顾一下太空竞赛的历史，我们要回到二十世纪五十年代。

在一九五五年七月，艾森豪威尔总统站出来宣布，美国将发射一颗科学卫星进入地球轨道。

那是他的目标。

他宣布了这个目标，但当美国不是第一个发射卫星的国家，而是俄罗斯人率先做到时，他感到很惊讶。

我们当时与俄罗斯人处于太空竞赛中，俄罗斯人发射了人造地球卫星，而那次人造地球卫星危机实际上推动了我们几十年。

直到今天，我们仍然会提起人造地球卫星，来思考我们是如何落后的，以及需要如何追赶。

所以在这里，美国感觉他们落后了，需要迎头赶上，而这种感觉促使政府采取了令人难以置信的行动。

于是我们有了《国防教育法案》。

它催生了奖学金、高级研究计划局、美国国家航空航天局。

我们投入了数额惊人的资金。

仅美国国家航空航天局的预算就急剧增加。

你会看到这个预算以惊人的速度增长，当时它就有六十亿美元。

按今天的价值计算，那相当于三百二十亿美元。所以，在二十世纪六十年代，我们把国家预算的很大一部分都花在了太空预算上。

如果我们问，花多少钱才是合适的？这很难说，但我们知道我们正在落后，而在那种比较之下，相对于俄罗斯人，我们是落后的。

他们在我们之前就把人造地球卫星送入了地球轨道，正是那种比较激励了我们。

它向我们提出了挑战，并激励我们去完成伟大的事业。

所以我们可以想想，如果重新表述这句话，你知道的，这是一个人的一小步，但结果却是一个巨大的飞跃，不仅对人类而言，更是美国对苏联的一大步。

社会比较在很多情况下都很重要，但在竞争对手之间，其重要性尤为突出。

竞争对手是特殊的比较对象。

竞争对手是指那些我们与之存在额外心理对抗关系的人。

击败一个竞争对手给我们带来的好处，是击败其他任何人所无法比拟的。

事实上，加文·凯尔多夫研究了赛跑中的竞争对手关系，分析了非常多的对抗案例，发现当参赛者比赛中有竞争对手时，他们会跑得更快。

所以，如果你与一个势均力敌的对手同场竞技，你很可能会取得更好的成绩。

不仅仅是赛跑运动员。

我们在许多不同的情境中都发现了这一点。

在这里，对于你们中那些铁杆篮球迷来说，你们会记得拉里·伯德与魔术师约翰逊之间的竞争。

对此，拉里·伯德曾说，我每天早上做的第一件事就是看比分数据，看看魔术师约翰逊做了什么。

其他任何事情我都不在乎。

这就是高度专注，对竞争对手的高度专注。

所以在这里，我们可以观察并思考动机的问题。

我之前也提到过北卡罗来纳大学焦油踵队和杜克大学蓝魔队之间的竞争。

这两支队伍在地理位置上非常接近。

他们都赢得过全国冠军。

而要赢得全国冠军，你需要具备很多条件。

你需要优秀的教练，你需要出色的球员。

你还需要强大的动力。

你看到的是，在一九九二年，杜克大学赢了。

一九九三年，北卡罗来纳大学赢了。

如果这种情况只发生一次，那确实引人注目，但随后你会看到相反的情况发生。

二零零九年，北卡罗来纳大学获胜，接着第二年杜克大学又赢了。

所以在这里，我们可以看到竞争对手之间相互激励，彼此给予对方巨大的动力。

这种现象存在于各种类型的关系中。

如果你观察姐妹关系，一项针对姐妹的研究发现，当一位姐妹在外工作而另一位在家时，决定其中一位女性是否外出工作的因素之一，就是她们丈夫的收入多少。

我们发现，如果一位女性的丈夫挣得比她姐妹的丈夫少，那么她家的家庭收入就会显得不够，这位女性就会产生外出工作的动力。

有趣的是，重要的不是金钱的绝对数量，而是相对数量才真正起作用。

所以，基本的观点是这样的。

也就是说，比较可以激励我们，并且在很多情况下，它可以是非常建设性的动力，但我们需要有所节制地看待它。

也就是说，并非所有的动力都是好的，接下来我们将会讨论其中的一些问题。

英文原文

I want to think about some of the consequences of comparisons.

And here I want to focus on the way comparisons can actually lead to very good outcomes.

And I want to focus on the link between comparisons and motivation.

So here's one of the things that can be very good and constructive about comparisons.

And I'll start off with a story about a Duke,Michigan game.

Duke was down by one point at halftime.

You can imagine what happened in that locker room.

You can think about the motivational speech the coach might have given them.

Duke came out roaring in the second half.

They exploded.

And what had been a really intense,close game became a blowout.

It turns out it wasn't unique to this Duke,Michigan game.

It turns out that if we looked at 18000 NBA games,which Jonah Berger and Dennis Pope did,they analyzed over 18000 games,and they found a discontinuity where teams down by one point at the half were actually more likely to win.

That is,in general,if one team's winning by a lot,they're likely to win the game.

So if you're ahead at the halftime,it generally helps predict who wins at the end of the game,except for if you're down by just a very little bit.

Because when you're down by a very little bit,you're motivated by that comparison,and that motivates you,it increases effort,and people down by one at halftime are actually more likely to win.

Now,here we find that it's not just in sports.

We can see this on the global stage.

We think about the space race.

Now,if we were to go back in the space race,we're going to go back to the 1950s.

And in July 1955,Eisenhower came out and said,the United States will launch a science satellite to orbit Earth.

That was his goal.

He came out with that goal and then was surprised when the U.S.wasn't the first to launch a satellite,but the Russians were.

We were in a space race with the Russians,and Russians launched Sputnik,and that Sputnik crisis has actually carried forward for decades.

And we still invoke Sputnik to think about how we're falling behind and need to catch up.

So here,the U.S.felt like they were behind and needed to catch up,and it motivated an incredible government action.

So we had the National Defense Education Act.

It led to scholarships,NARPA,NASA.

we invested an incredible amount of money.

The NASA budget alone took off.

You see this budget growing incredibly,where at the time it was$6 billion.

Today that would be$32 billion.So in the 1960s,we were spending a huge fraction of the national budget just on the space budget.

If we were to ask,what's the right amount to spend,it's hard to tell,but we knew that we were falling behind,and in that comparison,by comparison,we were down relative to the Russians.

They had launched Sputnik to orbit Earth before we did,and that motivated us because of that comparison.

And it challenged us and motivated us to accomplish great things.

So we can think about if we were to recast this,you know,one small step for man,but it turns out to be one giant leap,not just for mankind,but for America over the Soviets.

Now,social comparisons matter in a lot of cases,but no more so than in rivals.

Rivals are special comparisons.

Rivals are people with whom we have an extra psychological rivalry.

We get a benefit from beating a rival in a way we don't with anybody else.

And in fact,Gavin Keldoff has studied rivals in running races,analyzed lots and lots of rivalries,and found that runners run faster when they have a rival in that race.

So if you're racing against a close rival,you're likely to get a better time.

It's not just runners.

We find this in many different contexts.

And here,for those of you that are big basketball fans,you'll remember the Larry Bird-Magic Johnson rivalry.

And here,Larry Bird said,the first thing I would do every morning was look at the box scores and see what Magic did.

I didn't care about anything else.

This is intense focus,intense focus on a rival.

So here we can see and think about motivation.

And I already alluded to the Tar Heels and Blue Devils before.

These are rivals that are in close proximity to each other.

Both of them have won national championships.

And to win a national championship,you need a lot of things.

You need good coaching,you need great players.

You also need a lot of motivation.

And what you see is here in 92,Duke wins.

93,UNC wins.

Now,that would be remarkable if it happened once,but then you see the reverse happening.

In 2009,UNC wins,and then Duke wins the following year.

So here we can see rivals motivated,highly motivated by each other.

Now,it happens in all kinds of relationships.

If you look at sisters,a study of sisters where one's in the labor force and one stays at home,one of the things that drives whether or not one of these women works outside the home is how much their husbands make.

And we find that if the husband earns less than the sister's husband,that household income seems like it's not enough,and that woman is motivated to work outside the home.

Interestingly,it's not the absolute amount of money that matters,it's the relative amount that really matters.

So here's the broad idea.

That is,comparisons can motivate us,and in many cases,it can be very constructive motivation,but we need to think about it in check.

That is,not all that motivation is good,and we'll think about some of that next.

2-01-01.07_比较与欺骗

事实证明，比较不仅能让我们痛苦，还能激励我们从事一些我们本不该参与的行为。

想想两位滑冰运动员：南希·克里根，她在1992年是奥运会铜牌得主；以及坦雅·哈丁，她是唯一一位在比赛中成功完成三周半跳的美国运动员。

两人是争夺美国奥运代表队席位的竞争对手。

她们都训练得异常刻苦，然而可怕的事情发生了。

在那场被称为“震惊世界的一击”的事件中，一名男子在训练结束后走到南希·克里根身边，用一根管子猛击她的膝盖，迫使她数周无法训练。

结果发现，那不是随便什么人，而是坦雅·哈丁雇来除掉南希·克里根的。

所以，她们不仅通过加倍努力来竞争，还试图通过把别人拉下来进行竞争。

比较也可能激发不道德的行为。

我要谈谈另一场竞争。

这是维珍航空与英国航空之间的竞争，英国航空投入巨资，他们赞助了伦敦眼，随后布兰森花钱让一艘飞艇飞越伦敦，上面写着英国航空不行了，以此来嘲讽英国航空。

这场竞争最终不仅演变为互相贬损和建设性竞争，结果却是英国航空侵入了维珍的系统，查看他们的预订信息，采取不道德的手段试图窃取客户，最终给自己带来了真正的麻烦。

这种现象普遍存在。

也就是说，在亚当·格林斯基等人进行的一项关于职业足球竞争关系的研究中，他们通过分析比赛发现，这些比赛既有在不同城市举行的，也有在同一个城市举行的，也就是说，那些在比赛中双方都有主场的球队，由于同处一地，这些很可能成为竞争最激烈的对手。

在这些比赛中，他们发现了更多的黄牌和红牌，这是衡量不道德行为的一个指标。

还有另一个例子，这个例子与我自身关系更近一些：学术界。

在学术界，我们努力发表论文。但发表过程需要很长时间。在此期间，我们可以把论文上传到网上，有些网站会追踪论文被下载的次数。

当一篇论文被大量下载时，这意味着或暗示这篇论文非常重要。

事实上，我们许多同行会查看一篇论文被下载的次数，来判断这是否是我们应该阅读、应该关注的内容，我们将其用作衡量重要性的一个标准。

事实证明，用这个来衡量重要性有一个非常有趣的问题，那就是有时你可以操纵这些数字。

例如，你可以下载你自己的论文。

事实上，有些教员甚至编写程序来下载自己的论文。

那么，谁会这么做呢？

嗯，事实证明，比较能帮助我们理解这一点。

所以，当你的同行拥有很高的下载量时，这实际上是决定你有多大诱惑、多大可能去下载自己论文的一个重要因素。

还有一些参考点和目标也很重要。

如果你接近进入前十名，那也更容易促使人们从事这种行为。

我们可以更广泛地思考这个问题。

这是一个关于朗达的故事。

她从公司一批看起来很有前途的员工中被选中。

一位经理挑选她参加额外的课程，以提升她的计算机技能。

她正在被培养，准备晋升。

现在，这正是公司应该做的。

也就是说，我们应该关注那些有潜力的人，并培养他们以便晋升。

但这里存在一个比较问题，问题就在这里：也就是说，她的同事们环顾四周，正在进行比较，而且他们进行的这种比较让他们感到不快。

于是他们开始排斥她，不邀请她参加聚会，不给她传递口信。

因此她的工作受到了影响，结果朗达更难取得成功，她的处境也变得更不愉快。

这就像成为了“本月最佳员工”，却没人愿意跟你说话。

在某些情况下，这可能导致像朗达这样的人放松油门，最终投入更少的努力，因为他们不想成为那个老师的宠儿、那个本月最佳员工，或者那个被选中的员工。

所以我们需要思考，这些比较过程究竟会如何侵蚀我们真正想要实现的行为。

这告诉我们，比较不仅会让我们痛苦，还会增加变革。

英文原文

It turns out that comparisons can only make us miserable,they can also motivate us to engage in behavior we really shouldn't be engaging in.

Let's think about two skaters:Nancy Kerrigan,who in 1992 was the Olympic bronze medalist,and Tanya Harding,the only American to have ever landed a triple axle in competition.

The two are rivals competing for spots in the U.S.Olympic team.

They both trained incredibly hard,and yet something terrible happened.

In what was termed the whack heard round the world,a man came up and after practice,came up to Nancy Kerrigan and with a pole whacked her knee,throwing her out of practice for weeks.

It turns out it wasn't just anybody,it was somebody that Tanya Harding had hired to take out Nancy Kerrigan.

So not only were they competing by working extra hard,they're also competing by trying to pull somebody else down.

And comparisons can motivate unethical behavior.

I'll talk about a different rivalry.

This is a rivalry between Virgin and British Airways,where British Airways invested heavily,they supported the London Eye,and then Branson paid to have a blimp fly over London with the words BA can't get it up,taunting British Airways.

rivalry ended up spilling over not just to trash talking and constructive competition,but it ended up British Airways was hacking into Virgin's system,looking at their reservations,engaging in unethical practices to try to steal customers away in a way that ended up getting them in real trouble.

Now,it happens broadly.

That is,in a study of professional soccer rivalries that Adam Galinsky and others have done,they found that in analyzing matches,and these are matches between soccer teams playing in other cities as well as co-located cities,that is,teams that both have home teams in that match,

those are likely to be the most intense rivals because of the co-location.

And there,they found more yellow and red cards,a measure of unethical behavior.

Here's another example,and this involves something a little bit closer to my heart:academics.

Academics,we try to publish.Articles,but that publication process takes a long time.In the meantime,we can upload our articles onto the web,and there are websites that track how many times articles have been downloaded.

When articles have been downloaded a lot of times,it means or suggests that article is really important.

And in fact,a lot of our peers look to see how often an article has been downloaded to see if that's something we should be reading,something we should be paying attention to,and we use as a measure of what's important.

It turns out the one really funny thing about that as a measure of importance is that sometimes you can manipulate these numbers.

You can,for example,download your own article.

And in fact,some faculty have even written programs to download their own article.

Now,who would do that?

Well,it turns out comparisons help us understand that.

So when you have peers who have high download counts,that's actually an important factor in determining how tempted and how likely you might be to download your own article.

And there are also some reference points and goals that matter too.

If you're close to reaching the top 10,that also is more likely to push people to engage in this kind of behavior.

We can think about this more broadly.

So this is a story about Rhonda.

She was selected from a pool of people in her company who seemed to have great promise.

And she was selected by a manager to take additional classes,develop her computer skills.

She was being groomed for promotion.

Now,this is exactly what companies should be doing.

That is,we should be looking to look at the people who have promise and we should develop them for promotion.

But there's a comparison problem,and here's that problem:that is,her co-workers looking around are engaging in comparisons,and they're engaging in comparisons they don't like.

So they began ostracizing her,not inviting her to parties,not passing along messages to her.

So her work was suffering,and here as a result,it becomes more difficult for Rhonda to succeed,and it's also less pleasant for Rhonda.

It's like being the employee of the month that nobody wants to talk to.

And here,in some cases,it could lead people like Rhonda to take their foot off the gas and end up investing less effort because they don't want to be that teacher's pet,that employee of the month,or that selected employee.

So we need to think about how some of these comparison processes can actually erode the very behaviors we're actually looking to accomplish.

Now,this tells us that comparisons can make us not just miserable,but they can also increase change.

2-01-01.08_比较：寻找平衡点

我们已经探讨了比较的一些内在机制，比较带来的一些好处，以及比较带来的一些坏处。

所以，现在我想思考的问题是，我们如何才能找到恰当的平衡点？

我们知道，比较可以激励我们，而且这种激励可能非常有建设性，但它们同样可能引发怨恨，让我们痛苦不堪。

我们该如何找到那个平衡点呢？

我们想要获得动力，但同时也想感到满足。

这里有一些关键原则。

第一，我们要考虑下行比较，也就是与那些成就远不如我们的人进行比较。

例如，我们可以通过做志愿者或帮助有需要的人来实现这一点。

这样做会让我们更快乐。

所以，让自己更快乐的一个方法就是进行这种下行比较。

另一件需要考虑的事情是，上行比较如何激励我们。

就像我们之前想到的密歇根大学对杜克大学的比赛，半场落后一分，或者人造地球卫星的例子那样，这些比较可以极大地激励我们。

这些上行比较可以推动我们付出巨大努力，达到新的高度。

所以，下行比较能让我们更快乐，上行比较能激励我们，但它们也都会带来不好的影响，比如让我们感到不满足或动力减弱。

我们可以思考一下谈判过程中的比较，它们既激励我们，也影响我们的满意程度。

你可以想象，比如在谈判中，你可能会有某个目标，某个期望值，那是你试图达到的水平。

你也可以想想你的底线，也就是你愿意接受的最低条件。

所以，你有一个较高的目标，它能激励我们，推动我们努力；还有一个较低的底线，相比之下，它能让我们感到满意。

也就是说，在谈判中，大多数时候我们无法得到所有想要的东西。

所以，我们会达不到自己的目标，但很可能得到比我们的替代方案，也就是比我们的底线更好的结果，因此我们最终会落在中间的某个位置。

现在，这取决于我们把注意力放在哪里。

如果我们引导人们关注目标，如果我们专注于那个目标，我们会更有动力，但满足感会更低。

如果我们专注于自己的底线，我们的动力会减弱，但满足感会更高。

事实上，情况正是如此。

在亚当·格林斯基和他的同事们进行的这项研究中，那些关注目标的人最终比那些关注替代方案，也就是他们底线的人表现得更好，但那些关注目标的人，他们的满足感低于那些关注底线的人。

所以，在这里我们可以考虑如何利用比较来为我们服务。

也就是说，在谈判过程中，我们最好专注于自己的目标，但在谈判结束后，我们最好想想自己的底线，这能让我们更满足。

所以，我们既想要更高动力带来的好处，也想要更满足的感觉，而这可能涉及到注意力的转换。

这就是我们如何看待谈判中的比较。

但这不仅仅适用于谈判，它发生在更广泛的领域。

这里还有一个有趣的问题：我们思考一下在经济衰退时期毕业的好处。

那么，为什么会有什么好处呢？

如果你在经济衰退时期毕业，实际上找工作会更难，而且即使找到了工作，薪水也可能更低。

实际上，人们研究过，在经济衰退期毕业的影响是持久的。

所以，你的起薪会更低，而这种影响会伴随你很长时间。

但好处是什么呢？

嗯，事实证明，在经济衰退期找到工作的人实际上更快乐，尽管他们的收入要低百分之十五。

他们更快乐是因为比较。

他们更快乐是因为他们确实找到了一份工作，并且意识到他们许多同龄人最终做得不如他们好。

所以，在这里我们可以想到，比较帮助我们理解了许多不寻常的现象，无论是在谈判中，还是在我们的工作场所，乃至更广泛的领域。

以下是社会比较的三个关键原则。

我想思考三个关键点，它们能帮助我们找到平衡。

第一个观点是，我们要考虑那些有序或无序的比较。

这里说的有序或无序，我的意思是：这是否是预料之中的比较结果？

那么，如果我们是竞争对手，我们预期会怎样？

如果我们是兄弟姐妹，谁年龄更大？

我们之前谈到了戴维·米利班德和埃德·米利班德。

哥哥戴维被他的弟弟击败了。

现在，相比之下，想想肯尼迪家族。

以肯尼迪家族为例，这些兄弟姐妹是按顺序发展的，兄弟之间相互协作，因为他们互相帮助，一步步往上走，而且他们完全是按部就班地一步步前进。

网球界也是如此。

想想网球界最具统治力的姐妹组合之一，塞雷娜·威廉姆斯和维纳斯·威廉姆斯。最近一段时间，塞雷娜在网球界占据主导地位。

她的光芒盖过了她的姐姐，但事情是按顺序发生的。

是姐姐维纳斯首先占据主导地位。塞雷娜甚至说过，在她成长过程中，一切都是围绕维纳斯的，事情本就该如此。

在那里，当塞雷娜开始赢球并击败维纳斯时，她是在按顺序进行。

尽管她现在拥有辉煌得多的战绩，但这种按顺序发展被证明非常重要，而且这实际上使她们成为了极其高效的双打搭档。

事实上，她们拥有史上最令人印象深刻的女子双打搭档战绩之一，在女双决赛中的战绩是二十一胜一负，并且共同拥有三枚奥运会金牌。

所以，按顺序发展是让比较发挥积极作用的关键原则之一。

另一个关键观点是提供未来竞争的机会。

例如，奥运会之所以特别令人痛苦的一点是，对许多运动员来说，这是他们唯一的机会。

比如阿贝尔·基韦特，他输了，从未赢得过金牌，不是在那场比赛中，而且对他来说，未来也没有其他机会了。

所以，如果我们未来还有竞争的机会，那些比较的激烈程度就会降低。

第三个关键原则是考虑他人的视角。

当好事发生在我们身上时，我们通常非常高兴。

人们会说，哦，我真为你高兴。

你真的实至名归。

他们可能是真心的，也可能不是。也就是说，他们私下里可能非常沮丧，但我们通常听不到。

这表明这些比较确实非常强烈，而且这种现象在不同文化中都普遍存在。

我来分享一个俄罗斯寓言。

就像很多寓言故事一样，有一个人发现了一盏灯，他擦了擦，一个精灵出现了，精灵说，你可以许任何你想要的愿望。

但这里有个转折。在这个故事里，精灵说，转折点在于你的邻居会得到双倍。

所以你可以拥有任何你想要的东西，但你的邻居会得到双倍。

这个人来回踱步，揉着额头，非常深入、努力地思考，最后说，啊，我知道我想要什么了。

我要你戳瞎我的一只眼睛。

在这里我们可以看到，比较的过程是如此强烈，如此令人憎恶，以至于这个人非常担心得到好东西，因为相比之下邻居会得到更好的。

所以，在思考这些比较时，重要的是，即使好事发生在我们身上，也要认识到其他人会进行这些比较，他们可能不那么满意，至少不像他们表面上看起来那样满意。

英文原文

So we've thought about some of the mechanics of comparisons,some of the good in comparisons,and some of the bad in comparisons.

So the question I want to think about now is how do we find the right balance?

So we know that comparisons can motivate us,and that can be very constructive,but they can also create resentment and make us perfectly miserable.

How do we find that balance?

We want to be motivated,but satisfied.

And here are some key rules.

One,we want to think about favorable comparisons,that is,comparisons where we look down at people that haven't accomplished quite as much.

We can do this,for example,by volunteering or helping out people in need.

By doing that,it'll make us happier.

So one way to make ourselves happier is to engage in these downward comparisons.

Another thing to think about is how unfavorable comparisons can motivate us.

So just as we thought about with the Michigan Duke game being down by one at halftime,we can be incredibly motivated by these comparisons,or the Sputnik example.

These unfavorable comparisons can push us to great efforts to new heights.

So favorable comparisons can make us happier,unfavorable ones can motivate us,but they can both do things that aren't as good,like making us dissatisfied or less motivated.

We can think about comparisons in the negotiation process,where they both motivate us and influence how happy we are.

You can think,for example,in a negotiation,you might have some target,some aspiration,somewhere you're trying to hit.

And you can think about your reservation price,the least to be willing to accept.

So you have something up high that can motivate us and push us hard,and something lower,our reservation price,that can make us,in comparison,happy.

That is,in a negotiation,we're not going to get everything we wanted most of the time.

So we're going to fall short of our target,and we're likely to get something better than our alternative,what our reservation price is,and so we're going to end up somewhere in the middle.

Now,it depends on where we focus.

If we focus people's attention on targets,if we're focused on that target,we're going to be more motivated,but less satisfied.

If we focus on our reservation price,we're going to be less motivated,but more satisfied.

In fact,that's exactly what happened.

So here in this study that Adam Galinsky and his colleagues ran,people who focused on targets ended up doing better than people who focused on their alternatives,their reservation price,but people who focus on targeted targets.

Their target were less satisfied than people who focused on the reservation.

So,here we can think about trying to use comparisons to our advantage.

So,during the negotiation process,we like to focus on our targets,but then afterwards,we like to think about our reservation price,and that can make us more satisfied.

So,we want the benefits of that higher motivation as well as the benefits of feeling more satisfied,and that can involve shifting our attention.

So,that's how we can think about comparisons in negotiations.

But it's not just negotiations,it happens more broadly.

And here's another funny puzzle:we think about the benefit of graduating in a recession.

Now,why should there be a benefit?

If you graduate in a recession,it's actually harder to find a job,and if you do find a job,it's likely to be less highly compensated.

And actually,people have studied the effects of graduating recession are long-lasting.

So,you end up with a lower starting salary,and that follows you for a long time.

But what's the benefit?

Well,it turns out people who find a job in recession are actually much happier,even though they're making up to 15%less.

They're happier because of the comparison.

They're happier because they actually got a job and they realize that many of their peers ended up doing less well.

So,here we can think about comparisons helping us make sense of a lot of unusual phenomena both in negotiation and in our workplace and more broadly.

Here are three key principles of social comparisons.

I want to think about three key things that help us find our balance.

The first idea is that we want to think about comparisons that go in or out of order.

Now,by in or out of order,what I mean is:is this the expected comparison outcome that was anticipated?

So,if we're competitors,what do we expect?

If we're siblings,who's older?

So,we talked about David and Ed Miliband.

David,the older brother,was bested by his younger brother.

Now,in contrast,think about the Kennedys.

So,here we have the Kennedys,where these siblings were going in order,where the brothers collaborated because they were helping each other go from one step to the next,and they went from one step to the next completely in order.

The same is true in tennis.

We think about one of the most dominant sibling pairs in tennis,Serena and Venus Williams.Now,more recently,Serena has dominated on the tennis scene.

She's eclipsed her bigger sister,but things went in order.

It was Venus,the older sister,that was dominant first.And Serena even said that as she was growing up,everything was about Venus,that's how it was supposed to be.

And there,when Serena began to win and beat Venus,she was going in order.

And even though she now has a much more impressive record,that going in order turns out to be very important,and it's actually enabled them to be incredibly effective as doubles partners.

In fact,they have one of the most impressive doubles partners records of all time,where their record is 21 and 1 in women's doubles finals,and they have three Olympic gold medals to share.

So going in order is one of the key principles of making comparisons work.

The other key idea is providing opportunities to compete in the future.

So one thing that's particularly painful about,say,the Olympics is that for many athletes,this is their one chance.

For Abel Kivet,for example,he lost out,he'd never won the gold,it was not in that race,and there wasn't another future opportunity for him.

So if we have opportunities to compete in the future,those comparisons are going to be less intense.

The third key principle is to think about the perspective of other people.

When good things happen to us,we often are pretty happy.

And people will say,oh,I'm so happy for you.

You really deserve it.

They might or might not be.That is,they might be privately quite upset,but we don't typically get to hear that.

To suggest that these comparisons are really quite intense,and it really is a phenomenon that travels across culturally quite well.

I'm going to share a Russian parable.

And as a lot of parables happen,there's a man who finds a lamp,rubs it,a genie emerges,and the genie says,you can have any wish you want.

But here's the twist.In this case,the genie says,the twist is your neighbor gets double.

So you can have anything you want,but your neighbor gets double.

Well,the man paces back and forth,rubs his brow,thinks very deeply and hard about it,and finally says,ah,I know what I want.

I want you to poke out one of my eyes.

Here we can see that the comparison process is so intense,it's so invidious,that here the person's so worried about having something good because the neighbor in comparison will do even better.

And so to think about these comparisons,it's important even when good things happen to us,to recognize that others are going to make these comparisons and they might be less satisfied,at least than they might appear outwardly.

2-02-01.01_合作的挑战

接下来，我想思考一下合作带来的挑战。

我们如何让人们与我们合作，即使他们自己如果不那么努力或不帮助我们，日子可能会过得更好？

我想从一个故事开始，这是一个关于凶杀案侦探马歇尔·弗兰克的故事。

他是一位经验非常丰富的侦探，他遇到过一个案子，他知道保罗·罗尔斯有罪。

他知道，但他无法证明，而他真正想要的是得到一份认罪供词。

于是他和保罗·罗尔斯坐下来谈，在这个案子里，罗尔斯的邻居被勒死了，弗兰克侦探的目标就是得到这份认罪供词。

现在，在这次审讯中，有趣的是，罗尔斯知道这是个什么套路。

也就是说，他知道侦探想要一份认罪供词。

而在三十分钟内，弗兰克侦探最终拿到了那份认罪供词。

所以他最终让某个人配合了他想要的。

他想要这份认罪供词。

而且他做得相对较快。我想问的一个问题是，他是怎么做到的？

我想指出，这确实说明了合作这个概念。

我们如何让人们跨越界限来帮助我们，做我们想让他们做的事情，即使这不符合他们自己的最佳利益？

所以这与一些截然不同的问题相关。

比如，你会让一个完全陌生的人睡在你家吗？

嗯，通常不会，但这恰恰是爱彼迎赖以存在的基础。

也就是说，这是一个允许人们这样做的系统。

所以我们可以思考如何在一种社会困境中进行合作。

社会困境是一个多方参与的囚徒困境。

囚徒困境的情况通常只涉及两个人，但我们经常会遇到涉及多人的情况。

所以我们可以思考一些事情，比如我们如何共同努力减少汽车排放？

我们希望每个人都对汽车进行尾气检测，但就个人而言，我们宁愿不对自己的汽车进行尾气检测。

或者想想过度捕捞的问题。

我们宁愿其他所有人都减少捕捞，但就个人而言，我们宁愿尽可能多地捕捞。

所以，作为个人，我们有动力去背叛，或者去做最符合自身利益的事情，但作为集体，我们希望每个人都团结起来，做最符合集体利益的事情。

这些就是社会困境。

我们如何解决这些问题？

我们可以把囚徒困境看作是第一个案例。

也就是说，这是社会困境问题中的果蝇。

在经典的囚徒困境中，有两个人。

那么，你可以想想弗兰克侦探的案子。

你想得到认罪供词，如果他们认罪，整个法律程序就更容易推进，但对于那个潜在的罪犯个人来说，认罪对他们个人并不利。

现在，想象一下你抓住了两个人，他们可以互相告发并认罪，或者他们可以不认罪。

在这里，我考虑的是他们彼此之间的合作。

所以，想象一下这两个罪犯想要合作。

他们想要彼此合作，都不认罪。

那么，如果他们都不认罪，结果就是两人都得到轻判。

因为没有太多证据。

他们不会因为那件事受到很重的起诉。

所以，两人都得到非常轻的刑罚，比方说六个月。

现在，如果他们俩都认罪，两人都会被判五年。

所以，很明显，如果他们彼此合作，都不认罪，对他们双方都更有利。

现在，有趣的是：如果其中一人背叛，也就是说，其中一人与辩方合作，把整个事情都抖出来，而另一个人没有，那么，想象一下这里的侦探说，听着，我给你一个特别交易。

如果你把情况全抖出来，而另一个没有，你就可以自由离开，但另一个人会被判十年。

所以，从个人角度来看，面临这个问题的人确实面临一个两难境地。

他们可以尝试做对这个群体，也就是集体最有利的事情，选择合作，或者他们可以背叛，做对自己最有利的事情，在这种情况下，他们最终会得到更好的结果。

现在，在这个案例中，无论对方怎么做，他们总是能得到更好的结果。

所以，如果对方要开口，他们宁愿也开口。

如果对方不开口，他们开口仍然对自己更有利。

所以，从个人角度来说，他们仍然有这种动力去做最符合自身利益，也就是他们自己私利的事情。但我们想要推动人们去合作，即使这对他们来说代价高昂。

所以，我们要思考如何做到这一点？

我们如何让同事加班，承担额外的任务？

我们如何让我们的孩子多做些家务？

我们如何让配偶更多地帮助我们，即使他们更愿意窝在沙发上看电视，或者做别的事情？

所以，我们在工作中和家里都一直面临这个问题，试图让人们合作，即使他们自身的利益会把他们拉向相反的方向。我们可以思考很多社会困境。

我之前谈到了温室气体。

还有过度捕捞，但我们还想努力节约用水。

我们希望每个人都缩短淋浴时间，但我们自己却想洗个更长时间的澡，或者为像公共广播这样的事情做贡献，又或者是在一个项目上合作。

在许多谈判环境中，我们可以分享更多信息，这有助于创造价值，但这可能与我们试图索取价值的个人利益相冲突。

所以我们面临着这种张力。

作为管理者，他们一直在尝试解决这种社会困境。

他们试图让人们合作，而人们的天性可能正被拉向相反的方向。

这里有一些思路。

以下是一些能够促进合作的因素。

首先，我们要建立关系。

所以，人们越认同我们，效果就越好。

社会学家称之为过去的阴影。如果我们有团队凝聚力的经历，有共同的历史，这会将我们联系在一起，并营造出一种我们同舟共济的感觉。

我们在这里有一个共同的目标，而这个共同的目标能让人们更有效地合作。

这与共同身份的概念有关。

那么，我是否将自己视为这个群体的一部分？

就像我们称呼彼此的称谓。

我们是伙伴吗？

我们是员工吗？

我是否认为自己，我是否穿着带有公司标志的制服？

我是否视自己为这个组织的一员？

这种认同感越强，合作就越紧密。

然后，第三点，社会学家用未来的阴影这个词来描述我们未来互动的可能性有多大。

所以，如果我知道这是一种长期的关系，那么现在帮助你是一件更容易做到的事情，因为我知道将来某个时候你也有可能帮助我。

所以，未来的时间跨度越长，我们就越有可能获得合作。

所以是过去、身份认同，以及未来的阴影。

还有另外几件对合作很重要的事情。

一个是清晰的沟通。

所以我能否清楚地沟通我需要什么以及为什么需要它？

我们能否找到一种合作的方式？

所以沟通越好，合作就越有效。

这意味着面对面的沟通尤其重要。

面对面的沟通之所以重要，有很多不同的原因，我们之后会讨论。

但其中一个原因是，它能让我们获得最完整的沟通。

然后接下来，我们可以思考一下期望。

那么，我们对此抱有什么样的期望？

我是在传达我非常关心自己的利益吗？

还是在传达我们同舟共济的信息？

人们实际上做过用金钱或其他奖品来进行的囚徒困境游戏实验。

他们发现，当你把这个游戏描述成一个社区游戏时，人们的合作程度远高于你把它描述成华尔街游戏。

在华尔街游戏中，人们会戴上一种滤镜或心态，认为自己是在为自己而战，最终会变得更具竞争性。

所以我们描述事情的方式，我们设定的期望，会深刻地影响人们的合作程度。

他们在试图弄清楚我们玩的是什么游戏，而我们沟通的方式会深刻地影响这一点。

接下来，想想问责制。

那么，我们能观察到行为吗？

我之前谈到了节约用水。

现在，人们更有可能减少给草坪浇水，因为邻居们能看到。

缩短淋浴时间则更难被观察到。

当我们无法观察到人们是在合作还是背叛时，人们更有可能选择背叛。

而匿名性会损害合作。

像评级系统这样让爱彼迎有效运作的东西，则有助于合作。

然后更广泛地说，是信任。如果我们能建立一种信任关系，那么我们就能获得合作。

关于信任，我们稍后会多讲一点。所以，关键思路如下。

过去的阴影，我们过去所做的事情。共同的认同感。

我认同自己是这个群体的一员。

未来的阴影，我们未来将要进行的互动。

有效且清晰的沟通。

我们设定对合作的期望。

我们让人们对他们的行为负责。

这意味着我们可以观察他们做了什么，以及他们行为的后果。

比如，你可以想想税收。

我们有时会审计人们的纳税情况，并对不纳税的行为进行处罚。

这是一种让人们为了集体利益而合作的方式，尽管他们个人并不愿意。

然后是信任。我们的关系越信任，合作就越有效。

英文原文

Next,I want to think about the challenge of cooperation.

How do we get people to cooperate with us even when they might be better off themselves if they didn't have to work so hard or didn't have to help us out?

I want to start with a story,and this is a story about a homicide detective,Marshall Frank.

He's a very experienced detective,and he had this one case where he knew Paul Rawls was guilty.

He knew it,but he couldn't prove it,and what he really wanted was a confession.

So he sat down with Paul Rawls,and in this case,Rolls'neighbor had been strangled,and Detective Frank was going for this confession.

Now,in this interrogation,what's interesting is that Rawls knows that this is the game.

That is,he knows the detective wants a confession.

And in 30 minutes,Detective Frank ended up getting that confession.

So he ended up getting somebody to be cooperative with what he wanted.

He wanted this confession.

And he did it relatively fast.And one question I want to ask is how?

And I want to suggest that this really speaks to the idea of cooperation.

How do we get people to step over and help us out,do things that we want,even when it's not in their own best interest?

So it's related to other questions that are very different.

So would you let a complete stranger sleep in your house?

Well,generally not,but that's exactly what Airbnb is predicated upon.

That is,it's a system that allows people to do exactly that.

So we can think about how to cooperate in a social dilemma.

A social dilemma is a multi-party prisoner's dilemma.

So the prison dilemma case is just two people,but we often have a lot of cases with multiple people.

So we can think about things like how do we work together to reduce car emissions?

We want everyone to smog test their car,but individually we'd rather not smog test our own car.

Or we think about overfishing.

We'd rather everybody else cut back with fishing,but individually we'd rather fish as much as we could.

So individually we have incentives to defect or do what's in our own best interest,but collectively we'd like everybody to come together and do what's best for the collective.

So those are social dilemmas.

How do we solve those?

And we can think about the prisoner's dilemma as the first case.

That is,this is the fruit fly of the social dilemma problem.

Now,in the classic prisoner's dilemma,we have two people.

So,you can think about Detective Frank's case.

You'd like to get a confession,and if they confess,it's going to be easier for the whole legal process to go forward,but individually for that potential criminal,it's not great for them individually to confess.

Now,imagine you've caught two people,they could tattle on each other and confess,or they could not confess.

And here I'm thinking about cooperation with each other.

So,imagine these two criminals like to cooperate.

They'd like to cooperate with each other and not confess.

So,if they don't confess,then they both end up with a light sentence.

There isn't a lot of evidence.

They can't be prosecuted for that much.

So,they both get a very light sentence,say six months.

Now,if they both do confess,they both get five years.

So,clearly,they're better off if they both cooperate with each other and don't confess.

Now,here's what's interesting:if one of them defects,so one of them cooperates with the defense and spills the beans about the whole story,and the other one doesn't,well,imagine a detective here who says,look,I'm going to give you a special deal.

If you spill the beans,another one doesn't,you're going to go free,but the other person's going to get 10 years.

So,individually here,the person who's facing this problem really has a dilemma.

They could try to do what's best for that group,the collective,and cooperate,or they could defect and do what's best for themselves,in which case they end up with a better outcome.

Now,in this case,they always end up with a better outcome no matter what their counterpart does.

So,if their counterpart is going to talk,they'd rather talk.

If their counterpart's not going to talk,they're still better off talking.

So,individually,they still have this drive to do what's in their best interest,their own selfish interest.But we want to push people to cooperate,even though it's costly for them.

So,we want to think about how do we do that?

How do we get a coworker to stay late,take up an extra assignment?

How do we get our kids to do more chores around the house?

How do we get our spouse to help us out more,even when they'd rather hang out on the couch,watch TV,or do something else?

So,we have this constant problem,both at work and at home,to try to get people to cooperate,even when they're pulled in the opposite direction with their own self-interest.And we can think about a lot of social dilemmas.

So,I talked about greenhouse gases before.

And overfishing,but we want to try to conserve water.

We want everybody to take shorter showers,but ourselves we'd like to take that longer shower,or contributing to things like public radio,but working on a project.

And in many negotiation settings,we could share more information,which helps to create value,but it might be at odds with our own individual interest in trying to claim value.

So we have this tension.

Now,as a manager,managers are constantly trying to solve this social dilemma.

They're trying to get people to cooperate when people might naturally be pulled in opposite directions.

Here are some ideas.

Here's things that facilitate cooperation.

First,we want to build relationships.

So the more people identify with us,the better.

Sociologists call this the shadow of the past.So if we have team bonding experiences,we have a shared history,that'll bind us together and it'll create a sense of we're all in this together.

We have a shared goal here,and that shared goal gets people to cooperate more effectively.

It's related to this idea of a shared identity.

So do I see myself as part of this group?

So the names that we call each other.

So are we partners?

Are we employees?

Do I think of myself,do I wear logoed clothing that has my company name on it?

Do I see myself as part of this organization?

And the stronger that sense of identity,the stronger cooperation is.

And then,third,sociologists have this term shadow of the future for how likely we are to interact in the future.

So if I know this is a long-term relationship,then helping you out now is a much easier thing to do because I know there's going to be a time in the future that you might help me out as well.

So the longer the future horizon is,the more likely we are to get cooperation.

So the past,identity,and the shadow of the future.

A couple of other things that are important for cooperation.

One is clear communication.

So can I communicate what I need and why I need it clearly?

And can we figure out a way to collaborate?

So the better the communication,the more effective the cooperation.

And this is going to mean that face-to-face communication is particularly important.

Face-to-face communication is important for a lot of different reasons that we'll talk about.

But one is it allows the most complete kind of communication we can get.

And then next,we can think about expectations.

So what expectations do we have in this?

Am I communicating that I really care about my own self-interest?

Or am I communicating we're all in this together?

People have actually played the Prison Dilemma game with experiments for money or other prizes.

And what they found is that when you describe the game as a community game,people are far more cooperative than if people have described it as the Wall Street game.

In the Wall Street game,people put on this lens or mentality that they're in it for themselves and end up being much more competitive.

So the way we describe things,the expectations that we set,profoundly influence how cooperative people are.

They're trying to figure out what game are we playing,and the way we communicate is going to profoundly influence that.

Next,to think about accountability.

So can we observe behavior?

So I talked about saving water.

Now,people are more likely to cut back on watering their lawn because their neighbors can see that.

Taking a shorter shower is harder to observe.

When we can't observe people cooperating or defecting,people are more likely to defect.

And anonymity hurts cooperation.

And things like rating systems,which makes Airbnb effective,help cooperation.

And then more broadly,trust.If we can build a trusting relationship,then we get cooperation.

And we'll say a bit more about trust.So here are the key ideas.

Shadow of the past,what we've done in the past.A shared identity.

I identify myself with this group.

A shadow of the future,this future interaction we're going to have.

Effective and clear communication.

We set expectations for cooperation.

We hold people accountable.

That means we can observe what they do and the repercussions for what they do.

You can think about taxes,for example.

We sometimes audit people's taxes and their penalties for not paying taxes.

It's a way to get people to cooperate for the collective good,even though individually they'd rather not.

And then trust.The more trusting our relationships,the more effective cooperation is.

2-02-01.02_建立信任：展现脆弱

我们常常认为，一旦我们信任某人，我们就可以变得脆弱，但事实证明，变得脆弱实际上是建立信任的一个关键因素。我将从一个例子开始，这个人不被信任，而且她的信任很难建立。

这里说的是伊丽莎白·佩特拉基斯，就在她婚礼的前几天，她被要求签署一份婚前协议。

她的丈夫拥有大量房地产，而根据这份婚前协议，她保证在他们婚姻存续期间，每年能得到两万五千美元。

用她的话说，这份婚前协议是她心中的一根刺，这也是导致她离婚的原因之一。

所以在这里，婚前协议表现出低信任度，这代表着缺乏脆弱性，而这正是建立信任的障碍。事实证明，我们实际上可以让自己变得更加脆弱，当我们这样做的时候，我们最终反而能够建立信任。

我们可以做到这一点的一个方法是通过出丑。

通过做一些像打翻咖啡或掉笔之类的事情，我们犯的错误会让我们看起来更温暖、更平易近人。

现在，我们必须在这方面和能力之间取得平衡。

那么问题来了。

你更信任谁？

是打翻咖啡的人，还是没打翻咖啡的人？

我们可能会想，嘿，我为什么要信任一个表现出能力较低的人呢？

但事实证明，通过打翻咖啡，我们展现出一种人性、一种谦逊、一种脆弱，这可以让我们更讨人喜欢。

事实上，这正是几十年前做的一项研究，研究对象是为知识竞赛做准备的学生。

这里有一个重要的转折。结果发现，那些表现出高能力，答对了问题，然后打翻咖啡的人，是最受欢迎的。

如果你能力不是很强，那么打翻咖啡就没什么帮助了。

事实证明，精神科医生面临的正是这个问题。

他们需要在非常短的时间内走进一个房间，赢得某人的信任，让对方吐露内心最深处的秘密。

而要让对方吐露内心最深处的秘密，事实证明，如果他们在开始时打翻咖啡、掉笔或讲一个糟糕的笑话，会有所帮助。

这种展示温暖的做法正是人们试图去做的，无论是奥巴马养狗，罗恩·克莱恩谈论他的儿子，还是我们其他人犯些错误或做些自我表露。

现在，脆弱不仅仅在于分享失败，也可以通过像唱跑调这样的事情来实现，就像我们唱卡拉OK那样，或者和别人一起喝酒。

让自己在他人面前变得更加脆弱。

现在，我要在一个更严肃的背景下谈谈喝酒。

在这里，我们要把我们带到波斯尼亚战争，当时米洛舍维奇正处于战争之中，而美国非常努力地试图谈判达成和平。

于是，他们把主要人物拉到俄亥俄州的代顿，米洛舍维奇面对的是有史以来最伟大的谈判者之一，理查德·霍尔布鲁克。

霍尔布鲁克进行了谈判，他们花了数周时间进行谈判，一直到深夜。

他们喝着苏格兰威士忌，事实上，他们在研究地图时喝了非常多的苏格兰威士忌，以至于在划分前南斯拉夫时，他们最终将其中一条走廊命名为苏格兰路。

后来，他们宣布，我们找到了我们的路，苏格兰路，并在凌晨两点宣布达成协议。

事实证明，这种酒精，这种脆弱，帮助他们弥合了分歧，赢得了信任，达成了协议，但这也是有代价的。

这里的米洛舍维奇并没有全面考虑所有后果，此后不久，他最终被引渡到海牙，并因战争罪被起诉。

所以，当我们考虑建立信任时，脆弱实际上非常重要。

通过犯下像打翻咖啡或掉笔这样的错误，我们展现出那种脆弱，但我们也可以通过自我表露或承认失败来做到这一点。

但这里有一个风险，当我们展现出脆弱时，我们可能会像米洛舍维奇那样，没有考虑到所有我们应该考虑到的不同后果。

或者，你要确保展现脆弱或自我表露的方式，不会损害你的可信度。

所以，精神科医生可以掉笔并说，我的手一直不太灵巧，但外科医生不能这么说。

英文原文

We often think that once we trust somebody,we can become vulnerable,but it turns out that becoming vulnerable is one key ingredient for actually building trust.And I'll start off with an example of somebody that wasn't trusted and whose trust was hard to build.

Here,Elizabeth Petrakis,just days before her wedding,was asked to sign a prenuptial agreement.

And her husband had a large real estate holding,and she was guaranteed in this prenuptial agreement$25000 a year for every year they were married.

Now,in her words,this prenuptial agreement was a thorn in her side,and this is one of the things that led to her divorce.

So here,prenuptials demonstrate low trust,and that represents a lack of vulnerability,and that's an impediment to building trust.It turns out we can actually make ourselves more vulnerable,and when we do that,we can actually end up building trust.

And one way that we can do this is through Pratfalls.

By doing things like spilling coffee or spilling pens,we make mistakes that make us seem warmer,more approachable.

Now,we have to balance that with competence.

So here's a question.

Who do you trust more?

Someone who spills coffee or someone who doesn't spill coffee?

Now,we might think,hey,why would I trust somebody who's demonstrated lower competence?

But it turns out that by spilling coffee,we demonstrate a humanity,a humility,a vulnerability that can make us more likable.

And in fact,this is exactly the study that was done a couple of decades ago with students preparing for a quiz bowl competition.

And here's the important twist.It turns out the person who's demonstrated high competence,who gets these questions right,and then spills coffee,is the most liked.

If you're not very competent,then spilling coffee doesn't really help.

Now,it turns out this exact problem is the one that psychiatrists face.

In a very short period of time,they need to walk into a room and gain the trust of someone to spill their innermost secrets.

Now,to spill those innermost secrets,it turns out it helps if they spill coffee or spill their pens or tell a bad joke at the beginning.

And this demonstration of warmth is exactly what people are trying to do where whether it's Obama getting a dog,Ron Klein talking about his son,or the rest of us making some mistake or disclosure.

Now,vulnerability is not just about sharing failures,but it can also be done doing things like off-key singing,as we might do in karaoke,or drinking with people.

Making ourselves more vulnerable to others.

Now,I'll talk about drinking in a much more serious context.

And here,we're going to take us to the Bosnia War,where Milosevic was in the midst of a war,and the US worked very hard to try to negotiate a peace.

Now,here they pulled the lead people out to Dayton,Ohio,and Milosevic faced off one of the great negotiators of all time,Richard Holbrook.

So,Holbrook negotiated and they spent weeks negotiating,and it was late into the night.

They were drinking scotch,and in fact,they drank so much scotch as they're looking through maps,they ended up naming one of the corridors Scotch Road as they partitioned the former Yugoslavia.

Now,they announced that here we found our road,Scotch Road,and at two in the morning,they announced a deal.

It turns out this alcohol,this vulnerability,helped them bridge that gap,gain trust to reach a deal,but there's a downside.

Milosevic here wasn't thinking through the full range of consequences,and shortly after this,he ends up getting pulled to The Hague and prosecuted for warm crimes.

So,when we think about building trust,vulnerability is actually really important.

By making mistakes like spilling coffee or spilling pens,we demonstrate that vulnerability,but we can do it by self-disclosure or admitting failures.

But there's a risk that when we demonstrate vulnerability,we could,like Milosevic,not think through all of the different consequences we should be thinking about.

Or you want to think about making sure you don't demonstrate vulnerability or self-disclosure in a way that harms your credibility.

So,a psychiatrist can spill pens and say,I've never been very good with my hands,but a surgeon can't.

2-02-01.03_建立信任：融洽、温暖与平等

接下来我想谈谈有助于建立信任的其他三个关键问题：融洽关系、热情和平等。

现在，回顾一下之前提到的凶杀案侦探马歇尔·弗兰克。

当时，马歇尔·弗兰克面临这个挑战。

他试图让保罗·罗尔斯承认谋杀。

当然，保罗·罗尔斯肯定知道，如果承认谋杀，肯定要在监狱里待很长时间。

然而，侦探马歇尔·弗兰克却设法在三十分钟内拿到了供词。

他是怎么做到的？

嗯，事实证明，他成功的关键在于建立了融洽关系。

他通过许多不同的步骤建立了这种融洽关系，其中一些步骤看起来有点意思。

他基本上把这位谋杀犯当成了朋友来对待。

他坐得离他很近。

事实上，他坐得如此之近，以至于他们的腿几乎要碰到了。

他和对方说话时会身体前倾。

在那三十分钟的大部分时间里，他没有谈论谋杀犯或受害者，而是谈论家庭、日常生活。

弗兰克侦探说，我和他交了朋友。

也就是说，他是在交朋友。

他谈论的是朋友们会谈论的话题。

所以，我们把这看作是与任务无关的沟通。

也就是说，他没有直接切入正题，而是像朋友一样闲聊各种事情，这让他能够建立这种融洽关系，建立一种友谊感，从而产生信任感，最终让罗尔斯透露了所有这些信息。

所以，是以一种合作的方式行事，一种弗兰克侦探所期望的方式。

那么，一般来说，我们如何做到这一点呢？

嗯，我们通过这种与任务无关的沟通来建立融洽关系。

所以，与其直接谈正事，我们应该和人们聊聊当地的活动，问问他们的家庭、朋友、爱好、最近的体育赛事。

我们做一些与手头任务无关的事情，但这有助于建立融洽关系，使得当我们真正开始处理手头任务时，事情会变得容易得多。

我们也可以做一些事情，比如一起吃饭。

我们实际上可以一起参加活动，比如一起看体育比赛。

当我们一起做事时，这能让我们建立这种融洽感，而这确实有助于促进信任。现在，让我告诉你另一个故事。

这是关于一场选举的。

它发生在佛罗里达州的第二十二选区，故事是这样的。

罗恩·克莱因，一个政坛新手。

他要挑战克莱·肖，一位连任十三次的在任者。

在这场选举中，罗恩·克莱因对自己的东西很在行。

他是个政策专家。

他深知其中细节，并已为国会的到来做好了准备。

但克莱·肖是一位formidable的对手。

毕竟，他之前已经赢得过十几次选举。

他已准备好迎接所有挑战者。

但罗恩·克莱因很坚持。

然而，事实证明，罗恩·克莱因面临着一个挑战。

他被认为有能力，但很冷漠。

我们来想想人们对别人的这些看法。

我们经常根据他们的能力和热情程度来评判他们。

而在这里，罗恩·克莱因在谈论政策时，显得很有能力，但并不热情。

他没有与选民建立联系。

于是，他请来了这些顾问，并想出了如何克服这个关键挑战。

那么，他怎样才能既口齿清晰，又显得热情呢？

之前，人们觉得他很高冷。

他和这些顾问实际做了一次电视采访的练习。

他完整地完成了整个练习采访。

最后，顾问说，好的，我想让你看一遍你刚才做的采访，告诉我你会有什么不同的做法。

他说，嗯，其实还有一个要点我本可以提出来。

还有一些其他材料我本可以在这里引用。科恩说，听着，我想让你再看一遍。

我想让你看看，在整个采访过程中，你一次都没有笑。

这听起来有点意思。

为什么我们会希望一个政策专家笑呢？

但事实证明，如果你竞选公职，人们需要一种连接感。

他们需要信任你。

于是，他们发现，克莱因真正神采飞扬的时候，是在他谈论自己儿子的时候，谈论自己家庭的时候。

他们告诉他，听着，当你去发表竞选演说时，先从谈论你的家庭开始，先从谈论你的儿子开始，然后再转向谈论关键的政策问题。

结果，当他这样做的时候，他就能与选民建立联系。

他既展现了能力，也展现了热情，他变得更讨人喜欢，也更容易获得信任。

所以，有时我们需要做一些不同于仅仅展示纯粹能力的事情，来灌输信任。

事实上，我认为这是一种总统惯例，想想看，自艾森豪威尔以来，自从电视出现以来，每一位美国总统，当他们入主椭圆形办公室时，都会带一只狗。

这个惯例如此强大，甚至对从未养过狗的奥巴马总统也是如此。

而且理由很充分，他的一个女儿玛利亚对狗过敏。

然而，当他们搬进白宫时，奥巴马一家还是出去买了一只狗，一只低敏的狗，但他们需要一只狗。

所以你想这有多重要，你知道，为什么需要一只狗呢？

这里的关键是它能传递热情。

如果你赢得了全国大选，你已经展示了一定的能力。

这很难做到。

然后一个关键的挑战就是传递热情。

当你看到一位总统，一个位高权重的人，你会推定他有能力，然后你就在寻找那种热情，而养狗就能起到这个作用。

所以你会想做一些事情，比如花时间和家人在一起，分享故事，个人故事，和狗待在一起。

这些都是能传递热情感的事情，它们最终能建立信任。所以克莱因谈论他的儿子，总统们最终会养狗。

现在，这种与任务无关的沟通非常重要。

我们有共同的经历，比如一起去看体育比赛或一起吃饭，正确地称呼名字。

这些都是能建立融洽关系的事情。

如果我们有绰号，或者我们有共同的爱好，我们找到了共同点。

这些都能建立融洽关系，而这确实是建立信任的一个基本要素。

以上就是关于融洽关系的观点。

它与热情有关。

这个观点是，当我们表现出对他人的关心时，表现出善意时，花时间与朋友、家人、宠物在一起，或者做志愿者时，我们就能展示出热情。

我们在展示对他人的关心。

而这种关心会传递出一种热情感。

这是一个非常关键的组成部分。

信任包含着情感的部分，我们希望对方是热情的。

现在，与此相关的最后一点是平等的观念。

当我们准时出现时，我们是在表明我们的时间并不比别人的时间更有价值。

这传达了一种平等感，以及仁慈和热情的观念。

我们想要平等，所以我们不会坐在更高的椅子上。

我们不会强调我们之间的差异。

我们可以做一些事情，比如穿得相似。

我们传达一种平等感，这对建立信任也很重要。我们更有可能信任那些看起来不仅关心我们，而且把我们当作平等伙伴的人。

综上所述，这里有三个关键要素：建立融洽关系、展现热情和展现平等感，它们都是建立信任的关键要素。

I next want to think about three other key issues that help us build trust.Rapport,warmth,and equality.

Now,remember back to homicide detective Marshall Frank.

Now,Marshall Frank faced this challenge.

He was trying to get Paul Rawls to confess to murder.

Now,Paul Rolls certainly knew if you confess to murder,you're going to prison for a long time,for sure.

And yet,Detective Marshall Frank figured out how to get a confession within 30 minutes.

How did he do that?

Well,it turns out that the key to what he did was building rapport.

And he built rapport through a lot of different steps,and some of them seem kind of funny.

He essentially treated this murderer as if he were a friend.

He sat in close to him.

In fact,he sat in so close their legs were almost touching.

He leaned in when he talked to them.

He spent most of those 30 minutes not talking about the murderer or the victim,but talking about family,life in general.

Detective Frank talks about,I made friends with him.

That is,he's making friends.

He's talking about things that friends would talk about.

So,we think about this as non-task communication.

That is,rather than getting right down to business,he's chit-chatting about things as if they were friends,and that allowed him to build this rapport,to build a sense of friendship,that created a sense of trust that then led to Rawls revealing all of this information.

So,acting in a cooperative way,in a way that Detective Frank was hoping for.

Now,in general,how do we do this?

Well,we build rapport by this non-task communication.

So rather than getting right down to business,we should talk with people about local events,ask them about their family,their friends,hobbies,recent sporting events.

We do things that aren't about the task at hand,but that help build rapport that make it much easier when we do get to the task at hand.

We could also do things like share meals together.

We can actually go to events together,like sporting events together.

When we do things together,that allows us to build this sense of rapport,and that really facilitates trust.Now,let me tell you about another story.

This was about an election.

It happened in Florida's 22nd District,and it was right.

Ron Klein,a neophyte to the political scene.

He was taking on Clay Shaw,a 13-time incumbent.

Now,in this election,Ron Klein knew his stuff.

He was a policy wonk.

He knew the ins and outs,and he was ready for Congress.

But Clay Shaw was a formidable opponent.

After all,he had won over a dozen elections before.

He was ready to take on all challengers.

But Ron Klein was persistent.

It turns out,though,Ron Klein had a challenge.

He was perceived as competent,but cold.

And we think about these perceptions of people.

We often think about them in terms of their competence and how warm they are.

And here,Ron Klein,when he talked about policy,seemed competent,but he wasn't warm.

He wasn't connecting with voters.

Now,he brought in these consultants and he figured out how to overcome this key challenge.

So,how can he sound articulate but also warm?

So,people saw him as aloof.

He actually did a practice TV interview with these consultants.

He went through the entire practice interview.

And at the end,the consultant said,Okay,I want you to watch this interview that you just gave and tell me what would you do differently.

He said,Well,there's actually another point that I would have raised.

There's some other material I could have brought in here.And Cohen said,Look,I want you to watch it again.

And I want you to see that in this whole interview,you never smiled.

Now,it seems funny.

Why would we want somebody who's an expert in policy to smile?

But it turns out if you're running for political office,people need a connection.

They need to trust you.

And so,what they figured out is that what Klein really lit up with was when he talked about his son,when he talked about his family.

And they said,Look,when you go out on your political stump speeches,start off talking about your family,start off talking about your son,and then pivot to talking about the key issues in policy.

And it turns out as he did that,he was able to connect with voters.

He demonstrated warmth as well as competence,and he was more likable and trusted.

So,we need to do things sometimes that are different from just demonstrating pure competence to instill trust.

In fact,I think about this as a presidential imperative,where we think about every president since Eisenhower,since the advent of television,every U.S.president,as they've moved into the Oval Office,bring with them a dog.

And this imperative is so strong,it's true even for President Obama,who had never had a dog.

And for good reason,one of his daughters,Malia,is allergic to dogs.

And yet,when they move into the White House,the Obamas went out and bought a dog,a hypoallergenic dog,but they needed a dog.

And so you think about how important it is,you know,why would you need a dog?

And the key idea here is it projects warmth.

If you've won a national election,you've demonstrated some competence.

It's hard to do.

And then a key challenge is projecting warmth.

And when you see a president,a high-power person,you presume competence,and then you're looking for that warmth,and having a dog does that.

So you want to do things like spending time with family,sharing stories,personal stories,hanging around with a dog.

Those are things that project a sense of warmth,and they end up building trust.So Klein talked about his son,presidents end up getting dogs.

Now,it's this non-task communication that's really important.

We have experiences that we share in common,like going to sporting events or sharing meals together,using first names correctly.

Those are things that will build rapport.

If we come up with nicknames or we have shared hobbies,we find commonalities.

Those are things that are going to build rapport,and that's really an essential ingredient for building trust.

So that's the rapport idea.

And it's related to warmth.

The idea that we can demonstrate warmth when we demonstrate concern for other people,we demonstrate kindness,we spend time with our friends,our family,with pets,or volunteering.

We're demonstrating concern for other people.

And that concern projects a sense of warmth.

And that's a really key component.

There's an affective piece,an emotional piece to trust,and we want somebody who's going to be warm.

Now,one final point related to this is this idea of equality.

Now,when we show up on time,we're demonstrating that our time isn't more valuable than somebody else's time.

That's communicating a sense of equality,as well as this idea of benevolence and warmth.

We want to be equal,so we don't sit on a higher chair.

We don't accentuate differences between us.

We can do things like dress in similar ways.

We convey a sense of equality,and that's also important for building trust.We're more likely to trust people who seem to not only care about us,but also treat us as equal partners.

So taken together,here are three key elements:building rapport,demonstrating warmth,and demonstrating a Sense of equality,they're all key ingredients for building trust.

2-02-01.04_建立信任：相互依存、共同目标与共同敌人

共同目标对建立信任有着深远的影响。其中一部分原因来自相互依赖。

当我们相互依赖时，最终会建立起信任。塔耶费尔在20世纪70年代发现了一个有趣的现象，即使是名义上的群体，在这些实验中，仅仅将人们分到蓝队或红队，并称呼他们为红队或蓝队，就足以让人们偏袒自己的群体，对自己群体成员的信任超过了对我们群体成员的信任。

其深刻之处在于：如果我们在名义群体中都能看到这种现象，也就是说，你加入红队才五分钟，这个标签没有任何实际意义，那么你可以想象，当我们用部落、宗教或国家来划分时，这意味着什么。

也就是说，我们所属的群体深刻影响着我们对待群体内和群体外成员的方式。

塔亚·科恩做过一些很棒的研究，探讨了群体内的忠诚度，她发现，我们对自己群体成员越忠诚，就越能接受针对他人的战争和暴力。

所以，我们如何思考、如何界定“我们的群体”和“别人的群体”，这其中有着深刻的内涵。

现在，能够影响我们思考群体归属感的一个因素是共同的敌人。

当我们拥有共同目标时，它们会将我们凝聚在一起，而没有什么比共同的敌人更能起到这种凝聚作用了。

我们看到，911事件之后，巴基斯坦和美国的关系变得紧密得多。

以前协调得不太好的国家，之后在安全问题上开始进行极其密切的合作。

而且不仅仅是这两个国家。

想想俄罗斯和法国在中东遭遇袭击后，它们的互动方式发生了怎样的改变。

我们在现代政治中看到了这一点，但在过去很长一段时间里也是如此。例如，我们看到，美利坚合众国的形成就深受这种群体意识的影响，最初在法国-印第安人战争中，英国人与法国人作战，英国人利用殖民地居民来对抗法国人。

这是殖民地居民第一次真正地协同行动。

英国人最终训练了所有殖民地居民，其中包括一个名叫乔治·华盛顿的人。

而在这里，乔治·华盛顿实际上是和法国人作战的。

仅仅几年后，情况就完全改变了。在美国独立战争中，乔治·华盛顿再次将殖民地居民作为一个集体来使用，那群殖民地居民，他们正在与英国人作战，而谁帮助了他们呢？

嗯，法国人立刻加入了进来，因为他们非常渴望与英国人作战。

所以我们看到了这种竞争态势的转变，群体在变化，群体间的联盟也在变化。

这里的一个深刻见解是，共同的敌人可以帮助我们找到更高层次的目标，而这些更高层次的目标正是把我们团结在一起的动力。

所以，当我们能够想到与某个外部竞争者竞争时，某个外部敌人，或者当我们想到需要共同应对的事情时，比如为我们的组织解决一个问题，或者共同解决一个环境问题，这些更高层次的目标对于帮助我们建立信任至关重要。总而言之，我想回顾一下信任的基石。

在整个模块中，我们讨论了热情和能力。

我们要展现高度的热情和高度的能力。

但同时我们也要考虑展现脆弱性。

如果我们已经展现了能力，那么展现脆弱性可以帮助我们展现热情。

沟通过程非常重要，而且我们可以信任制度，在某些情况下，制度可以替代对个人的信任。

例如，即使我们不太信任某个人，我们也可以信任我们签署的合同。

声誉帮助我们解决了很多关键问题。我们过去认为流言蜚语是建立声誉的一种工具，但现在我们认为在线声誉极其重要。

而我们拥有的共同目标将我们紧密联系在一起，并帮助我们建立信任。

英文原文

Common goals play a profound influence in building trust.Part of this comes from interdependence.

When we rely on each other,we end up building trust.Now,there's something interesting that Tajfeld found in the 1970s,where just even nominal groups,in these experiments,assigning people to a blue group or a red group and just calling them red or blue caused people to favor their group,

trusting their group members more than they trusted our group members.

Here's what's profound.If we do this with nominal groups,that is,you've only been part of the red group for five minutes and it doesn't have any particular meaning,you could imagine what it means when we think about things in terms of a tribe,a religion,or a country.

That is,the groups that we're in profoundly influence how we treat both the in-group and the people outside of our group.

Some great work that Taya Cohen has done looked at loyalty within groups and found the more loyal we are to our group members,the more we're accepting of warfare and violence against others.

So there's something profound about how we think about and how we identify what is our group and what is somebody else's group.

Now,one thing that can influence how we think about our group membership are our common enemies.

And when we have common goals,they bind us together,and there's nothing quite as profound as a common enemy in doing that.

We saw after 9-11,Pakistan and the United States grow far closer.

Countries that hadn't been well aligned before began to coordinate incredibly closely on security issues afterwards.

And it's not just these two countries.

You think about Russia and France after attacks in the Middle East,how they changed their dynamics.

And we see this in modern politics,but the same has been true for a long period of time in the past.So we saw,for example,the formation of the United States was profoundly influenced by this sense of group,where initially in the French-Indian War,the British were fighting against the French,

and the British used the colonists to fight against the French.

This is the first time the colonists had actually acted together and in concert.

And the British end up training all the colonists,including somebody named George Washington.

And here,George Washington actually fought against the French.

The dynamics completely changed just a couple years later,when it was in the American Revolutionary War,George Washington again used the Colonists as a collective,that group of colonists,they're fighting against the British,and who helped them?

Well,the French jumped right in because the French were so eager to now fight the British.

So we see these shifting sands of competition where we think about the groups and these shifting alliances between groups.

And one of the profound ideas here is that common enemies can help us find superordinate goals,and these superordinate goals are what drive us together.

So when we can think about competing with some other outside competitor,some other outside enemy,or if we think about something that we need to tackle together,like solving a problem for our organization or solving an environmental issue together,those superordinate goals turn out to be incredibly important in helping us build trust.In summary,I want to think about the building blocks for trust.

And so across this module,we've thought about warmth and competence.

We want to demonstrate high warmth and high competence.

But we also want to think about vulnerability.

If we've demonstrated competence,vulnerability can help us demonstrate warmth.

The communication process is very important,and we can have trust in institutions that can,in some cases,substitute for trust in individuals.

So,for example,we might trust a contract we signed even if we don't trust the person as much.

And reputations have helped us solve a lot of our key problems.We used to think about gossip as a tool for building reputations,but now we think of online reputations being incredibly important.

And then the common goals we have bond us together and help us build trust.

2-02-01.05_建立信任：沟通与制度

接下来，我想谈谈在建立信任过程中的沟通和制度。在沟通方面，其中一个关键思想是确保我们的言语与行动相符。

我想告诉你们一个关于2008年的故事，当时美国三大汽车制造商来到华盛顿特区，请求联邦贷款。

他们要求获得250亿美元的贷款，但后来曝出，这三家公司的首席执行官，也就是来到华盛顿特区的这三位，都是各自乘坐公司的专机来的。

嗯，这是他们通常的出行方式。

这似乎显得很不协调，他们一边说迫切需要资金，一边却又各自乘坐私人飞机前来。

所以，当他们第二次来的时候，他们都改乘混合动力汽车了。

你需要考虑你的言语如何与行动相匹配，以达到最大的信任效果。关于沟通的另一个关键思想是，你要以平等的姿态进行沟通。

以平等的姿态沟通，这意味着我们要准时出现。

也就是说，我们不是在暗示自己的时间比别人更重要。

我们可以尽量减少其他差异，比如座位、衣着等方面的差异。

所以语言很重要，不仅在于我们如何沟通，也在于我们使用的词语。

瓦尔达·利伯曼做过一项研究，研究的是同样的经济激励措施，但分别称之为“社区游戏”和“华尔街游戏”。

结果发现，在同样的激励下，人们在“社区游戏”中的合作程度远高于“华尔街游戏”。

当我们称某人为“伙伴”而不是“对手”，当我们称一名员工为“团队成员”而不是“雇员”时，你触发的是一种不同的思维模式，而这种思维模式会改变我们彼此相处的方式。

这不仅仅体现在语言上。

我之前谈到了行动，这体现在我们如何就坐上。

所以，当我们一起坐在桌子的同一边时，这种座位安排，意味着我们是在共同解决问题，传递出我们正在合作的信息。

而这有助于建立信任。这不仅体现在沟通上，想想制度。

我们可以信任其他人，但我们也可以信任像法院系统这样的制度。

而我们信任法院系统的方式会产生深远的影响。

我们通常对制度怀有敬畏之心，但这在世界范围内并非普遍共识。

我想给你们讲一个关于阿尔顿·洛根的故事。

我这里放了一张安德鲁·威尔逊的照片，想说明他们俩，你得想象一下二十年前，他们长得很像。

事情是这样的，1982年，芝加哥一家麦当劳餐厅发生了一起枪击案。

现场非常混乱，并且有目击证人。

根据证词，这些证词足以给阿尔顿·洛根定罪。

但有一个问题。

阿尔顿·洛根当时根本不在现场。

他和那起枪击案毫无关系。

凶手是安德鲁·威尔逊。

更糟糕的是，为安德鲁·威尔逊辩护的律师，因为另一起案件为他辩护，而他实际上还犯下了其他谋杀案。

安德鲁·威尔逊向他的律师承认，麦当劳的那起谋杀是他干的。

与此同时，阿尔顿·洛根被定罪并继续在监狱服刑。

律师们恳求安德鲁·威尔逊坦白。

毕竟，他已经因谋杀罪被判刑了。

难道他就不能也承认那起罪行吗？

他们知道，阿尔顿·洛根是被冤枉入狱的。

然而，这里有个问题。

在美国，我们有律师-当事人保密特权。

律师不能单方面披露这些信息，这些会对其当事人不利的信息，这些是在保密情况下披露的信息。

这个原则很重要，因为为了获得最佳的辩护，我们需要确保罪犯或嫌疑人能够向他们的律师披露信息，而不必担心这些信息会被用来对付他们。

所以这是一个重要的原则。

事实证明，正是这个原则指导了律师们的行为。

他们实际上写了一份宣誓书，但把它封存了起来，藏了起来，而阿尔顿·洛根则在监狱里度过了26年。

直到安德鲁·威尔逊在狱中去世后，他们才站出来披露了这些信息，阿尔顿·洛根最终才重获自由。

这个故事最令人惊叹的部分在于。

他的姑姑在迎接他时，说他们做了他们必须做的事，表现出对这种制度令人难以置信的尊重。

现在，我还想从其他方面来思考制度。

这里有一个有趣的制度：那就是闲言碎语这种非正式制度。

这是一个放在教堂前的广告牌，上面写着：如果你的朋友对你说别人的闲话，你就知道他们也会对别人说你的闲话。

现在，我们认为闲言碎语名声不好。

闲言碎语当然有一些非常负面的特点，但它也有其他作用。

它帮助我们沟通什么是规范，什么是预期的行为。

它传递着关于声誉的信息。

闲言碎语不是什么好东西，但它实际上以一种比我们通常意识到的更深刻的方式，帮助我们约束行为。

我们现在已经开始用评分系统将其正规化了。所以，如果我问你这个问题，你会让一个完全陌生的人睡在你家吗？

而答案竟然是响亮的“会”。

我们已经通过评分系统解决了这个问题。如果你去看看爱彼迎的网站，他们有一个专门讨论信任的网页。

在他们的所有资料中，他们始终如一地谈论信任。他们发现，事实上，人们是非常值得信赖的。

而评分系统则带来了巨大的改变。

其他关键问题也是如此，比如，你会让你的孩子和一个你不认识的人同坐一辆车吗？

这里的答案同样是“会”。

优步也再次通过评分系统解决了这个问题，帮助我们信任其他人。

e Bay和其他电子商务网站也是如此，它们已经发现，声誉可以有效地帮助我们解决信任问题。

I next want to think about communication and institutions as we build trust.When it comes to communication,one of the key ideas is to make sure our words match our deeds.

I want to tell you a story about 2008 when the three big American car manufacturers came to Washington,D.C.asking for federal loans.

They were asking for$25 billion in loans,and it came out that all three of them,the three CEOs who came to DC,had all flown on separate corporate jets.

Now,this is how they usually traveled.

It just seemed incongruous to say we desperately need money when they'd flown separately on their private jets.

And so the next time they came for their second trip,they went in hybrid vehicles.

You want to think about how your words match your deeds to affect the most trust.Another key idea about communication is you want to communicate as equals.

And by communicating as equals,what that means is that we show up on time.

That is,we're not signaling that our time is more important than somebody else's.

And we can minimize other differences like in the seating,in the clothing,and so on.

So language matters,not just in how we communicate,but the terms that we use.

There was a study that was done that Varda Lieberman did looking at the same economic incentives,but calling it the community game versus the Wall Street game.

It turns out with the same incentives,people cooperated far more in the community game than they did in the Wall Street game.

When they call somebody a partner versus an opponent,when you call an employee a team member versus an employee,you're triggering a different mindset and that mindset shifts the way we relate to each other.

It's not just in language.

I talked about deeds before,and that's manifest in how we sit.

So when we're sitting together on the same side of the table,that seating,we're tackling a problem together,communicates an idea that we're working together.

And that can help build trust.It's not just in communication,think about institutions.

So we can trust other people,but we can also trust institutions like the court system.

And the way we trust the court system has profound consequences.

We often have this reverence for institutions,but they're not universally shared throughout the world.

I want to tell you a story about Alton Logan.

And I've put up a picture here of Andrew Wilson to suggest that the two of them,and you have to imagine 20 years earlier,they looked pretty similar.

It turns out there was a shooting in 1982 in Chicago at a Mc Donald's.

It was a chaotic crime scene,and there was eyewitness.

Testimony,and that testimony was enough to convict Alton Logan.

There was one problem.

Alton Logan wasn't even there.

He had nothing to do with that shooting.

It was Andrew Wilson.

Now,making matters worse,lawyers for Andrew Wilson representing him for another crime,and he had actually committed other murders.

Andrew Wilson admitted to his attorneys that he had committed that murder in the Mc Donald's.

Meanwhile,Alton Logan was convicted and remained in prison.

The lawyers begged Andrew Wilson to come clean.

He was,after all,already convicted of murder.

Wouldn't he confess to that crime too?

Alton Logan,they knew,was wrongfully imprisoned.

However,there's a problem.

In the United States,we have attorney-client privilege.

The attorneys couldn't unilaterally disclose that information,information that would harm their client,information that was disclosed in secret.

This principle is important because to get the best representation,we need to ensure that criminals or suspects can disclose information to their lawyers without the fear of having that be used against them.

So that's an important principle.

And it turns out that principle guided the lawyers'behavior.

They actually wrote an affidavit,but they sealed it away,they hid it away,and Alton Logan was in prison for 26 years.

It was only after Andrew Wilson died in prison they came forward and disclosed that information and Alton Logan finally went free.

Here's the most amazing part about the story.

His aunt,on receiving him,said they did what they had to do,demonstrating an incredible reverence for this institution.

Now,I want to think about institutions in other ways too.

And here's a funny institution:it's the institution of gossip.

Here's a billboard that was put in front of a church that read:If your friends gossip to you,you know they also gossip about you.

Now,we think that gossip gets a bad rap.

Gossip,of course,has some very negative characteristics,but it does other things too.

It helps us communicate what the norms are,what expected behavior is.

It communicates information about reputations.

Now,gossip isn't a great thing,but it actually helps us police behavior in a more profound way than we typically acknowledge.

We've now begun to formalize that with rating systems.So,if I ask you this question,would you let a complete stranger sleep in your home?

And the answer turns out to be a resounding yes.

And we've solved that with rating systems.And if you were to look at Airbnb's website,they have a website devoted to trust.

Throughout their materials,they talk consistently about trust.And they find that people are,in fact,incredibly trustworthy.

And the rating system makes a profound difference.

And the same is true of other key questions,like would you let your kids drive in a car with someone you don't know?

And the answer here again is yes.

And Uber's figure this out again with rating systems that help us trust other people.

And this is true with e Bay and other electronic commerce sites that have figured out that reputations can be effective in helping us solve the trust problem.

2-02-01.06_信号传递与信任

我们经常要问的一个关键问题是：我们该相信某人发出的信号吗？

人们经常向我们传递信息，我们也向其他人传递信息。

我们为什么不相信别人发给我们的信息呢？

我们又该如何发出让别人信任的信息呢？

关键在于，我们必须传达一些无法直接观察到的信息。

比如，你对这段关系的承诺有多深？

或者，这个候选人对这份职业的兴趣有多大？

或者，这个候选人的智商有多高？

又或者，这个合作伙伴真的确信这个产品能成功吗？

我们都在试图做出这些判断。

我们在试图信任他人。

而我们常常不得不依赖这些不可观察特征的信号。

就拿一个人对一段关系的承诺程度来说吧。

他们可以做些什么来表明自己的承诺呢？

通常，我们会想到一些解决这个问题的东西，比如礼物。

比如有人送来一打红玫瑰。

这就是一个承诺的信号。

他们在传达“我在乎你”的信息。

我在乎这段关系。

现在，我想做的是仔细思考一下“信号”这个概念。

我将从两个关键维度来思考信号。

这里的关键是，信号可以是清晰的。

信号可以非常清晰。

同时，信号也可以是强有力的。

我所说的“强有力”，是指这种无法观察的信息试图以某种方式被传递出来。

这种方式对于某些人来说，是不是代价太高昂了？

而对另一些人来说，是不是又相对便宜？

所以，当我说我想用一打红玫瑰来表示我在乎你，这个信号是清晰的。

每个人都能明白这个意思。

但“强有力”方面又如何呢？

假设我并不真的在乎这段关系。

也许我的期望是短期的。

我还能负担得起送你一打红玫瑰吗？

我想给出的答案是，通常是可以的。

也就是说，有时候这些信号并不那么昂贵。

当我们在审视信号时，我们需要从“强有力”的角度仔细考量。

这里有一些想法。

要表明我们对关系的承诺，昂贵的礼物可以解决这个问题。

比如说，我们似乎也在人际关系中解决了这个问题。

玫瑰花不错，但珠宝更好。

而如果我们真的对一段关系非常认真，我们还有一个终极选择。

那就是钻戒。

注意这个做法巧妙之处在于，我们花了很多钱，而且还有一套约定俗成的规则，告诉我们该花多少钱。一个人赚得越多，就应该在戒指上花更多的钱。

也就是说，这个花费应该让人觉得，嗯，恰到好处地“心疼”。

它很昂贵，代价很高，但一个人的资源越多，这个代价就应该越高、越昂贵。

所以，昂贵的礼物可以帮助我们解决“该不该相信某人的意图”这个问题。

他们真的对这段关系投入了吗？

注意，真正重要的是成本，因为我们把钱花在了那些很难观察到的钻石戒指的特性上。

比如，钻石戒指的切割有多完美，未经训练的人用肉眼是很难评估的，但我们在意这些，就是因为它们的成本。现在，我们可以思考，一个人对这个职业的投入程度如何？

他们对在我的公司工作有多大的兴趣？

如果他们愿意接受无薪实习，或者愿意在研究生阶段为数不多的假期里花掉一个暑假，他们就是在为这段关系、这份职业进行投资。如果他们不是真正投入的话，这种投资代价就太高了。

注意，有时候人们会为面试做准备。

他们读五篇关于公司的文章，为面试做好了准备。

这是一个清晰的兴趣信号，但不是强有力的信号。

花时间实习才是一个强有力的信号。

或者，我们想表明自己很聪明。

我们该如何发出这个信号呢？

嗯，事实证明，有一个代价高昂的昂贵信号可以做到，那就是高等教育。

所以我们投资于教育，通过这种方式来表明我们的聪明才智。

如果我们不那么聪明，就很难去投资，去观看所有这些视频，阅读所有这些书籍，参加所有这些考试。

对某些人来说，这代价太高了；而对另一些能够负担得起并从中获益的人来说，代价相对较低。

或者，我们有多大把握这个产品会成功？

担保或保修之类的措施有助于发出这个信号。

关键在于，当我们发出信息时，应该关注清晰度。

这条信息是否传达了正确的含义？

比如你出现时，带了一打百合花给别人。

这可能就不是一个非常清晰的信息。

我们要仔细思考信息的清晰度如何。

接收信息的人能明白你的意思吗？

第二点是关于“强有力”的。

所以，当别人向我们发送信息时，他们发送的是那些，嗯，是预期的信号吗？

比如，我的一个朋友在一家公司工作。

在他入职周年纪念日那天，他收到了一篮鲜花。

这篮鲜花里附着一张纸条：我们很在意你和你对公司的投入。

我们非常重视你所做的一切。

一周后，他被解雇了。

那么，公司能负担得起发送像那篮鲜花所传递的信息吗？

我的答案是，嗯，当然可以。

即使他们并非真心实意，他们也能负担得起发送那种信息。

所以有时我们可以发送一些并不强有力的信息。

而作为接收方，我们应该检验这个信号的“强有力”程度。

所以，就指导原则而言，发送信号要清晰。

就接收方而言，我们应该相信强有力的信号。

这些信号既可以在时间上强有力，也可以在金钱上强有力。

如果某人的时间有限，比如一个首席执行官能安排的午餐约会有限，那么和你共进午餐，或者在圣诞节给你打电话，这些都占用了他有限的时间预算。

我们可以从时间和金钱两个方面来考量信号的“强有力”程度。

但这是两个关键的维度。

清晰度，尤其是在我们发送信号时；以及强有力程度，尤其是在我们接收信号时。
