Now,in this case,it's a very disturbing course of events,but I want to think about it from a threat perspective and this credibility perspective:what's going on?

That is,how are they able to effectively change international policies?

And they're able to do that by following through on a very disturbing threat.

So we can look at threats and figure out:you know,sometimes they work,sometimes they don't.

And we want to think about when they do and when they don't.

Now,here's this idea about using threats:willingness.

Are you willing to follow through?

The threat has to be credible,and you want to avoid threats that are going to hurt you more than your counterpart,but often following through on threats is very costly to you.

So it was costly to Reagan to fire all those workers and replace them.

It was costly for the home rail meatpackers to hire all new workers,at least in the short run.

But we need to make sure we have a threat that's really costly to the counterpart.

In the GM example,the threat was more costly to the other side,and that makes it effective.

We want the demands to be reasonable.

Can the other side comply with the demands?

So notice that in that hostage-taking example,the first threat was not reasonable.

It built credibility.

The second threat,though,gave a month to remove 51 people.

That was a more reasonable demand,and that ended up gaining compliance.

Okay,let's think about interests.

So,what are their interests?

What are your interests?

We want to avoid rash threats.

We want threats to come from a place of calculation where we want to gain compliance to further somebody else's interests.

So,we don't want to punish people,we want to motivate people.

So,if we can all get back to work,we'll be productive.

And here's a way to avoid some bad consequence as opposed to a bullying kind of threat,which is likely to promote reactance.

Now,still,some of the examples we talked about showed effective threats that were really bullying,but they're not a foundation for a long-term relationship.

And they're likely to motivate people to try to retaliate.

Now,we also want to think about saving face.

So,we don't want irrational threats or wimpy threats.

We want to make it easy for the other side to meet demands as if they're choosing.

Because,again,we can incite reactance.And revenge.

So we want to build respect and build credibility.

Those are the key ideas rather than just throwing out threats as a way that can actually undermine our credibility if we don't follow through or people call us on them because they're calling our bluff.

And then finally,we want to be exact when we're conveying a threat.

So we want to be very clear about if you do this,then here's what's going to happen.

So we want to set a clear deadline.

We want to be very clear about consequences.

We want to be specific.

And remember,if we don't follow through,we lose credibility.

And if we do follow through,it's often costly,at least in the short run.

So that's the idea about delivering threats.

The next idea is how we deal with threats.

So when people make threats,we should recognize that these threats push our neurological buttons.

We really crave retaliation.

That is,we want to go beat up that person that issued a threat.

This is one reason why we should be very judicious and careful when we issue threats because we're pushing somebody else's buttons and that reactance is likely to blow up back in our face.

Now,when it's happening to us,my recommendation is to avoid escalating conflict.

We want to be very careful about being just reactive,even though that might be what feels best in the moment.

Now,on the other side,we want to be very careful about conceding too quickly,because if we concede to somebody who's making threats,we're encouraging them to operate that way,and we lose power.

So,one thing we might do is ignore a threat.

In fact,this is what a lot of hostage negotiators do.

Hostage negotiators will frequently talk through a threat deadline.

So,some hostage will say,look,this is the deadline.

And right before the deadline,the negotiators will get on the phone,they'll start talking through,and they'll try to move the conversation forward somewhere and never go back to,like,you know,hey,you know,you said you were going to throw somebody off a building,you never did,haha.

They don't come back to it,but they talk through it.

So they're ignoring that threat.

And often,you know,we look at these studies,negotiators abandon their threats most of the time,77%of the time,when the threat goes unreciprocated.

As we respond to threats,we want to think about a few key things.

One is trying to figure out the motivation.

So,what's behind that threat?

It could be that the person who's issuing the threat feels like a victim.

So,they feel frustrated or offended,they feel neglected,and this threat is coming out of a desire to be.Heard.

So they feel like they can't grab attention unless they issue that threat.

If that's the motivation,it's really important.

They're calling out for attention.

They care deeply about this issue.

We want to give them careful attention.

It could be they're just being pragmatic.

So they have a really strong alternative,and this is how they're going to deal with you.

This is how they see the playing field.

And they want to gain leverage with this threat.

The third case is they're just bluffing.

This is how they have done business in the past or flex insecurity.

The threat really isn't serious.

They just found that issuing threats are a good way to gain compliance.

So we want to think about where this threat is coming from.

And we want to respond appropriately.

So if somebody is just trying to gain attention,we want to express understanding.

We want to listen.

We want to figure out what their grievances are and express understanding for their troubles.

So we want to soothe their concerns.

Now,we should also ask questions.

So how intense is this threat and how intense is their feeling about it?

And if it's a pragmatist,we can come up with creative solutions to address it.

Now,if it's somebody who's just bluffing just to gain compliance as a matter of practice,we want to label that behavior and we really want to counter it.

So we like to call it out or ignore it completely.

And sometimes when we're really stuck,what we have to do is deliver a counter threat.

Now,remember,I said this could escalate conflict,but sometimes to establish credibility,we issue a counter threat saying,look,if you do that,here's what we'll be forced to do.

But none of us wants to end up in that place.

Let's try to get somewhere else.

Or I understand that you're feeling upset.

If you take that course of action,here's the response that we're going to have to follow through with.

But let's see if we can figure out a more creative way for us both to get what we need.

So we like to remove beyond threats and really de-escalate them,but you can't just give in to every threat because we'll lose our own credibility,our own power,and that could be in the long run what's really most important.

2-04-01.09_目标的好处

目标设定其实是一种极其强大的工具。

它是激励的基础组成部分。

目标设定可以推动我们成就伟大的事情。

目标设定也可能驱使我们做出非常糟糕的事情。

但首先，我想思考一下目标设定的好处。

有超过四百项管理学研究关注了目标设定，还有数不清的研究探讨了目标设定中的行为，无论是送邮件、焊接、缝纫，还是在体育运动中的表现。

当人们拥有具体且具有挑战性的目标时，他们会加倍努力，更加坚持不懈，并且表现会更好。

这是普遍的结果，也是一个非常可靠且可重复验证的发现。

事实上，一些最具奠基性的目标设定学者曾说过，目标设定对任务绩效的积极影响是心理学文献中最可靠、最可重复的发现之一。

确实如此。

也就是说，从心理学角度看，仅仅设定一个有挑战性的目标就能提升表现。

在很大范围内，目标难度与任务表现之间的关系几乎是线性的。

也就是说，目标越难，表现越好。

这对于基于努力的任务尤其如此。

所以，对于那些只需要人们更努力一点的任务，更大的目标会激发动力，并常常提升表现。

我们也知道，目标的接近程度很重要。

因此，当人们接近目标时，你需要把目标分解成更小的部分。

比如，月底快到了，我们几乎要达到目标了，这时人们的动力特别足。

所以，接近那个目标时，人们会格外努力地工作。

你可以观察到这一点。有关于跑步者的研究。

如果你观察一场马拉松比赛，在整数时间点附近会出现很大的冲刺峰值。

人们都力争在特定时间内完赛。

目标之所以有效，是因为它们能集中我们的注意力，增加我们的努力，并提升我们的毅力。

因此，我们要想利用目标设定的好处，就需要设定清晰、具体的目标。

这些目标应该具有挑战性，但也要切合实际。

如果我们有过去的表现数据，比如之前比赛跑多快，或者这条生产线上的工人能完成多少产量，或者基于过去业绩的销售目标，我们应该把目标设定在第八十到第九十百分位的表现水平。

这样既有挑战性，又可信。

而且，如果我们能设定一系列短期目标，比如月度目标而非年度目标，我们很可能会从目标设定中获得更大的益处。

下一步涉及到对目标的承诺。

这也是目标必须切合实际的一个原因。

人们必须相信自己能够达成目标。

所以，如果他们设想目标实现的情景，把它写下来，告诉其他人——要注意，有时候如果我告诉了别人，如果我没能达成，那会很丢脸。

这会坚定我实现目标的决心。

我们还需要考虑制定一个计划。

那么，我该如何实现这个目标呢？

需要采取哪些步骤才能达到目标？

那个行动计划会帮助我们最终达成目标。

当然，清晰的反馈也很重要。

也就是说，我们要确保在整个过程中都能得到反馈。

并且要记住，当我们特别接近目标时，那才是最能够提升表现的时候。

英文原文

Goal setting turns out to be an incredibly powerful tool.

It's a fundamental part of motivation.

Goal setting can drive us to do great things.

Goal setting can also drive us to do very bad things.

But first,I want to think about the benefits of goal setting.

There are over 400 managerial studies that have looked at goal setting,and there are dozens and dozens more that have looked at behavior in goal setting,whether it's delivering mail,it's welding,it's sewing,in athletics.

When people have specific challenging goals,they increase their effort,they increase persistence,and they increase performance.

That's the general result,and it's a very robust and replicable finding.

In fact,some of the most foundational goal setting scholars have said the beneficial effects of goal setting on task performance is one of the most robust and replicable findings in the psychology literature.

And indeed,it is.

That is,psychologically,just setting a challenging goal will boost performance.

And the relationship between goal difficulty and task performance over a wide range is almost linear.

That is,the more difficult the goal,the higher the performance.

This is particularly true for effort-based tasks.

So,tasks where we just need people to work a bit harder,greater goals will boost motivation and often boost performance.

We also know that goal proximity matters.

So,you want to break down goals into smaller pieces when people are close to reaching that goal.

So,the end of the month,and we're almost at the goal,that's when people are particularly motivated.

So,close to that goal,people work extra hard.

You can look at this.There are studies of runners.

If you look at a marathon race,there are big spikes right by round numbers.

People are racing to get in under a specific time.

Now,goals work by focusing our attention,they're increasing our effort and boosting persistence.

So,what we want to do to harness the benefits of goal setting is to set clear,specific goals.

They should be challenging but also realistic.

If we have past performance,so how fast we've run on prior races,or how much people on this factory line can perform,or sales goals based on past performance,we want to set goals around the 80th to 90th percentile performance.

So challenging,but also credible.

And if we can set a series of short-term goals,like goals every month rather than goals for the whole year,we're likely to see greater benefits to setting goals.

The next part involves committing to goals.

And this is one reason why the goal has to be realistic.

People have to believe they can get there.

So if they visualize it,they write it down,they tell other people,and notice sometimes if I tell other people,it'll be embarrassing if I fall short.

So that'll steal my resolve to that goal.

We also want to think about developing a plan.

So how can I achieve that goal?

What steps do I need to take to get there?

That action plan will all help us get to the goal.

And of course,clear feedback is important.

That is,we want to make sure we're getting feedback along the way.

And remember that when we're particularly close to the goal,that's what's going to boost performance the very most.

2-04-01.10_设定目标的陷阱

除了目标设定的好处之外，也存在一些重要的隐患，或者说目标设定的弊端和丑陋面。

让我给你讲一个关于2016年富国银行的故事。

他们发起了一项宏伟的计划，GR-8计划。

他们为员工设定了一个目标，即向每位客户销售至少八种金融产品。

这里所说的金融产品，指的是支票账户、借记卡、信用卡。

他们希望每位客户至少拥有八种金融产品。

这也被称为交叉销售。

所以，你来开一个支票账户，或者你来办理房屋抵押贷款，他们就会试图向你推销其他金融产品。

现在，我们都知道目标设定可以提升动力和绩效。

它激励人们做得更多。

问题来了。

如果你正在努力实现那个目标却遇到困难，会发生什么？

那该怎么办？

我们知道，从心理学角度讲，未能实现目标的感觉很糟糕。

这给员工或其他试图达成目标的人带来了一个两难境地。

而经常发生的情况是，人们会偷工减料，走捷径。

在富国银行的案例中，他们开设了200万个虚假账户来满足这些销售目标。

也就是说，员工在客户未授权的情况下，以客户的名义开设了账户。

富国银行最终解雇了5300名员工，并支付了1.85亿美元的罚款。

现在，有人可能会说，嗯，这里有一些害群之马。

是一些不好的员工做了错事。

我的观点是，问题不在于员工，而在于体制。

任何时候，如果你因为同一个问题不得不解雇超过5000名员工，那就不只是几个害群之马了。

这是一个更具系统性的问题。

而这里，问题就出在目标设定上。

实际上，当时的首席执行官约翰·斯坦普夫站出来说，我们要取消产品销售目标，因为我们希望确保客户完全相信，零售银行家始终关注的是客户的最大利益。

所以他们取消了这些目标，因为目标本身就成了问题。

这让我想到了我和同事们所做的一项研究，我们将其命名为《目标失控》，因为目标除了能带来非常积极的影响外，也可能导致一些负面后果。

它们可能使注意力过于狭窄。

也就是说，我们只专注于实现那个目标。

想象一下一个跑步者。

他正努力达到那个目标。

他专注于达到那个时间，却忽略了膝盖的疼痛。

也许这样做是对的。

也许不对，但目标就是以这种方式集中注意力，从而推动绩效。

目标也可能增加冒险行为。

所以我们为了努力达成目标，会承担更多风险。

也就是说，因为我们非常在意达成目标，特别是当我们接近目标时，我们可能会冒险，以便能够实现目标。

而且，差一点没达成和差很多没达成，对我们来说可能没那么重要。

目标也可能导致不道德行为。

富国银行的案例并非孤例。

还有很多其他的例子。

这里有一个关于狭隘目标的例子。

多年前，通用汽车设定了一个关于百分之二十九的目标。

在2002年，他们拥有美国市场百分之二十八点二的份额。

他们设定了获取百分之二十九市场份额的目标。

所以他们制作了带有数字29的徽章和别针，供高管们佩戴。

于是这些高管们戴着写有29的别针走来走去。

目标是增加市场份额。

结果，通用汽车扩大了免息贷款和零首付激励措施的提供范围。

他们试图让人们购买汽车，以达到百分之二十九的目标。

在努力实现这个目标的过程中，他们每卖出一辆车都在亏钱。

你可能会说，嗯，他们在努力达成目标，但他们忽略了更广泛的焦点。

也就是说，目标设定过程将他们的注意力狭隘地集中在百分之二十九的市场份额上，但这当然不是真正的目标。

真正的目标是同时实现盈利。

所以他们忽略了全局，因为目标设定过程限制了他们的视野。

结果，正如《福布斯》所说，他们固守于这个目标。

公司接着做出了一个又一个灾难性的决策，这些决策将其拖到了破产的边缘，然后越过了破产的边缘。

所以通用汽车最终破产了，因为他们最终追求的这个狭隘目标，并没有反映他们更广泛的目标。

还有其他案例。

在英国，健康委员会报告称，斯塔福德郡医院有400例死亡，原因是他们过度关注某些指标。

所以我们在不同行业、不同时期都看到了这种情况。

人们最终因为目标设定而缩小了关注范围，目标设定本质上就会让人们聚焦于具体的指标。

接下来，冒险行为。

目标设定也会助长更大的冒险行为。

2003年，房利美和房地美，这是一个旨在为所有美国人，特别是低收入人群提供抵押贷款支持的大型机构。

他们设定了一个目标，即让百分之二十的抵押贷款面向较低收入和极低收入家庭。

这比前几年的百分之十四有所提高。

所以在1990年代末，有百分之十四的抵押贷款是面向低收入和极低收入家庭的。

2001年和2003年，他们的目标是将这一比例提高到百分之二十。

结果他们发放了非常糟糕的贷款，这些贷款风险极高，质量极差，最终导致他们在2008年申请破产并寻求政府救助。

所以在这里，他们设定了一个目标，结果承担了他们无法承受的更高风险。

在我们自己的研究中，我们考察了目标设定，发现在追求目标时，人们更有可能参与冒险和不道德的行为。

我们在谈判研究中也看到了这一点。

设定了目标的人，达成的协议盈利性更差。

他们会提出更大的要求。

人们也在其他领域讨论过这种破坏性的目标追求，比如1996年的珠穆朗玛峰山难。

当人们试图实现登顶山峰的目标时，他们承担了太多风险，有时会带来灾难性的后果。

现在，目标设定也可能让我们陷入大麻烦。

例如，绿巨人公司推出了一项计划，你知道，在收获蔬菜时，他们要确保蔬菜里没有昆虫。

所以他们设定了收集昆虫的目标，并为收集昆虫的人员设定了指标。

结果，他们的员工开始随身在口袋里携带昆虫，然后把它们放进蔬菜里，以便稍后把它们拿出来，从而达到他们从蔬菜中挑出昆虫数量的目标。

还有20世纪80年代的Mini Scribe公司，他们有季度收益目标。

他们有出货量要达到足够产品的目标。

结果发现，员工们不仅发货产品，还发货砖块，因为他们试图在非常狭隘的意义上达成这些目标。

1990年代的西尔斯汽车维修中心，他们设定了特定计费工时的目标。

他们希望每小时有147美元的可计费销售额。

结果发现员工对工作收费过高，并进行不必要的维修。

在秘密调查中，他们发现大量西尔斯汽车维修中心的员工都建议进行不必要的工作，这使其声誉受损多年。

我自己与同事进行的实验表明，当人们设定了具体而有挑战性的目标，并且未能达成这些目标时，他们常常会作弊。

在这个实验中，他们在检查自己的工作以达成目标时作弊。

所以，在多个领域，我们都看到目标导致了非常不尽人意的结果。

我这里再分享一个例子。

2009年，亚特兰大学区的总监贝弗莉·霍尔被誉为年度国家总监。

所以，这是一个被树立为他人学习榜样的人。

从2001年开始，他们学区有5万名学生参加标准化考试，而她成功地提升了亚特兰大的成绩。

但结果发现，她所做的是向教育工作者施压，要求他们实现这些卓越的成就目标。

但当州调查人员调查这些成绩时，他们确定超过一半的学区存在作弊行为。

超过180名教师卷入了这起丑闻。

也就是说，教师为了让学生达到成绩目标，代表学生在标准化考试中作弊，以便他们能通过这些分数。

所以，目标会驱使我们做一些非常不可取的事情。

综合来看，我们可以看到目标可能助长不道德行为。

它们可能通过引导人们使用不道德的手段来实现目标，从而助长不道德行为。

就像富国银行的员工开设客户并未要求的账户一样。

我们也可以看到人们为了达成目标而谎报自己的绩效。

也就是说，他们声称自己达成了目标，即使实际上并没有。

在这两种情况下，目标都在激励人们，但它们是在激励人们走捷径，而这些捷径可能会对个人、团队和组织造成灾难性的后果。

英文原文

In addition to the good in goal setting,there are also some important pitfalls,or the bad and the ugly,about goal setting.

Let me tell you a story about Wells Fargo in 2016.

They launched the great initiative,GR-8 initiative.

They set a goal for their employees to sell at least eight financial products to their customers.

By a financial product,what I mean is a checking account,a debit card,a credit card.

They wanted at least eight financial products per customer.

This is also known as cross-selling.

So you come in and open a checking account,or you come in and have a home mortgage,and they try to sell you other financial products.

Now,we all know that goal setting can boost motivation and boost performance.

It motivates people to do more.

Here's the problem.

What happens if you're struggling to hit that goal?

What then?

We know psychologically it feels terrible to fail to meet a goal.

And it presents a dilemma for employees or other people who are trying to hit a goal.

And what often happens is that people will cut corners.

And in the case of Wells Fargo,they opened 2 million fake accounts to meet these sales goals.

So employees were opening accounts with customers that customers had not authorized.

Wells Fargo ended up firing 5300 employees,and they paid$185 million in fines.

Now,one idea is to say,well,there's some bad apples here.

There's some bad employees doing the wrong thing.

My view is it's not the employees,it's the system.

And anytime you have to fire over 5000 employees over the same problem,it's not a few bad apples.

It's a problem that's more systemic.

And here it's goal setting that's the problem.

And the CEO,John Sumpf,actually came out and said,we're eliminating product sales goals because we want to make certain our customers have full confidence that retail bankers are always focused on the best interest of customers.

So they're eliminating the goals because the goals were a problem.

Now,this brings me to this idea of some work that I've done that we titled Goals Gone Wild,because goals can do,in addition to very positive things,some negative things.

They can focus attention too narrowly.

So that is,we're focused on hitting that goal.

So,think about a runner.

They're trying to hit that goal.

They're focused on hitting that time and they're ignoring the pain in their knees.

Maybe that's the right thing to do.

Maybe it's not,but goals focus attention in a way that can drive performance.

Goals can also increase risk-taking.

So we take on more risk to try to hit that goal.

That is,since we care deeply about hitting that goal,particularly when we're close to it,we might take risk that might allow us to reach the goal.

And the difference between falling short by a little and falling short by a lot may not be that important to us.

Goals can also lead to unethical behavior.

The Wells-Fargo case is not an isolated case.

There are many others.

So here's the idea about a narrow goal.

General Motors years ago set a goal for 29.

Now,in 2002,they had 28.2%of the U.S.market.

They set a goal for capturing 29%.

So they created buttons and pins for executives to wear with the number 29.

So these executives were walking around with pins that said 29.

And the goal was to increase market share.

Well,it turns out that GM expanded the offering of interest-free loans and no-money-down incentives.

They're trying to get people to buy the cars to reach their 29%goal.

They were losing money on a per-car basis in the effort to meet this goal.

Now,you could say,well,they're trying to meet the goal,but they're missing the broader focus.

That is,the goal setting process narrowed their focus on 29%of market share,but of course,that's not really the goal.

The goal is to be profitable at the same time.

So they were missing the broader picture because the goal setting process had narrowed their focus.

So they ended up saying,well,this is what Forbes said:fixate on this target.

The firm went on to make decision after disastrous decision that helped drag it to the brink and then past the brink of bankruptcy.

So GM ended up going bankrupt because they ended up pursuing this narrow goal that really didn't reflect their broader goal.

There are other cases.

So in the United Kingdom,the Health Commission reported that there were 400 deaths at Stafford Hospital because they had excessive focus on certain targets.

So we see this across industries across time.

People end up narrowing their focus because of goal setting that really does,by its inherent nature,focus people on specific.

Now,risk-taking.

Goal setting also promotes greater risk-taking.

In 2003,Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac,a large institution designed to support mortgages for all Americans,but particularly people with lower incomes.

They set out a goal to have 20%of mortgages for lower,very low-income families.

This was up from 14%in the preceding years.

So at the end of the 1990s,14%of the mortgages were for low-and very low-income families.

2001 and 2003,they had a goal of boosting that to 20%.

They ended up making very bad loans,loans that were so risky and so bad,they ended up filing for bankruptcy and a government bailout in 2008.

So here they set a goal and they ended up taking on more risk than they could handle.

In our own research,we've looked at goal setting and found that people are more likely to engage in risky and unethical behavior when they're pursuing a goal.

So we've seen this in negotiation studies.

People with goals are reaching less profitable agreements.

They're making larger demands.

And people have talked about the destructive goal pursuit in other domains too,like the 1996 Mount Everest disaster.

As people were trying to reach their goal of summiting the mountain,they took on too much risk and sometimes with disastrous consequences.

Now,goal setting can also get us into deep trouble.

The Dolly Green Giant,for example,rolled out a plan where,you know,as they harvest vegetables,they want to make sure there are no insects along with those vegetables.

So they set out a goal for collecting insects,and they set targets for people collecting insects.

And it turns out their employees ended up starting carrying insects around with them in their pockets that they'd put into the vegetables so they could take them out later to hit their goals of number of insects pulled out of vegetables.

Now,Mini Scribe in the 1980s,they had quarterly earnings.

They had goals to ship enough products.

And they found that employees were actually shipping not just products,but also bricks because they were trying to hit these goals in a very narrow sense.

Sears Automotive,the 1990s,they set a goal for certain billable hours.

They wanted$147 in billable sales per hour.

They found the staff overcharged for work and made unnecessary repairs.

In undercover investigations,they found that a vast number of Sears automotive employees were suggesting unnecessary work,and it damaged the reputation for years.

My own experiments with my colleagues have demonstrated that when people have specific challenging goals and they fail to meet those goals,they'll often cheat.

In this case,they were checking their own work to hit that goal.

So,across several domains,we've seen goals lead to very undesirable outcomes.

And I'll share one other example here.

The Atlantic School Superintendent Beverly Hall in 2009,she was heralded for the National Superintendent of the Year award.

So,here's someone who was held up as an example for others to follow.

And they had 50000 students standardized tests starting in 2001,and she was able to boost performance in Atlanta.

Now,it turns out what she done is she had pushed goals on educators to produce these great achievement goals.

But when state investigators looked into this performance,they determined that cheating had occurred in more than half of the districts.

Over 180 teachers were implicated in this scandal.

That is,teachers who were cheating on standardized tests on behalf of the students to hit performance goals so they can meet these marks.

So,goals can push us to do things that are very undesirable.

Taken together,we can see that goals can promote unethical behavior.

They can promote unethical behavior by guiding people to use unethical means to meet that goal.

So,like Wells Fargo employees opening up accounts that customers didn't ask to create.

And we can also see people misrepresenting their performance to meet the goal.

So,they're saying they met the goal even when they didn't.

In both cases,goals are motivating people,but they're motivating people to cut corners in ways that can have disastrous consequences both for individuals,groups,and organizations.

2-04-01.11_最大化目标设定的效果

那么，我们该如何最大程度地利用目标设定呢？

有时，目标能激励我们成就伟业，但目标也可能将我们引入歧途，做出不道德和糟糕的事情。

那么，我们还应该使用目标吗？

注意，在我们之前谈到的一些例子中，高管介入并直接决定取消富国银行、西尔斯的的目标设定流程。

这就带来了一个挑战。

我们该如何决定如何使用目标呢？

我们知道，目标对于引导努力非常有效，特别是当任务是基于努力的，当参数清晰，并且我们能够准确地将我们试图完成的关键维度纳入其中时。

目标对于告知和沟通我们所关心的事情也非常有效。

而且它们对于直接明了的任务非常有用。

所以在很多情况下，目标确实非常重要，它们确实是激励的基础组成部分。

它们是沟通和让人们朝着特定方向前进的关键机制之一。

但目标应该谨慎使用。

我认为，我们应该表现出对过程的关注，同时也要监控人们在追求目标时所从事的行为。

当人们接近目标时尤其如此。

因此，如果是一个销售目标，月底应该是我们非常留意、警惕人们行为的时候。

所以当人们接近目标时，就是目标对他们动机影响最强烈的时候，我们要小心人们正在做什么。

我们要表明我们在乎过程。

所以他们关心过程，就像亚特兰大的学校老师一样，我们确实关心考试的诚信。

如果那是我们衡量目标绩效的方式，我们要非常小心，确保我们在乎那个过程。

这里有一些相关的想法。

我们可以有绩效目标与学习目标之分。

所以当我们出去，比如说你去打网球，绩效目标是赢得网球比赛。

学习目标是提高自己，让你的反手击球达到最佳状态。

在任何领域都是如此，无论是教育领域还是工作领域，我们在做一个项目。

目标是绩效，还是有一个学习目标？

结果是，我们越能转向学习目标，也就是我们不断努力改进，试图让它越来越好，我们就越接近学习目标，效果就越好。

这样，在长期来看我们会处于更有利的位置。

我们发现人们会表现得更好，他们对反馈的反应更好，随着时间的推移，他们最终确实会学得更好，表现得更出色。

因此，我们想要从绩效心态转向学习目标心态。

另一个关键理念是组织文化。

组织文化确实很重要。

这与我们关心过程的理念相关，而关心道德规范的强大文化，确实可以降低由目标设定引发不道德行为的风险。

所以，这里的理念是，如果我们有一种组织文化，我们就可以限制目标设定可能造成的损害，因为我们表现出了对道德的关注和对过程的关注。

所以，简而言之，我想发出一个警告。

那就是，目标可能会在组织中引发系统性问题，因为它们会缩小关注点，它们会增加冒险行为，它们可能助长不道德行为，损害学习，损害合作，并降低追求我们真正希望人们去做的事情的内在动力。

但另一方面，它们也可能产生非常积极的结果。

所以，我们应该使用目标设定，但应该谨慎为之。

英文原文

So how do we make the most of goal setting?

Sometimes goals can motivate us to do great things,but goals can also lead us astray to do unethical and terrible things.

So should we ever use goals?

Notice that in some of those examples we talked about before,executives come in and just decide to remove the goal setting process at Wells Fargo,at Sears.

And it presents this challenge.

How do we decide how to use goals?

We know that goals can be very effective for directing effort,particularly when it's an effort-based task,when the parameters are clear and we can accurately incorporate the key dimensions of what we're trying to do.

Goals are also very powerful for informing and communicating what we care about.

And they're very useful for straightforward tasks.

So in many cases,goals are really important,and they really are a foundational part of motivation.

They're one of the key mechanisms for communicating and getting people on board to drive in a particular direction.

But goals should be used carefully.

And I'm going to argue that we should demonstrate a concern for the process and also monitor the behavior that people are engaging in as they're pursuing that goal.

This is particularly true when people get close to that goal.

So if it's a sales goal,the end of the month should be when we're very mindful and watchful,vigilant of what people are doing.

So when people get close to the goal,that's when goal is going to be most intense in their motivation,and we want to be careful about what people are doing.

We want to demonstrate that we care about the process.

So they care about the process,like the Atlanta school teachers,that we do care about the integrity of the test taking.

If that's how we're measuring goal performance,we want to be very careful that we're caring about that process.

Now,there's some related ideas here.

We could have performance goals versus learning goals.

So when we go out,let's say you're going out to play tennis,the performance goal is winning the tennis game.

The learning goal is improving so that your backhand becomes the best that it can be.

And the same is true in any domain,whether it's educational or at work,we're doing a project.

Is the goal performance or is there a learning goal?

And the upshot is that the more we can get to a learning goal,that is we're constantly trying to improve,we're trying to get this to be better and better,the closer we are to a learning goal,the better.

Better off,we're going to be in a long-term situation.

We find that people are better,they react better to feedback,they actually do end up learning and performing better over time.

And so,we want to move away from a performance mindset to a learning goal mindset.

Another key idea is organizational culture.

The culture in the organization really matters.

And this is related to the idea that we care about process,and strong cultures that care about ethics can really curtail the risk of unethical behavior being driven by goal setting.

So,the idea here is that if we have an organizational culture,we can limit the damage that goal setting may cause because we demonstrate a concern for ethics and a concern for process.

So,in short,I want to issue a warning.

That is,goals may cause systematic problems in organizations because they narrow focus,they increase risk-taking,they can promote unethical behavior and harm learning,harm cooperation,and decrease intrinsic motivation to pursue what we really want people to do.

But on the other hand,they can also have very positive consequences.

So,we should use goal setting,but we should do so carefully.

2-04-01.12_跨越终点线

在这最后一部分，我想探讨一下收尾的重要性，以及我们如何结束一件事，会影响我们如何开始下一件事。

我想分享一个关于我朋友安赫尔·卡尔萨迪利亚的故事。

他是佛罗里达州迈阿密的一名危机谈判专家。

有一天，他被叫去处理一起事件。

一个名叫帕里斯的人拖着三个手提箱，翻过铁丝网，爬上了一座塔。

在这座无线电塔的顶端，他正在往下扔传单，上面写着“听帕里斯说”。

当时，塔下聚集了一群人。

交通也因此受阻。

特警队被召来了，需要一名危机谈判专家说服这个人下来，别再制造这场骚乱。

他们赶到了现场。

一开始他们不知道如何与他沟通，直到最后他们想出了办法，可以通过直升机来沟通。

于是安赫尔登上直升机，在大的纸板上写字，让帕里斯用点头或摇头来回应，从而与他沟通，并最终说服他下来。

这个过程花了几个小时。

时间长得甚至需要给直升机重新加油。

最终，安赫尔说服了他，如果你现在下来，你就可以下来，我会让你对媒体讲话。

谁知道呢，可能另一个故事会爆发，你会失去你的机会，你有话要说，现在是时候说出去了。

最后，安赫尔说服帕里斯下来了。

他下来了，他们以为他可能带着炸弹，结果发现他没有。

他下来了，特警队又累又乏，他们想把帕里斯扔进车里。

安赫尔介入说，不行，我知道你们很烦，很累，只想把这家伙扔进去，但我们得说，不行，我答应了他可以跟媒体讲话，我要兑现这个承诺。

所以安赫尔让他对媒体讲话。

他跑到媒体那边说，即使你们没有胶片，也把灯打开，让他说话。

于是他们让那个人讲了话。

结果发现他有一些非常不寻常的要求。

他想要减少沥青路面。

他想要更多的马，更多的自行车。

那是1996年。

他想成为鲍勃·多尔的竞选搭档。

而最有趣的要求是这个。

他希望结束，不是结束所有色情内容，而是希望结束俄罗斯的色情内容。

不知为何，是那种类型特别困扰他。

这个故事有趣的地方在于。

首先，结果他有点滑稽，他确实兑现了这个收尾的承诺。

但第二部分是，事情并没有就此结束。

几个月后，几个月后，帕里斯被监禁后又释放了，毕竟他没有炸弹。

他不被认为是对社会的威胁。

几个月后，安赫尔在家里踱步。

他和家人在一块儿。

他收到一个传呼。

他低头一看。

他想，哦，一个传呼。

他简直不敢相信。

那天可是复活节周日。

他收到了一个传呼。

他赶过去，出现在现场。

有个人在那儿。

他们对安赫尔说，看，安赫尔，这儿有个人，他想跟你谈谈。

果然，是帕里斯，他爬上了一座高压电线塔，并且提出了类似的要求。

第二次谈判进行得非常快，非常顺利。

他们之前已经建立了关系。

帕里斯相信安赫尔会兑现承诺。

所以你看，安赫尔结束第一次互动的方式，影响了第二次互动的走向。

这里还有一点非常有趣，就是我们通常认为危机谈判是单次事件。

也就是说，安赫尔很容易会说，你知道吗，这是一锤子买卖。

人在这儿了。

我们搞定了。

把他扔进车里吧。

但安赫尔兑现了承诺，他认识到即使在非同寻常、古怪的情况下，有时看似单次的案例，也可能演变成重复互动。

也就是说，对于危机谈判，我们并不指望会有回头客，但有时事情会出乎我们的意料。

接下来，我想在更大的层面上思考收尾。

在世界舞台上，我们来思考一下冷战的结束。

这是一场在苏联和美国之间持续了几十年的对抗。

最终，柏林墙倒塌了。

随着墙的倒塌，人们涌过边界，这被西方国国家，美国和西欧，誉为伟大的胜利。

它为德国的统一创造了机会。

这也标志着苏联开始走向终结。

对美国来说，这似乎是一场伟大的胜利。

但当时的乔治·赫伯特·沃克·布什总统并没有沾沾自喜。

他对此甚至没有大肆宣扬。

他表现得极其低调，因为他知道，要与苏联领导人戈尔巴乔夫合作，他需要促成合作。

他知道，如果他对那场胜利表现得欣喜若狂，那会使他未来与戈尔巴乔夫的合作变得困难得多。

这种关于收尾的理念在很多不同的领域都适用。

想想谈判。

当然，我们可以想象在达成协议后感到高兴。

也许达成了对我们非常有利的协议，然而，正如柏林墙倒塌时不要幸灾乐祸很重要一样，在谈判中最终达成好协议时，不沾沾自喜也很重要。

在这里，你甚至要小心，在达成谈判协议后，笑得太开心都不行。

英文原文

In this last segment,I want to think about the importance of endings and how we end things influences how we start what comes next.

And I want to share a story about one of my friends,Angel Calzadilla.

He's a crisis negotiator in Miami,Florida.

Now,one day he was called to an incident.

A man named Paris had hauled three suitcases over a barbed wire fence and up a tower.

At the top of this radio tower,he was throwing down leaflets that read,listen to Paris.

Well,a crowd had gathered below.

It was being to stop traffic.

The SWAT team was called in,and a crisis negotiator needed to convince this guy to come down and stop creating all this commotion.

Well,they got there.

They didn't know exactly how to communicate with him until they finally figured out,well,we can communicate by helicopter.

So Angel goes up in a helicopter,is writing on these large sheets of paper,and is getting Paris to shake his head yes or no to get him to communicate,to eventually persuade him to come down.

It takes hours.

It takes so long they have to refuel the helicopter.

Finally,Angel persuades him,if you come down now,you can come down and I'll let you speak to the media.

Who knows,another story could break,you could lose your opportunity,you have a message,now's your time to get it out.

Finally,Angel persuades Paris to come down.

He comes down,they think he might have a bomb,it turns out he didn't.

He comes down,the SWAT team is tired,they're exhausted,they want to throw Paris in the van.

Angel intervenes and says,no,I know you're sick,you're tired,you just want to throw this guy out,but we're saying,no,I promised him he could speak to the media,I'm going to follow through on that promise.

So Angel lets him speak to the media.

He runs over to the media and says,even if you have no film,just turn your lights on,let the guy speak.

So they let the guy speak.

And it turns out he had some very unusual demands.

He wanted less asphalt.

He wanted more horses,more bicycles.

And this was 1996.

He wanted to be Bob Dole's running mate.

And here's the most interesting demand.

He wanted an end,not to all pornography,he wanted an end to Russian pornography.

For some reason,that was the variant that was really bothering him.

Now,here's the funny part about the story.

First,it turns out he had a funny,he followed through on this ending.

But the second part is that it doesn't end there.

Months later,months later,after Paris had been incarcerated but then released,he didn't after all have a bomb.

He wasn't deemed a threat to society.

Months later,Angel's pacing around his house.

He's hanging out with his family.

He gets a page.

And he looks down.

He's like,oh,a page.

I can't believe it.

It's Easter Sunday.

He gets a page.

He goes up,shows up on scene.

There's a guy.

And they say,look,Angel,here's a guy,and he wants to talk to you.

And here it is,Paris,he's climbed up a pylon,and he has similar demands to make.

Now,the second negotiation goes very quickly,very smoothly.

They had already built a relationship.

Paris trusted Angel to follow through.

So here,how Angel had ended that first interaction influenced the way that second interaction went.

And something else really interesting here is that we often think of crisis negotiations as single-shot events.

That is,it would be easy for Angel to have said,you know what,this is a one-shot deal.

Here's the guy.

We got him.

Let's throw him in the van.

But Angel follows through,recognizing that even in unusual,weird cases,sometimes what seems like a single-shot case is a repeated interaction.

That is,when it comes to crisis negotiations,we're not expecting repeat business,but we can sometimes be surprised.

Next,I want to think about endings on a bigger scale.

Here on the world stage,we think about the end of the Cold War.

This is a war that raged for decades between the Soviet Union and the United States.

Now,finally,the Berlin Wall fell down.

And as it fell down,people streamed across the border,and it was heralded as a great victory for the Western countries,the United States and Western Europe.

And it created an opportunity for Germany to become reunited.

And it marked the beginning of the end of the Soviet Union.

Now,for the United States,it seemed like a great victory.

But President George Bush at the time didn't gloat.

He didn't even make much of a deal about it.

He was incredibly understated about this because he knew that working with Gorbachev,the leader of the Soviet Union,he needed to affect cooperation.

And he knew that if he gloated about that victory,it would make it much more difficult for him to work with Gorbachev going forward.

And this idea about ending is true in a lot of different domains.

Think about negotiations.

Of course,we can think about being happy after we've been.

Reached a deal,perhaps even a deal that's really great for us,and yet,just like it's important not to gloat when the wall falls down,it's important not to gloat when we end up with a good deal in a negotiation.

And here,you want to be careful even smiling too much after you reach a negotiated agreement.

3-01-01.01_课程介绍

欢迎来到《影响力》课程。

我是凯德·梅西。

我是沃顿商学院运营信息与决策组的实践教授。

这门课程，我已经向高管MBA和MBA学员讲授了十年，最初是在耶鲁管理学院，最近则是在沃顿商学院。

我还教授其他课程。

我教授谈判、决策制定、人员分析。

这门课程是我非常用心投入的。

我为此倾注了大量心血。

在过去的十年里，我从我的学生以及关于权力与影响力的文献中学到了很多。

我喜欢它的原因之一，是它和谈判一样，不仅仅关乎工作。

它在你个人生活、家庭以及人际关系中，与在工作中同样重要。

我还喜欢它，是因为它几乎处于社会科学和临床心理学的一个绝佳交汇点。

这是一门非常个人化的课程。

如果你报名参加，我希望你准备好进行一些自我反省和拓展，因为这里的动机是，我们相信通过鼓励你、激励你，并为你提供成为更具影响力的人的新工具，我们能够对你的生活产生影响。

开设这门课程的最初动机，是为了武装我们的MBA学员，让他们在离开我们的项目、开始在组织中摸索前进之路时，能够有所准备。

事实上，它最初的名称，第一个版本，叫做《navigating organizations》(在组织中游刃有余)。

当时的想法是，商学院的很多课程都是关于如何运营整个组织，例如，如何设计一个组织，而对于当你离开商学院、成为中层管理者、仍在努力向上攀登时会发生什么，则涉及不够。

这些工具旨在帮助你穿越组织，在组织中游刃有余。

所以，这就是我的出发点。

这也是这门课程旨在实现的目标。

我会简要介绍一下第一周的学习路线图。

第一周我们有几个主题。

首先是一个介绍，阐述关于权力与影响力的一些基本概念，为你提供一些基本框架，并介绍一两个例子，我们将在后续课程中反复用到这些例子。

然后，在本周的后半段，我们将从个人视角转向更具组织性的视角。

关于权力与影响力的内容，很多都集中在个人层面。

但在一开始就强调情境和背景的力量至关重要。

因此，在第一周的后半部分，我们将更多地探讨背景和组织。

这就是我们本周的学习方向。

第一周。

祝您学习愉快。

英文原文

Welcome to Influence.

My name is Cade Massey.

I am a practice professor here at the Wharton School in the Operations Information and Decisions Group.

This is a course that I've been teaching with executive MBAs and MBAs for 10 years now,first at Yale School of Management and more recently here at Wharton.

I teach other things.

I teach negotiation,decision-making,people analytics.

This is a course that's very close to my heart.

I've poured a lot into it.

Over the last 10 years,I've learned a lot from the students I've been working with and from the literature on power and influence.

One of the reasons I like it is that,like negotiation,it's about more than just work.

It's as important in your personal life,in your family,and your relationships as it is at work.

I also like it because it's this nice intersection of it's almost social science and clinical psychology.

This is a very personal class.

If you're signing up for it,I hope you're ready to do some introspection and some stretching because that's the motivation here is that we think we can make a difference in your life by encouraging you and motivating you and giving you new tools for becoming a more influential person.

The initial motivation for this course was to arm our MBAs as they left our program and they began navigating their way through organizations.

In fact,the initial title,the first version,was called Navigating Organizations.

The idea was that so much of the business school curriculum is about running an entire organization,how do you design an organization,for example,and not enough about what happens when you leave business school,when you're a middle manager,while you're still traversing your way.

These tools are intended to help you traverse your way,navigate your way through organizations.

So that's where I'm coming from.

That's what the course is intended to do.

And then in the second half of the week,we're going to talk about,we're going to move from the kind of individual perspective to a more organizational perspective.

So much happens in Power and Influence that focuses on individuals.

And so in the second half of week one,we're going to look more at context and organization.

Week one.
