3-02-01.08_常见错误

那么在本讲中，我们将讨论人们在建立网络和培养关系时常犯的几个错误。

第一个，也可能是最重要的一个错误，就是等到有了目标才开始networking。

我们今天讨论的这些理念，更多地关乎一种生活方式。

它是一种手段，而非目的。

你应该从社会资本的角度来思考。

你应该把你的非正式网络看作是你建立和培养的社会资本，就像你建立自己的人力资本一样。

你的网络是你带到任何情境中去的东西，就像你的教育背景一样，而且你应该随着时间的推移，为了它本身而逐步地、增量地发展它。

第二个常见错误，专注于向上社交。

试图去认识那些已经掌权的人很有吸引力，甚至令人向往，但这有几个问题。

第一，竞争更激烈。

这是一种稀缺资源，那些身处权力高位的人，能给予的时间甚至比基层的人更少。

这也会过度关注正式的组织架构，如果你只看那些身居要职的人，你也会忘记那些非正式的权力来源。

最后，一个非常实际的考虑是，你网络的最大来源之一，将是你现在认识的人以及他们随着时间的推移如何发展。

那些和你一起上学的人，那些和你一起创业的人，随着时间的推移，会进入有影响力的位置。

如果你在这个过程中忽略了他们，那么当他们真正处于能够发挥作用的职位时，你就不会拥有这些网络了。

第三个常见错误，认为你的正式职位与非正式网络无关。

我们花了这么多时间讨论非正式网络。

我们不想忽略的是，你的正式职位会带来关系上的后果，网络上的后果。

所以工作本身可以驱动网络。

事实上，它会让你处于接近的位置。

它会让你与特定的一群人定期互动。

实际上，这是思考那份工作的重要方式。

这个正式职位会损害还是促进什么样的非正式网络？

这也减轻了一些你需要进行非正式社交的压力，因为你知道其中一部分会来自正式职位带来的。

最后，有些人犯的错误是，把建立联系本身当作终点。

他们想认识某个人。

却忽略了这个人的网络。

你遇到的每个人都嵌入在他们自己的网络中。

希望你能从这次讨论中带走的一点是，每个人都会受到影响，每个人都带来资源，每个人都带来他们网络的约束。

所以当你认识别人时，不仅仅是认识那个人，你是在了解他们生活和工作的背景，即社会背景。

这有助于更好地理解他们。

这也有助于你更好地理解可能存在的机会，以及存在的约束。不过这里有一点需要注意，那就是把别人当作接触其网络的工具的危险。

当你开始把人当作达成自己目的的手段时，你在很多方面都如履薄冰。

所以，尽管我们希望你在他们网络的背景下去考虑他们，但我们不希望你去考虑他们。

仅仅因为他们的网络。

英文原文

So in this lecture we'll talk about a few common mistakes that people make as they build a network and cultivate relationships.

The first and probably most important is the mistake of waiting to network until you have an objective.

The ideas we've been talking about today are much more about a way of life.

It is a means rather than an end.

You should think in terms of social capital.

You should think about your informal networks as social capital you build and cultivate just as you might build your human capital.

Your network is something you bring to any situation,just like your education,and it's something you should grow in and of for itself incrementally over time.

Second common mistake,focusing on networking up.

It's appealing,alluring even to try to get to know those who are already in positions of power,but there are a few problems with this.

One,there's more competition.

It's a scarce resource,and the folks in those positions of power have even less time to give than those at lower levels.

It also puts an undue focus on formal hierarchy,and you forget,if you're only looking at those in positions of power,you forget the informal sources of power as well.

And then finally,a very practical consideration is one of the greatest sources of your network is going to be who you know now and how they evolve over time.

The folks you were going to school with,the folks you were starting your organizations with,will move into positions of influence over time.

And if you've neglected them along the way,then you won't have those networks when they're actually in the positions where they can really make a difference.

Third common mistake,thinking that your formal position is unrelated to the informal network.

We've spent so much time talking about informal network.

We don't want to neglect that there are relationship consequences,network consequences that come along with your formal position.

So the job itself can drive the network.

In fact,it's going to put you in proximity.

It's going to give you regular interaction with a distinct set of people.

It's an important way to think about that job,actually.

What is the informal network that's going to be impaired or facilitated by the formal position?

It also takes a little bit of pressure off of the need to do the informal networking because you know that some of it's going to come from the formal side.

And then finally,some folks make the mistake of thinking of a tie as an endpoint.

They want to get to know a person.

They neglect the network that that person sits.

Everybody you meet is embedded in their own network.

Hopefully one of the things you carry away from this discussion is how everybody is influenced and everybody brings a resource and everybody brings the constraints of their network.

So when you're getting to know people,it's not just that person,you're getting to know the context,the social context that they live and work in.

So it helps better understand them.

It also helps you better understand opportunities that might exist,also the constraints that exist.One caveat here is the danger of treating people as a means to get to their network though.

You're on thin ice in many ways when you start thinking about people as a means to your end.

So even though we want you to think about them in the context of their network,we don't want you to think about them.

Only because of their network.

3-02-01.09_关于社交网络的总结思考

以下是关于非正式网络讨论的几个关键要点。

首先，网络是社会资本。

它类似于你的人力资本。

是你带到任何情境、任何组织中去的整体能力组合的一部分。

网络的有效性在很大程度上取决于结构洞。

这是我们今天要推介的一个新观点，一个有点不同寻常、反直觉、甚至有些挑衅性的观点。

这是网络理论中最重要的观点之一：网络的效率和有效性，即那种社会资本的力量，取决于结构洞，也就是网络各部分的disconnected程度。

最后一点，网络是赢得的，而不是构建的。

你无法像我们希望的那样，事先准备好，刻意为之。

这需要你将其作为一种生活方式。

你通过从互惠的角度思考，超越互惠的常规，来创造能量。

要时刻把社交网络当作你每天都在进行的事情，而不是因为有一个必须立即达成的目标才去做。

所以，我们在这个话题上讨论的理念，与本课程的其他部分相互关联。

例如，理解对方，就是我们贯穿课程始终都在讨论的一个理念。

这对于创造宝贵资源、促成互惠、战略性管理你的网络以及认识到其中的权衡取舍至关重要。

这是我们几乎每一步都会谈到的东西。

如果这些策略你可以放心使用，无需担心用得太多，或者可以在所有情况下使用，那当然很好。

但生活比这要复杂一些。

影响力也比这要复杂一些。

你所做的每一个选择都伴随着权衡取舍。

最后，是意图性。

以最大化其效用的方式构建网络，需要更多的策略性，这可能比你习惯于带入人际关系中的策略性要多一些。

一种思考方式是，我们敦促你对你的网络抱有意图性，而对你的人际关系不要抱有意图性。

我们理解那种不适感。

事实上，我们主张，对于将过多的意图性带入人际关系和个人交往中，应该保持这种不适感。

但我认为，我们可以安心地、策略性地规划更广泛的网络，以及我们关于工作、位置和如何安排时间的决定，同时在我们建立的个人关系中，仍然保持非意图性和更人性化的态度。

最后，通过你的网络来增加影响力，这绝非令人反感之事，反而是提升你能力的关键途径之一。

权力的发展和运用需要成事，而成事——尤其是在当今时代——几乎总是需要通过与他人合作才能实现。

如果你不能通过他人成事，你就无法取得他人所能取得的成就。

正如杰夫·普费弗所言，执行上的失败，几乎毫无例外都是因为未能成功建立有效的联盟。

英文原文

So a few key takeaways from our discussion of informal networks.

The first is that networks are social capital.

They're the analog to your human capital.

They're part of the portfolio that you bring to any situation,any organization.

The effectiveness of the network depends heavily on structural holes.

This is the new idea,kind of the unusual,counterintuitive,somewhat provocative idea we're pushing today.

It's one of the most important ideas in network theory,that the efficiency and effectiveness of a network,the power of that social capital,depends on structural holes,how disconnected the network is.

And finally,that networks are earned,not built.

You can't do this stuff quite as ready-made,as intentional as we'd like.

This is something you need as a way of life.

You create energy by thinking about it in terms of reciprocity,going beyond the norm of reciprocity.

Very much thinking about social networks as something you're doing on a daily,weekly basis,not because you have an objective that has to be met by it right away.

So the ideas we've been talking about on this topic connect to the rest of the course.

Understanding the other party,for example,is an idea that we've been talking about throughout the course.

It's critical for creating valuable resources,generating reciprocity,strategically managing your network,recognizing trade-offs.

This is something we talk about pretty much every step of the way.

It would be nice if these were tactics that you could use without worrying about using them too much,or if you could use them in all circumstances.

But life is a little more complicated than that.

Influence is a little more complicated than that.

There's going to be trade-offs associated with every choice that you make.

And finally,intentionality.

Building networks in a way that maximizes their effectiveness requires a little more strategy,and it might be a little more strategy than you're comfortable bringing to your relationships.

One way to think about it,we would urge you to be intentional about your network and to be unintentional about your relationships.

We understand the squeamishness.

In fact,we advocate having squeamishness about bringing too much intentionality to relationships and individuals.

But I think we can sit comfortably about being strategically about the broader network and the decisions we make about jobs,about where we sit,about how we spend our time,while still being unintentional and more human in the individual relationships that we build.

Finally,far from being distasteful,increasing influence through your network is one of the key ways to leverage your ability.

The development and use of power requires accomplishing and accomplishing almost always,especially these days,requires working through other people.

You can't accomplish what others can if you can't work through other people.

As Jeff Pfeffer puts it,failures of implementation are almost invariably failures to build successful coalitions.

3-02-01.10_联盟简介

在本讲中，我们将讨论联盟。

首先，我想举一个近期新闻中的例子。

几年前，有一则关于俄罗斯和中国之间达成大型天然气协议的公告。

这是《金融时报》的头条新闻，在所有人看来，这像是一笔双边协议。

但如果你阅读文章，就会发现第三方对该协议的影响有多频繁。

事实上，此举的动机之一就是俄罗斯想在天然气市场上抢在美国之前进入中国。

中国对美国液化天然气的兴趣与日俱增。

俄罗斯不希望这种情况发生，所以他们想敲定这笔交易，以便为自己保住市场。

这就是美国的影响。哈萨克斯坦。

他们必须确定这条管道的路线。

他们必须穿越多个国家修建管道，才能从俄罗斯到达中国。

最短的路线是穿过哈萨克斯坦。

哈萨克斯坦不想参与这笔交易，因为作为前苏联加盟共和国，他们长期以来对俄罗斯有种伪依赖关系。

另一方面，与中国接壤的蒙古则希望管道经过。

他们可能也想稍微减少一点对那个大国邻居中国的依赖，但中国不希望蒙古拥有这条管道。

所以他们不得不一路向东绕行。所以我们可以看到，即使在这个相对简单的例子中，看起来像是一笔大型双边交易，但实际上，第三方影响了这件事的动机和选址。

这就是我们今天要讨论的出发点。

联盟是一个极其重要的话题。

它们时时刻刻影响着谈判、组织和个人。

然而，我们并没有真正看到太多关于联盟的著作。

我们看到对联盟的研究也不多。

我们想与大家分享一些我们在过去几年中观察到和研究的成果。

为此，让我们从一个最近的MBA学员的例子开始，讲述她在自己的组织中使用联盟的经历。

我们来看看她的描述。

她写道，在我的上一份工作中，我为一个为心理健康诊所提供咨询和培训以帮助改善其临床服务的组织工作。

当时，我们被要求创建一个专注于诊所业务运营的新服务项目。

我的团队里有几位成员在向诊所提供临床培训方面经验非常丰富，他们强烈认为我们应该使用相同的项目模式来提供这些业务服务。

然而，作为唯一的客户联系人，我从客户那里得知，使用这种模式并不能满足他们的业务需求。

作为团队中资历最浅的成员，至少年轻了十五岁，当我试图将这一点传达给整个团队并提出新的解决方案时，我很快就被主要的临床专家压制并驳回了。

我们先停在这里，问一下，你们熟悉这种情况吗？

我想你们很多人都熟悉。

你没有正式职权。

你可能处于一个相对不那么有影响力的位置，但你却想以某种方式影响决策。

她该怎么办呢？

于是她给我们很好地展示了联盟以及接下来发生的事情。

她说，我发现团队中两位主要成员，他们来自业务和运营部门，更认同我的看法。

他们只是不想公开反对其他高管，宁愿把精力花在其他问题的争论上。

我开始与这些团队成员单独会面，分享我的想法，并根据他们的反馈进行修改。

一旦获得了他们的支持，我就安排了与那些更保守的团队成员的会议，他们来自各种业务和临床背景。

我告诉他们，这些想法来自他们同为高管的同事，并征求他们的反馈和意见。

我还让不同的团队成员参与进来，帮助我完善某个想法的部分内容，因为我知道这些部分与他们个人的目标是一致的。

例如，我请我们的财务专家帮我思考改进我们财务建模培训的策略，并让他负责为最初的试点项目进行培训。

当我最终向整个团队展示一个新的拟议项目模式时，只有那位临床负责人之前从未听过这个方案。

当其他所有人都支持这个想法时，他也默许了。

在我的整个三年工作期间，我运用了这种逐一沟通、想法归属和协调目标的策略，推动了两项新的重大项目。

在我离职前的最后一次团队会议上，我们的临床负责人宣称，我们最新的项目是我们有史以来最大、最成功的项目推广，而且他从一开始就知道这个项目注定会成功。

所以，我们这里有了一个绝佳的例子，展示了如何从一个相对无权的位置运用联盟，从而在组织中实际施加影响。

这正是我们今天讲座中想要研究和学习如何做到的事情。

英文原文

In this lecture,we'll talk about coalitions.

And to start that,I want to give an example from recent news.

There was an announcement a couple years ago of a big gas deal between Russia and China.

Here is the headline in the Financial Times,and it looks to all the world like a two-party deal.

But if you read the article,you see how often third parties influence the deal.

In fact,one of the motivations for this was that Russia wanted to beat the U.S.to the Chinese market.

There is increasing interest in liquefied natural gas from the U.S.in China.

Russia doesn't want that to happen,so they want to land this deal so they can preserve the market for themselves.

That's the influence of the U.S.Kazakhstan.

They have to locate this pipeline.

They have to build it across countries to get from Russia to China.

The shortest distance would be through Kazakhstan.

Kazakhstan didn't want to be in on the deal because of their long-standing pseudo-dependence on Russia as a former member of the Soviet Union.

On the other hand,Mongolia,next to China,wanted the pipeline.

They wanted perhaps a little less dependence also from their big neighbor,China,but China didn't want Mongolia to have the pipeline.

So they had to take it all the way to the east.So we can see,even in this relatively simple example,it looks like a big two-party deal,but in fact,third parties influence the motivation and the location of this thing.

That's where we're coming from today.

Coalitions are an incredibly important topic.

They affect negotiations and organizations and individuals all the time,every day.

And yet,we don't really hear that much written about them.

We don't see them studied that much.

We want to share with you some of the things we have seen and studied in the last few years.

So to do that,let's start with an example from a recent MBA talking about her use of coalitions in her organization.

So let's just walk through this.

She writes,In my last job,I worked for an organization providing consultation and training to mental health clinics to help improve their clinical services.

We were being asked to create a new offering that focused on their business operations.

There were a few members of my team who were very experienced in providing clinical trainings to clinics,and they felt strongly that we should use the same program model to deliver these business services.

However,as the sole client contact,I heard from our clients that using this model wasn't working for their business needs.

The most junior member of the team by at least 15 years,when I tried to communicate this to the entire team and propose a new solution,I was quickly shut down and dismissed by the lead clinical expert.

So let's stop here and ask,are you familiar with this kind of situation?

I suspect many of you are.

You don't have formal authority.

You might be in a relatively less influential position,and yet you want to somehow impact the decision-making.

What is she going to do?

So she gives us a nice illustration of coalitions and what follows.

She said,I identified that two of my main team members who came from business and operations functions were more sympathetic to my opinions.

They just didn't want to actively disagree with the other executives,preferring to pick their battles on other issues.

I began to meet with these team members individually,sharing my ideas and refining them based on their feedback.

Once I had their buy-in,I set up meetings with the more conservative team members who came from a range of business and clinical.

backgrounds,telling them that the ideas had come from their fellow executives and asking them for their feedback and input.

I also engaged different team members in helping me build out parts of an idea that I knew aligned with their personal goals.

For example,I asked our financial expert to help me think through the strategy for revamping our financial modeling training and lead the training for the initial pilot.

When I finally presented a new proposed program model to the entire team,only the clinical lead had never heard the proposal before.

And when everyone else backed the idea,he acquiesced as well.

I used this strategy of individual check-ins,idea attribution,and goal alignment to push through two new major programs throughout my three years.

In one of our last team meetings prior to leaving my job,our clinical lead declared our latest program had been our biggest and best program rollout yet,and that he had known from the beginning that it was destined to be a success.

So here we have a fantastic example of using coalitions from a relatively powerless position in order to actually exert influence in their organization.

This is the kind of thing we want to study and learn how to do in today's lecture.

3-02-01.11_联盟的类型

联盟的哲学非常直观，政治哲学家埃德蒙·伯克对此阐述得很好。

当人们联合在一起时，他们能轻松迅速地互通任何邪恶图谋的警报。

他们能够共同商议，洞悉其阴谋，并以团结的力量加以抵抗。

而当他们分散各处，缺乏协调、秩序或纪律时，沟通就不确定，商议就困难，抵抗就变得不可行。

所以，好处是显而易见的，这是一个相当高尚的理性描述，但联盟实际上也非常基础。

当我们想了解某种人类行为有多基础时，我们会去灵长类动物中寻找。

我们基本上是在更低等的生命形式中寻找。

通过研究灵长类动物的行为，各种心理行为，我们发现，因为我们在那里看到了它，所以我们知道它对我们来说更为根本。

我们天生就会做这些事情。

联盟也是如此。

这里引用弗朗斯·德瓦尔的话，他是最著名的灵长类动物学家之一，写过一本很棒的书叫《黑猩猩的政治》。

他说，根据经验，冲突中的双方，冲突中的黑猩猩双方，知道第三方站在哪一边。

因此，第三方仅仅通过一个眼神或一个支持的手势就能影响局势。

对第三方的依赖在黑猩猩的等级制度中扮演着如此突出的角色，以至于基本的关系都完全被掩盖了。

考虑到黑猩猩社会的等级制度如此森严，这一点尤其引人注目，联盟甚至在那里也影响着它们的行为。

这表明，从埃德蒙·伯克到黑猩猩，联盟对人类行为是多么重要和基础。

为了深入探讨联盟的类型以及联盟的来龙去脉，让我们从一个例子开始。

这个例子来自一个名为“三方组织”的谈判练习，这是哈佛谈判学院的经典练习。

我们至今每年还在使用。

在这个谈判中，有三方，海王星、冥王星和金星，他们试图决定如何分配一笔资金，一笔钱，或者积分，随便你怎么叫。

如果他们作为一个三方团队合作，他们总共有二十四点可以分配。

他们也可以决定只两方合作，那样会有不同的收益。

海王星和冥王星合作，他们就有二十点可以两人分。

冥王星和金星合作，他们有十二点。

而如果金星和海王星合作，他们有十八点。

我们在这个小表格上为你列出了收益。

你会看到。

从这些收益来看，海王星在这次谈判中似乎有更大的权力。

他们是实力更强的一方。

所以我想问问你，在这次练习中你会怎么做。

我们今天不会真的做这个练习，但它可以引出我们接下来要讨论的一些内容。

如果你是其中较弱的一方，冥王星或金星，假设你是最弱的那一方。

假设你是金星。

你会如何处理？

而且你会知道这是一个关于联盟的练习。

所以开始之前，你可能会想，好的，我是和海王星结盟，还是和冥王星结盟？

我应该尝试和冥王星结盟吗？

你觉得你会怎么考虑？

这个决定。

你甚至会如何思考这个决定呢？

所以，你可以通过计算积分和数字来思考，但你也可以考虑一下个人因素。

谁扮演海王星这个角色？

我和他们是什么关系？

我和他们之间有多少信任？

对冥王星也是如此。

所以，你会综合所有这些信息，然后做出决定：好吧，我是要把赌注押在大佬海王星身上，还是押在那个中等规模的冥王星身上，去尝试组建联盟？

这个决定抓住了我们在世界上看到的两种主要联盟类型：一种是权力平衡。

这是我们在政治学中长期看到的一种动态，即单一主导力量的存在导致较小力量联合起来。

所以，在我们刚才的例子中，冥王星和金星想要合作，以某种方式制衡更强大的海王星。

但还有另一种类型——跟风，这是另一种联盟，即较小的力量相互竞争，以便与单一的dominant力量结盟。

所以，这是金星在说，嘿，我既然能投靠大海王星，为什么要去找小小的冥王星呢？

那样赢面更大。

这就是我们看到的两种类型，而当你作为较弱的一方，试图决定组建哪种联盟时，这通常是你面临的选择。

那么，你怎么知道该走哪条路呢？

如果你要组建联盟，是走权力平衡路线，还是走跟风路线？

有时你只是旁观别人之间的这种动态。

那么，你如何预测接下来会发生什么？

会是权力平衡联盟，还是跟风联盟？

如果我们能理解这一点，我们就能更好地理解联盟。

所以，概括来说，联盟有两个基础：一个是利益。你可以把这看作是一种安排的经济层面。

另一个是身份认同。

你可以把这看作是该安排或联盟的情感层面。

所以，让我们深入探讨一下基于利益的联盟和基于身份认同或者说基于情感的联盟。

一个基于利益的例子，有个非常生动的名字，叫“浸信会教徒和私酒贩子”。

这可以追溯到二十世纪八十年代对美国立法的研究。

他们讨论的具体例子是在美国，所谓的“蓝色法律”，即在一周中的某些日子限制酒类销售。

例如，在某些州或某些城市，你周日不能卖啤酒和葡萄酒。

那么，这是怎么来的呢？

顺便问一下，为什么这些法律有些至今还存在？

分析表明，基本上有所谓的“浸信会教徒”，他们不一定真的是浸信会教徒，但他们是宗教领袖。

他们给联盟带来的是道德制高点，是事业的理由。

但同时还有私酒贩子，这些人是从中获取经济利益的人。

对于这些蓝色法律，他们是酒吧老板。

他们乐于看到周日除了酒吧无处可买酒，所以他们的利益是经济上的。

为了实现这一点，他们可以提供竞选资金。

所以，你就有了这个非常强大的联盟，你未必会料到他们能走到一起，他们看起来不像会合作的人，但因为拥有共同的经济利益，他们组成了强大的联盟。

当然，这很有效，因为从立法机构的角度看，你既有道德制高点，说你是出于宗教原因这么做，同时你又能获得竞选资金，因为私酒贩子可以提供这个。

布鲁斯·扬德尔在八十年代初创立了这个理论，他说，当两个截然不同的群体都要求某种持久的社会管制时，这种管制就会出现。

所以，需要这种互补性，再加上共同的经济利益，才能形成一个非常强大的联盟。

最近，我们看到一些例子，比如韩国能源，大的金融利益集团介入支持绿色能源，尤其是在加利福尼亚州。

表面上看是为了环保原因，但实际上，如果你深究其原因，会发现有监管上的优势，实际上他们是为了投资。

当然，他们本来就是干这个的。

但因为同时有了道德制高点和经济利益，这就成了一个互补的、强大的、基于经济的联盟。

所以，当你基于利益做这些决定时，有一个非常理性的计算方法可用。比如，与甲方结盟的预期价值是多少，对比与乙方结盟的预期价值是多少？

就是计算一下。

甲方获胜的概率乘以甲方获胜后我得到的收益，对比乙方获胜的概率乘以乙方获胜后我得到的收益？

这听起来非常理性，也非常狭隘，而这正是其主张——许多联盟恰恰是依据这些理由形成的。

简而言之，哪一方更可能赢？如果那一方赢了，作为合作伙伴，我会受到怎样的对待？

这类联盟面临的挑战之一是它们是动态的，人们总是在跳来跳去，试图找到更好的交易。

博纳议长，一位长期担任美国众议院议长的人，有句名言，我喜欢把我的工作描述为，试图让二百一十八只青蛙乖乖待在独轮车里，时间足够长到通过一项法案。

这很难做到。

二百一十八是众议院通过法案所需的简单多数票。

之所以难，是因为他可能让每个人都排好队，但马上就会有人开始试图挖墙脚。

而且因为他们在做这种计算，他们可能正好能把赌注加高一点，让他们跳出独轮车，去和别人结盟。

我最喜欢的一个例子，也是最有说服力的例子之一，来自一项关于联盟形成和内战的研究。

这是近年来的一项研究，研究对象是内战，多派系内战，所以在近两百年的时间跨度里，存在着联盟形成的空间。

这里的封面是阿富汗，但实际上，他们研究了五十三个不同地区的内战。

这是福蒂尼·克里斯蒂亚。

她写道，历史上充斥着交战的领袖们改变立场的例子。

这对我们来说是令人惊讶的，因为我们倾向于认为，特别是从这个封面来看，这些冲突会是基于宗教的、非常道德的、基于部落的冲突。

但实际上，他们观察到，交战团体旨在与赢家结盟，只要他们能得到可靠的保证，保证赢家在胜利后不会剥夺他们的权力。

看来不存在所谓的“不可能的联盟”。

这是很棒的研究。

这不是直觉能想到的。

这不是我们预期的。

但他们发现，利益，这种理性的计算，如此强烈地驱动着行为，以至于它能克服那些看似根深蒂固的身份认同问题。

我曾与特种部队的学生交流过，他们以前是特种部队的，他们谈到在战场上，亲眼看到有人在战斗中真的改变立场，因为战斗中的形势计算发生了变化，一方看起来更有可能获胜。

另一种形式的联盟，联盟形成的另一个基础，是身份认同，更多是基于情感的，可能是忠诚。

它导致人们为了这些其他目标而牺牲狭隘的经济利益。

另一个来自军事领域的例子是一战中的英法联盟。

一战爆发时，他们并没有正式的条约。

他们之前有一些关系，但没有正式条约。

当德国入侵比利时，然后入侵法国时，英国必须决定是否站在法国一边参战。

这是英国内阁外交部的一份备忘录。

他们写道，认为没有书面盟约约束我们与法国的说法严格来说是正确的。

没有合同义务，但英法协约已经建立、加强、经受考验，并以一种足以让人相信一种道德纽带正在形成的方式得到庆祝。

如果英法协约的整个政策不意味着在一场正义的争吵中，英格兰会站在她的朋友一边，那它就毫无意义。

这种光荣的期望已经被唤起。

我们不能背弃它，否则我们的好名声就会受到严厉批评。

你看，这与我们之前谈到的计算，是截然不同的联盟基础。

这是道德，这是荣誉，而事实上，大英帝国确实加入了法国一方参战。

我们不知道这份备忘录有多大影响，但我们知道当时确实有人提出了这样的论点。

这是同一个故事，用视觉化的方式呈现。情绪可以发挥很大作用，驱使受委屈的各方，较弱的各方联合起来，实施报复。

所以概括来说，我们有利益与身份认同之分。

诉诸自身利益或经济利益意味着联盟的候选人池很广。

你可以拉拢任何人，只要你能证明他们的经济利益能得到很好的满足。

但这意味着你与任何你拉拢进来的人的联系都相对薄弱，相对肤浅。

或者，你可以诉诸身份认同或情感，这能提供更强的联系，但会极大地限制你可以结盟的人数。

这就是权衡取舍。

没有正确的答案。

没有哪种方式更好。

这是我们看到的联盟形成的两种不同方式。

两者都很重要。

底线之一是，忽视任何一方都是有风险的。

它们对你来说都是组建联盟的机会，对你来说也是他人试图挖走你联盟伙伴的风险。

英文原文

The philosophy of coalitions is pretty intuitive and stated well by the political philosopher Edmund Burke.

Whilst people are linked together,they easily and speedily communicate the alarm of any evil design.

They are enabled to fathom it with common counsel and to oppose it with united strength.

Whereas when they lie dispersed without concert,order,or discipline,communication is uncertain,counsel difficult,and resistance impracticable.

So clearly there are benefits,and this is a pretty high-minded intellectual description of it,but coalitions are also pretty fundamental.

When we want to understand how fundamental human behavior is,we look for it in the primates.

We look for it in lower forms,basically.

And we found by studying behavior in primates,all kinds of psychological behavior,that because we see it there,we know that it is more fundamental to us.

We're hardwired to do these things.

Such it is with coalitions.

So here's a quote from Franz De Waal,one of the best-known primatologists out there,has a great book called Chimpanzee Politics.

He says,from experience,the conflicting partners,the conflicting chimpanzee partners,know on whose side the third party stands.

Consequently,the third party can influence the situation by a mere look or gesture of support.

Dependence on third parties plays such a prominent role in the chimpanzee hierarchy that the basic relationships are completely overshadowed.

This is especially dramatic given how hierarchical the chimp societies are that influence that coalitions influence their behavior even there.

And it shows from Edmund Burke down to the chimps how important and fundamental coalitions are to human behavior.

To dig into the kinds of coalitions and the ins and outs of coalitions,let's start with an example.

And this example is from a negotiation exercise called Three-Way Organization,long-standing exercise out of the Harvard Negotiation School.

We still use it every year.

So in this negotiation,there are three parties,Neptune,Pluto,and Venus,and they're trying to decide how to divide up a pot,pot of money,pot of points,whatever you want to call it.

If they work together as a three-team organization,they have 24 points to divide.

They could also just decide to work in twos,in which case there are different payoffs.

Neptune and Pluto work together,they have 20 to divide amongst themselves.

Pluto and Venus work together,they have 12.

And then if Venus and Neptune work together,they have 18.

So we've laid the payouts out for you here on this little chart.

So you'll see.

And from these payouts,it looks like Neptune has more power in this negotiation.

They're kind of the bigger party.

So I want to ask what you would do in this exercise.

We're not going to do this exercise today,but it kind of motivates some of what we're going to talk about.

So if you were one of the smaller parties,Pluto or Venus,let's put you in the smallest position.

Let's put you in the Venus position.

How would you go about this?

And you would know that it's a coalition exercise.

So going in,you might think,okay,do I form a coalition with Neptune or should I form a coalition with Pluto?

Should I try to form a coalition with Pluto?

How do you think you would?

About that decision.

How would you even think about that decision?

So,you can go through the math and the points and think about it that way,but you might also think about the individuals.

Who is in the role of Neptune?

What relationship do I have with them?

What kind of trust do I have with them?

And the same with Pluto.

So,you would take all this information in and then you would make a decision:all right,am I going to place my chips with the big guy,Neptune,or the smaller guy,the kind of medium-sized person,Pluto,as I go in and try to form a coalition?

And that decision captures the two main kinds of coalitions that we see in the world:one being the balance of power.

This is the long-standing dynamic we see in political science where the presence of a single dominant power leads smaller powers to band together.

So,in our example,we just came from,Pluto and Venus want to work together to kind of counterbalance the bigger Neptune.

But there is another kind of bandwagoning is the other kind of coalition where the smaller powers vie with each other in order to ally with the single dominant power.

So,this is a Venus saying,Hey,why would I want to go to little Pluto when I can go to big Neptune?

More likely to win that way.

So,these are the two kinds that we see,and this is often the decision that you face when you are a smaller party trying to decide what kind of coalition to form.

So,how do you know which way to go?

If you're going to form a coalition,you go with balance of power or do you go with bandwagoning?

And sometimes you're just observing this happen with other people.

So,how do you predict what's going to happen?

Is it going to be a balance of power coalition or is it going to be a bandwagoning coalition?

If we can understand that,we'll better understand coalitions.

So,broadly,there are two bases for a coalition:one is interest.Think of this as kind of the economics of an arrangement.

Another is identity.

You can think of this as kind of the emotions of the arrangement or the coalition.

So,let's dive into both the interest-based coalitions and the identity/slash/emotions-based coalitions.

So,an example of interest-based comes with the very colorful name Baptists and Bootleggers.

This goes back to 1980s research on U.S.legislation.

And the particular example they're talking about are in the U.S.,they're called blue laws,where the distribution of alcohol is restricted on certain days of the week.

So,for example,in some states or some cities,you can't sell beer and wine on a Sunday.

So,where does this come from?

Why do these laws some of these laws still exist,by the way?

So,the analysis says that basically there are quote Baptists,they're not necessarily actual Baptists,but they are religious leaders.

And what they bring to the coalition is the moral high ground,the kind of the explanation of the cause.

But they're also the bootleggers,and these are the people with the financial interest in making this happen.

So,with these blue laws,they are the bar owners.

They would love for there to be no other place to get alcohol except bars on Sundays,and so their interest is financial.

And to make that happen,they can provide campaign funds.

So,you have this very powerful coalition you wouldn't necessarily expect together,they don't seem like the kinds of people that would work together,but because they have common economic interest,they form a strong coalition.

And of course,it's effective because for The legislature's perspective,you have the moral high ground saying you're doing it for religious reasons,but you also get campaign funds because the bootleggers could provide that as well.

Bruce Yandel,who created this theory back in the early 80s,says durable social regulation occurs when it's demanded by both of two distinctly different groups.

So it takes that complementarity,but with a common economic interest,to form a very strong coalition.

So more recently,we've seen examples such as Korean Energy,where big financial interests have come in to back green energy,especially in,say,California.

And it looks like it's for environmental reasons,but in fact,if you look at the reasons,there's regulatory advantages,and actually they're in there for investment.

That's what they do,of course.

But because they've got kind of the moral high ground and the financial interest,it's a complementary and strong economic-based coalition.

So there's a very rational calculus available when you're making these decisions based on interest.What's the expected value of allying with A,party A,for example,versus the expected value of allying with party B?

So just go through the math.

What's the probability that A wins times the payoff to me if A wins versus the probability that B wins times the payoff to me if B wins?

So this sounds very rational and very narrow,and that's the claim here that many coalitions get done on exactly those grounds.

In short,which party is likely to win,and how will I be treated as a partner to that party if they do?

So one of the challenges with these kinds of coalitions is that they're dynamic and that people are kind of always hopping around trying to find a better deal.

There's a great quote from Speaker Boehner,a longtime speaker in the U.S.House,who said,I like to describe my job as trying to get 218 frogs in a wheelbarrow long enough to pass a bill.

It's hard to do.

218 being the one vote majority to pass legislation in the House.

The reason it's hard is because he might get everyone lined up for a moment and then somebody else is going to start trying to poach them.

And because they're doing this calculus,they might be able to raise the ante just enough that they'll jump out of the wheelbarrow and form a coalition with somebody else.

My favorite example,and one of the most powerful examples,comes from a study of alliance formation and civil wars.

So this was done in recent years looking at civil wars,multi-party civil wars,so there is this,so there's room for coalitions over an almost 200-year period of time.

So the cover here is from Afghanistan,but in fact,they looked at civil wars in 53 different areas.

And this is Fotini Christia.

She writes,history is replete with warring leaders changing sides.

This is surprising to us because we tend to think,especially from the cover here,that these would be religious-based conflicts,very moral,tribal-based conflicts.

But in fact,they observe that warring groups will aim to side with the winner so long as they can have a credible guarantee that the winner will not strip them of power once victory is accomplished.

There appears to be No such thing as an impossible alliance.

This is great research.

This is not intuitive.

This is not what we would have expected.

But they find that interest,this rational calculus,drives behavior so much that it can overcome these very seemingly deeply held identity issues.

I've talked with special forces students,students who previously were in the special forces,who talk about being in the field and seeing men actually change sides during battle as the calculus changes during battle and one side looks more likely to win.

Now,the other form of coalitions,the other basis on which coalitions get formed,are identity,more emotion-based,could be loyalty.

And it leads one to sacrifice narrow economic interests in service for these other objectives.

An example also from the military world comes from the UK and France alliance in World War I.

So they did not have a formal treaty when World War I started.

They had some previous relationship,but they didn't have a formal treaty.

And when Germany invaded Belgium and then France,the UK had to decide whether to come into the war on the side of France.

This is a memo from inside the Foreign Secretary Office in Great Britain.

And they write,The argument that there is no written bond binding us to France is strictly correct.

There is no contractual obligation,but the Entente has been made,strengthened,put to the test,and celebrated in a manner justifying the belief that a moral bond was being forged.

The whole policy of the Entente can have no meaning if it does not signify that in a just quarrel,England would stand by her friends.

This honorable expectation has been raised.

We cannot repudiate it without exposing our good name to grave criticism.

So you see,this is such a different basis for the coalition than the calculus we talked about before.

This is morality,this is honor,and indeed,Great Britain did join on the side of France.

We don't know what influence this memo had,but we know that there were people making exactly this kind of argument.

Here's the same story in kind of visual terms.Emotions can play a big role,drive the abused parties,the smaller parties together to team up and exact revenge.

So broadly,we have this interest versus identity.

Appealing to self-interest or the economics means the coalition candidate pool is broad.

You can bring anybody in as long as you can show that their economic interests are well served.

But it means that your ties to anybody you do bring in are relatively weak,relatively shallow.

Alternatively,you can appeal to identity or emotion,which provides a much stronger connection,but it greatly restricts the number of people you can ally with.

These are the trade-offs.

There's no right answer.

There's no better way to go.

It's two different ways we see coalitions formed.

Both matter.

One of the bottom lines is that it's risky to neglect either one.

They're both opportunities for you to form a coalition,and they're also risks to you from others trying to poach your coalitional partners.

3-02-01.12_联盟案例

我们来看两个来自截然不同领域的简短例子。

一个是来自电视，情景喜剧《老友记》。

这部剧在九十年代是个巨大的意外成功。

在剧集开播前，这六位演员基本都还是无名之辈。

按照电视行业的常规做法，他们各自单独签订了合同。

然而，这部剧真的火了。

然后有趣的事情发生了，他们开始集体谈判。

是作为一个整体单位与制片公司谈判，而不是六个独立的演员。

有趣的是，他们拿的片酬都一样。

所以，尽管比如说詹妮弗·安妮斯顿的名气要大得多，他们实际上拿的片酬是一样的。

从第三季到第十季，都是这样的安排。

到剧集结束时，他们每人的片酬达到了每集一百万美元。

他们每年拍摄二十到二十四集。

所以这些人通过联盟，每人赚了两千万美元。

那么，他们为什么要这么做呢？

你觉得他们为什么会接受平等片酬？

你认为从长远来看，他们的情况更好了吗？

为什么会这样？

所以有些人认为，这改变了片场的氛围，某种程度上维系了他们之间的关系。

也许如果没有那种平等的安排，他们根本不可能走到第十季，也不可能取得那么好的成绩。

但是，除了通过联盟，马特·勒布朗又怎么可能通过其他方式拿到和詹妮弗·安妮斯顿一样的片酬呢？

另一个例子来自南太平洋的金枪鱼渔业。

这个例子出自《石板》杂志的一篇文章。

金枪鱼渔业的故事是这样的，历史上，那些大型捕捞船队，从日本、英国或美国远道而来，进入这些岛屿周围的当地水域，也就是它们的领海。

当这样做的时候，你必须付费。

而他们基本上就是让这些岛屿相互竞价。

谁收我们最少的费用，允许我们在他们的水域捕鱼？

而这些岛屿，因为这是它们最重要的收入来源之一，没有多少议价能力。

结果捕捞权就被越压越低。

多年来，情况一直如此。

后来，它们终于意识到，嗯，我们需要合作，本质上。

我们需要组建一个联盟。

它们这么做了，开始作为一个整体进行谈判，完全扭转了谈判局面。

现在，轮到它们让船队之间相互竞价了，问谁愿意付最高的价钱在我们的领海捕鱼。

它们发现自己拥有了巨大的议价能力，甚至能够改善渔业的健康状况。

特别是，金枪鱼船队可以在国际公海捕鱼。

没人能限制这一点。

但这对于当地的金枪鱼渔业是有害的，因为金枪鱼可不知道自己是在领海还是公海游动。

如果你想尽可能健康地管理渔业，你就需要以某种方式限制国际公海上的活动。

通过组建这个联盟，这些国家获得了巨大的议价能力，它们甚至能够强制限制船队在国际公海上的活动。

这是一个绝佳的例子，展示了联盟的力量，以及弱势一方看到这一点，并因此扭转谈判桌的绝佳例子。

英文原文

So let's look at two quick examples from two very different places.

One is from television,the sitcom Friends.

This was a huge kind of a surprise hit in the 90s.

And before the show started,these six actors were essentially unknown.

And as is typically done on television,they negotiated their contracts individually.

However,the show really took off.

And then the interesting thing that happened is that they started negotiating collectively.

It was a single unit negotiating with the production company instead of six individual actors.

And interestingly,they all took equal pay.

So despite having quite a bit of disparity between the celebrity of,say,Jennifer Aniston,they were actually paid the same.

So in years three through 10,this was the arrangement.

And by the time they were done,they were paid a million dollars per episode per actor.

And they shot 20 or 24 episodes a year.

So these guys were making$20 million each through a coalition.

Now,why would they do such a thing?

Why do you think they might accept equal pay?

Do you think they were better off in the long run?

Why would that be?

So some people think that it changed the dynamic on the set,that it preserved the relationships in a way.

Maybe they would never have made it to year 10 and done as well if they hadn't gone in with that kind of equal arrangement.

But by what other means,other than a coalition,would Matt Le Blanc have ever been paid the same as Jennifer Aniston?

Another example is from the tuna fisheries in the South Pacific.

This example comes from a Slate magazine article.

And the story with the tuna fisheries is that historically the fleets,the big fleets,have come down from Japan or the UK or the US and gone into these local waters,the territorial waters around these islands.

And when you do that,you have to pay.

And they would basically just auction these islands off against each other.

Who's going to charge us the least to allow us to fish in their waters?

And the islands,because this is one of their most important sources of revenue,didn't have much bargaining power.

And they got these fishing rights bid down.

And for years,this was the arrangement.

And then finally,they realized,well,we need to work together,essentially.

We need to form a coalition.

And they did that and started bargaining as a block and completely turned the bargaining tables.

So now they were auctioning the fleets off against each other,asking who was going to pay the most to fish in our territorial waters.

And they found they had so much bargaining power that they were able to improve the health of the fisheries.

In particular,a tuna fleet can fish in international waters.

Nobody can restrict that.

But that's damaging to the tuna fisheries down there because tuna don't know whether they're swimming in territorial waters or international waters.

If you want to manage the fishery as healthily as possible,you want to restrict in some way what's going on in the international waters.

By forming this coalition,the countries had so much bargaining power,they were able to enforce restrictions on what the fleets could do even in the international waters.

Fantastic example of the power of coalitions and a smaller party seeing that and flipping the negotiation table as a result.

3-02-01.13_联盟的建议

好的，在本次讲座中，我们来谈谈关于联盟的实践方案。

我们观察到的最佳实践有哪些？

你如何组建一个联盟？

你又如何维系一个联盟？

我们为你准备了四大要点。

广泛撒网，考虑博弈大局，开好会前会，最后是，先予后取。

我们来逐一讨论这几点。

首先，广泛撒网。

我想引用布鲁斯·布恩诺·德·梅斯奎塔的话。

他是纽约大学的教授，除了做研究之外，他还为大型公司和国家提供咨询，试图预测那些重大难题的走向，比如伊朗在核弹问题上会怎么做，巴基斯坦军方会采取什么行动，诸如此类。

在他的书中，他写道，本质上，该模型寻找的是那些如果认为对己方有利，就愿意相互靠拢的参与者之间可能形成的组合。

简而言之，这个模型预测的就是联盟。

他的模型常常得出令人惊讶的结果。

它不仅系统地梳理了我们所知道和预期的那些显而易见的问题，也梳理了我们未曾察觉的那些隐性问题。

多年审视他的模型让他发现，冲突几乎总是有隐藏的解决方案。

他的模型之所以能起作用，原因之一就是他尽可能广泛地寻找可能性。

他会考虑所有可能的联盟。

这不是我们自然而然会做的事。

因此，一个重要的实践方案就是：广泛思考，创造性地思考联盟伙伴。

我们在哈佛的同事，拉克斯和塞贝纽斯，在他们2006年关于谈判的书中，指出了其中一些可能的相关方。

比方说，如果你在和某人谈判，你可能需要考虑的不仅仅是那个必须给予正式批准的人。

想想那些能影响决策者的人，比如那些能在他们耳边说话的人。

谁对你提供的东西估值最高？

这一点对于那些试图向组织销售产品或服务的企业家来说至关重要。

在那个组织里，谁最能从这个产品或服务中受益？谁可能是潜在的联盟伙伴？

谁能阻止决策？

谁的动机与你不同？

谁需要执行你谈判达成的协议？

这些都是关键的成员。

他们可能有助于你渡过难关，或者可能是实际完成某件事所必需的。

第二个实践方案，考虑博弈大局。

如果你把谈判框定得太狭隘，就会错失机会。

如果你认为你只是在谈判或试图影响某个非常具体的事情，而忘记了所有与之相关、其他人可能正在考虑的事情。

那么，如果其他人正在考虑建立一个更广泛的联盟、拥有更广泛的利益，你就容易受到他们能带来而你却没想到的人的影响。

那么，建立联盟还有哪些其他基础呢？

嗯，我们提到了经济方面，利益，一个方可能拥有的狭隘的理性利益，但还有那些情感上的考量。

比如身份认同、忠诚度，在某些情况下，是怨恨或愤怒，在某些情况下，是善意。

所以关键在于，你要知道对方在意什么。

他们在意的东西不一定和你一样。

你可能认为这纯粹是一场经济谈判或一个纯粹的经济联盟。

但实际上，他们可能拥有这些情感或基于身份的利益。

这对你来说是错失的机会，而对于其他与你作对的人来说，则是一个机会。

实践方案三：这是一个非常基本的，但也许是最重要的一点：开好会前会。

我总是惊讶地发现，有些专业人士居然不经常使用这一招。

这绝对需要成为你工具箱里的一员。

谈判总是会受到影响的，常常受到限制，有时甚至在正式会谈开始前很久就已经尘埃落定了。

所以，在这些预先的会面中，你要做一些情报收集、试探一下、建立信任、打好基础。

在某些情况下，你是在建立联盟。

这张图片里，我们看到几个人坐在酒吧的角落里。

会议的形式不一定非得是这样。

这可以是路过某人的办公室，敲敲门，在饮水机旁碰见他们，给他们发短信，打个电话，发封邮件。

这些都算作是开过会前会。

这些是在你真正坐下来之前，与各方进行接触的方式。

丘吉尔有句名言：与盟友并肩作战固然有诸多不利，但最糟糕的莫过于孤军奋战。

你希望在进入会议之前就知道自己是否有盟友。

实践方案四，第四个也是最后一个实践方案：先予后取。

这个观点与心理学和社会学研究了数十年的一个主题相关。

人性使然，我们倾向于对他人做出对等的回应。

近年来亚当·格兰特在他的书《给予与索取》中对这一点阐述得很好。

但普遍的观察是，无论行为采取何种形式，积极的形式，比如好意、礼物、尊重和谈判中的让步，我们都倾向于以同样的方式回报。

这也适用于所有负面行为。

所以，当我们亏待别人，或者他们亏待我们时，我们都会倾向于做出回应。

这既是组建联盟的机会，如果你使用这些负面行为，也会阻碍你组建联盟，这是一种风险。

这一点，我们再次在猿类身上看到。

让我们回到弗朗斯·德瓦尔对黑猩猩的研究，看看联盟是多么基础，这种互惠行为又是多么根本。

他说，黑猩猩的群体生活就像一个市场，交易着权力、性、情感、支持、不容忍和敌意。

两个基本规则是：善有善报，以及以眼还眼，以牙还牙。

所以，我们天生就是如此。

我们生来如此。

我们从观察黑猩猩中知道这一点。

德瓦尔还举了另一个例子，灵长类动物学家托希沙达·纳希达描述了莫哈莱山脉一只阿尔法雄性黑猩猩的案例，它通过一套精密的贿赂系统，将它的头衔维持了异常长的时间，超过十年。

十年太离谱了，因为黑猩猩通常处于等级制度顶端的时间也就十八个月左右。

所以，这差不多算是个三西格玛偏差事件。

它是怎么做到的呢？

它有选择性地把肉分给那些它可以用其支持来对抗潜在挑战者的个体。

所以，猿类也会这样做。

猿类也在使用联盟，而这正在影响它们的影响力。

这显然是我们也能做到的事情。

其中一个启示是，你可能需要承担一些。

代价，才能建立一个更稳定、更可持续的联盟。

因此，你可能会通过接受较低的回报——甚至在短期内可能被视为不公平的回报——来改善你的长期地位。

所以，这可能就是我们确实看到一些联盟中，回报的差距比你预期的要更加平等的原因之一。

我最喜欢的一个例子来自大学体育，美国的大学体育联盟。

各队作为联盟的一部分进行比赛。

学校们组成联盟。

学校需要做的一件事就是决定如何分配他们的电视转播收入。

这是他们收入的主要来源。

他们从大学体育项目中获得的收入，有很大一部分来自这些巨额电视转播合同。

你如何在联盟的所有不同成员之间分配这笔钱呢？

以美国两个不同地区的不同联盟中的两个组织为例，德克萨斯大学和阿拉巴马大学。

阿拉巴马红潮队，这是过去一二十年里最成功的橄榄球项目，也是有史以来最成功的项目之一。

他们可以说是东南联盟的旗舰项目。

而东南联盟被认为是稳定的、成功的，可能是过去一二十年里美国最好的橄榄球联盟。

他们如何分配电视转播收入呢？

这是主要的收入来源，他们平均分配，每个学校拿相同的一份。

所以，从强大如阿拉巴马，到规模较小、可能不那么强的范德堡大学，他们拿到的电视转播费是一样的。

事实上，他们的联盟如此强大，以至于同等的一份还会分给联盟办公室。

他们就是这样看重他们的联盟，而且他们在分配上比你预期的要平均得多。

结果，他们拥有了令人难以置信的……这也是其他因素共同作用的结果。

但其中一个因素就是这个平均分配。

他们拥有这个强大的联盟。

相比之下，德克萨斯大学和十二大联盟，则以最不稳定的联盟之一而闻名。

在过去几年里，随着学校纷纷离开，他们已经失去了一些大学成员。

学校们经常给出的一个原因，观察家们认为发生这种情况的原因之一，是因为他们不把钱在学校之间平均分配。

德克萨斯大学，可以说是十二大联盟的旗舰机构，总是要求并从电视转播合同中获得远比其他学校多的收入。

我们认为这是他们联盟较弱的原因之一。

当然，德克萨斯可以辩称这很公平。

他们拿得多才公平，但这需要付出代价。代价就是联盟变弱了，而从长远来看，他们最终得到的可能会更少。

我们不确定，但这很好地说明了，作为谈判桌上实力更强的一方，你可能需要少拿一点，你可能需要少拿一点，来巩固一个更强大的联盟，并获得更可持续的长期回报。

以上就是四个实践方案。

广泛撒网，考虑博弈大局，开好会前会，先予后取。

英文原文

All right,in this lecture,we want to talk about prescriptions for coalitions.

What are the best practices we see out there?

How do you make a coalition?

How do you hold a coalition?

We have four big ones for you.

Cast a wide net,consider the metagame,have the meeting before the meeting,and finally,give to get.

Let's talk a little bit about each one of these.

So,cast a wide net.

I want to quote from Bruce Bueno de Masquita.

He is a professor at NYU who,in addition to doing research,he consults to large companies and countries trying to predict what's going to happen on these big,hard questions like what's Iran going to do around nuclear bombs,what's the Pakistan military going to do,that kind of thing.

In his book,he writes,in essence,the model looks for possible groupings of players who would be willing to shift their positions toward one another if they thought that doing so would be to their advantage.

In short,the model predicts coalitions.

His model often produces surprising results.

It methodically works through not only the obvious coalitions we know and expect,but also the invisible ones that we don't.

Years of peering at his model have shown him that conflicts almost always have hidden solutions.

One of the things that's going on with his model is that he's looking as broadly as possible.

He's considering all possible coalitions.

This is not what we do naturally.

And so one of the big prescriptions is think broadly,think creatively about coalitional partners.

Our colleagues at Harvard,Lax and Sabanius,in one of their books on negotiation in 2006,suggests who some of these parties might be.

So if you're negotiating with somebody,for example,you might want to think beyond just the person who has to give formal approval.

Think about those who influence the decision makers,who might be in their ear,for example.

Who has the highest value for what you offer?

This is something that's terrifically important to entrepreneurs who are trying to sell into an organization a product or a service.

Who is it in that organization who would most benefit from that product or service,possible coalitional partner?

Who can block decisions?

Who has misaligned incentives?

Who has to implement something that you negotiate?

These are all critical members.

They might be helpful in getting over the hump or they might be necessary to actually get something done.

Second prescription,consider the meta game.

So you miss opportunities if you frame negotiations too narrowly.

If you think you're only negotiating or trying to influence on a very particular matter and you forget all the matters that are related to it that others might be thinking about.

So if others are thinking about a broader coalition,broader interest,you're going to be exposed to people they can bring to the table that you're not thinking about.

So what are additional grounds for coalitions?

Well,we've named the economic side,the interest,the narrow rational interest a party might have,but there are also those emotional considerations.

So identity,loyalty,in some cases,spite or anger,in some cases,beneficence.

So what's critical is that you know what the other party cares about.

They don't necessarily care about the same things you do.

You may think it's a strictly economic negotiation or a strictly economic coalition.

But in fact,they might have these emotional or identity-based interests.

Those are missed opportunities for you,and it's an opportunity for somebody else who's working against you.

Prescription number three:this is a very basic one,but perhaps the most important one:have the meeting before the meeting.

I'm always surprised to find professionals who don't use this all the time.

This needs to be in your toolbox for sure.

So,negotiations are always influenced,often constrained,and sometimes even settled long before the official talks begin.

So,in these advanced meetings,you're going to do some intelligence gathering,temperature taking,credibility building,groundwork laying.

In some,you're doing alliance creating.

In this picture,we see a couple of guys sitting in a bar in a corner.

It doesn't necessarily have to be the style of meeting.

This can be just swinging by somebody's office,knocking on the door,bumping into them at the water cooler,texting them,giving them a call,dropping an email.

These all count as meeting before the meetings.

These are ways of touching base with parties before you actually sit down.

There's a great quote from Churchill:There is only one thing worse than fighting with allies,and that is fighting without them.

You want to know before you get into the meeting whether or not you have allies with you or not.

Prescription four,the fourth and final prescription:give to get.

So,this ties into a topic that's been studied in psychology and sociology for decades.

And the human nature is we're inclined to respond in kind to other people.

It's been talked about very well by Adam Grant in recent years in his book,Give and Take.

But the general observation is that,regardless of the form behavior takes,positive form,favors,gifts,respect,and negotiation concessions,we're inclined to give back in kind.

This applies to all negative behavior as well.

So,when we mistreat people or when they mistreat us,we're inclined to respond.

This is an opportunity for forming coalitions,and it's a risk if you're using these negative behaviors that'll get in the way of your forming coalitions.

So,this again,we see in the apes.

Let's go back to Franz De Waal and his study of chimpanzees,looking at how fundamental coalitions are and how fundamental this reciprocity behavior is.

He says,chimpanzee group life is like a market in power,sex,affection,support,intolerance,and hostility.

The two basic rules are:one good turn deserves another,and an eye for an eye,a tooth for a tooth.

So,again,we're wired this way.

We're hardwired this way.

We know it from watching it in the chimps.

Another example from De Waal talks about a primatologist,Toshishada Nashida,describing the case of an alpha chimp in the Mohale Mountains who maintained his rank for an extraordinarily long time,over a decade,through an elaborate system of bribery.

So,a decade's ridiculous because chimps are usually at the top of the hierarchy for 18 months or so.

So,this is something like a three-stander deviation event.

How did he do it?

He distributed meat selectively to those individuals whose support he could use against potential challengers.

So,apes are doing this.

Apes are using coalitions,and it's making a difference in their influence.

This is clearly something available to us.

One of the implications is that you might bear some.

costs in order to have a more stable,sustainable coalition.

So you might improve your long-term position by accepting lower,perhaps what even might be seen as unfair payoffs in the short term.

So this may be one of the reasons we do see coalitions where the disparity in payoffs is more equal than you might expect.

So one of my favorite examples comes from University Athletics,Collegiate Athletics in the United States.

Teams compete as a part of a conference.

So schools group together in conferences.

And one of the things schools have to do is decide how to share their television revenues.

This is the primary source of their revenues.

A huge percentage of what they receive from college athletics come from these big television contracts.

How do you divide that money across all the different members of the conference?

Take,for example,two organizations in two different parts of the country in different conferences,the University of Texas and the University of Alabama.

So Alabama Crimson Tie,this is the most successful football program of the last 10 or 20 years and one of the most successful of all times.

They're kind of the flagship program of the Southeastern Conference.

And the Southeastern Conference is known as being a stable,successful,probably the best football conference in the country in the last 10 or 20 years.

How do they divide their television revenues?

The primary source of revenues,they divide it equally,equal parts to each school.

So from big,strong Alabama down to little,maybe not so strong Vanderbilt,they receive the same television monies.

In fact,they have such a strong coalition that another equal share goes to the league office.

That's how much they value their coalition,and they pay more equally there than you might expect.

As a result,they have this incredibly,the result of other things as well.

But one of the factors is this equal split.

They have this strong coalition.

Contrast that with the University of Texas and the Big 12,known as being one of the most unstable coalitions.

They've lost university affiliates over the last few years as they migrated away.

One of the reasons schools often give,one of the reasons observers think this happens,is because they don't share their money equally across the schools.

So the University of Texas,kind of the flagship organization of Big 12,has always demanded and received far more pay from the television contracts than the other schools.

We think that this is one of the reasons that they have a weaker one.

Now,Texas could argue it's fair.

It's only fair that they get paid more,but it comes at a cost.It comes at the cost of a weaker coalition,and in the long term,they may end up with less.

We don't know for sure,but it's a great illustration of you might take a little bit less as the bigger party at the table,you might take a little bit less to secure a stronger coalition and a more sustainable long-term payoff.

So four prescriptions.

Cast a wide net,consider the metagame,have the meeting before the meeting,and give to get.

3-02-01.14_案例：华盛顿广场公园

咱们做一个微型案例研究，一个真实的例子，探讨一下在需要的时候，你可能会如何去组建一个联盟。

这个例子来自纽约市，位于格林威治村核心地带的华盛顿广场公园，以及一场持续了数十年、但在五十年代真正白热化的斗争。

这里的关键人物是罗伯特·摩西。

我们之前在课程的另一讲中听说过罗伯特·摩西，他曾担任纽约市的交通负责人、交通专员长达数十年，被认为是纽约历史上最有影响力的人物之一。

他掌权大约有四十五年之久。

在那之前，他提出的项目从无败绩。

他这次遇到了什么？

他遇到了简·雅各布斯。

这是简晚年的照片。

这张照片拍摄于二十一世纪初，距离他们那场斗争已经过去足足四五十年了。

但让我们来看看当时发生了什么。

事情的起因是，摩西想将第五大道穿过公园。

第五大道从北边延伸下来，在到达华盛顿广场公园那个著名的拱门处时就终止了。

摩西想让它穿过公园，把公园一分为二，这不仅会彻底改变公园的面貌，还会因增加该区域的交通流量而改变整个社区。

这是一个高度拥挤的休闲区，当地居民对此反对声浪很高。

简·雅各布斯就住在这个区域，她虽然不是第一个发起这个联盟的人，但她很早就加入了联盟，并且事实证明，她对联盟至关重要。

所以问问你自己，如果你在五十年代住在华盛顿广场公园附近，而摩西想修建一条穿过你所在社区的四车道、又宽又大的繁忙大道，你会怎么做？

你面对的是纽约最有影响力的人物。

你怎么才能阻止他？

你会想什么办法去阻止他？

想想看你会怎么去组建一个联盟。

我们相信联盟的原因之一是，当你没有权力、处于这些相对没有影响力的位置时，联盟是你拥有的最佳资源之一。

那你会怎么做呢？

你可能会想到的一个办法是，嗯，当然先去找我的邻居们，搞个请愿书，收集一些签名。

当然，这也是他们最初采取的行动。

而这一步是否足够，取决于该提案背后的支持力量有多强。

结果证明，这样做是不够的。

那你下一步该做什么？

他们开始尝试引入媒体，并且用了很有创意的方式。

比如说，他们组织抗议活动，而且深谙媒体运作之道，他们让孩子们出来亮相，并极力强调这对孩子们的影响。

最终，人们开始报道这件事。

顺便提一句，那时正是《村声》周报初创之际。

《村声》周报，美国第一份另类周报，在纽约创刊，就始于那个时代，他们当然很支持这项事业。

他们还招募了为一些大报、日报撰写建筑专栏的作家，也为他们的事业发声。

他们就这样把媒体拉了进来。

他们还会做什么？

他们开始与年轻的政治家合作。

那些位高权重的老牌政治家不愿与摩西对抗，但也许一些年轻政客愿意。

比如，埃德·科赫，他最终成为了纽约市长，他当时参与进来，是因为他需要一个事业来打响自己的名号。

他们开始考虑名人效应。

结果发现，当时美国最著名的女性之一，埃莉诺·罗斯福，就住在格林威治村，她非常乐意用自己的名人效应支持这项事业。

就这样，每采取一步行动，每增加一个联盟成员，他们的力量就增强一分。

最终，经过多年努力，他们终于建立了足够强大的联盟，吸引了足够的关注，使得他们能够去找那个区域里唯一可能真正阻止摩西的政治人物——那就是州务卿迪萨皮奥。

迪萨皮奥有能力施加足够的影响力。

他看到了这些人想要什么，以及他们多年来积聚起来的力量，最终成功阻止了摩西将第五大道穿过公园的计划。

所以，在斗争最激烈的时候，摩西最后一次绝望地试图阻止预算委员会关闭公园禁止车辆通行，但未能成功，他说，没有人反对这个计划，没有人，没有人，没有人，只有一群母亲。

嗯，事实证明，母亲们如果能组建起联盟，也能产生巨大的影响力。

他们已经超越了母亲和孩子的层面，联合了像科赫这样的政治家，联合了埃莉诺·罗斯福，最终联合了州务卿迪萨皮奥。

顺便说一下，简·雅各布斯后来声名远扬。

她写了一本书，叫《美国大城市的死与生》。

她甚至没有受过城市政策、城市发展方面的专业训练，但她写的这本书，却被全美国的公共政策学院用作教材。

我们从这个案例中学到了什么？从雅各布斯身上得到的一些启示。

她的联盟之所以如此有效，一个原因在于它在多个层面运作。

她组织了普通民众的街头抗议。

她获得了报纸的报道和社论支持，不只一家报纸，而是多家报纸。

她向多个政府部门和候选人施加了政治压力，她还得到了名人的公开支持。

你看，这涉及多少个不同的层面。

最成功的联盟正是要在多个层面上运作。

当然，摩西也在试图做同样的事情。

摩西拥有各种手段，他会在媒体上说一套，背地里又会进行秘密会谈。

所以他面对的压力也很大。

他们面对的压力也很大。

需要那样一个精心策划的联盟才能办成这件事。

这也是一个极具战略眼光的联盟。

她是有意为之的。

他们对于如何构建这个联盟是有明确意图的。

他们赢得了每一层新的支持。

他们必须在一个层面上建立起来，才能扩展到下一个层面。

联盟背后的一个重要理念是，你往往无法直接攻击你的目标。

你必须迂回曲折，间接地接近目标。

这些人不可能直接去找迪萨皮奥。

如果他们第一天就直接去敲迪萨皮奥的门，他根本不会听他们的。

他根本不会在意。

但他们积累了足够的支持，直到他不得不去倾听他们的声音。

所以，最后总结一下关于联盟的几点思考。

第一点，也许也是最重要的一点教训是，你应该广泛地寻找潜在的联盟。

它们是弱势群体的关键资源，也是强势群体的主要威胁。

你难免会处于弱势的谈判地位。

有时在这种情况下，你最有力的筹码就是一个联盟。

另一方面，你有时也会处于强势地位。

那么最大的风险是什么？

最大的风险就是出现一个反对你的联盟。

所以我们都需要从正反两方面留意这些联盟的存在。

最后一点，执行上的失败，几乎毫无例外都是因为未能成功建立有效的联盟。

这是你影响力工具箱中的一项关键工具。

英文原文

Let's do a mini case study,real-world example,and ask how you might have gone about forming a coalition when one was needed.

The example comes from New York City,Washington Square Park in the heart of Greenwich Village,and a battle that took place over multiple decades,but really got heated in the 50s.

The key actor here is Robert Moses.

We've heard about Robert Moses in another lecture earlier in the class,but he was the director of transportation,the transportation commissioner in New York for decades and known as being one of the most influential men in the history of New York.

He held power for something like 45 years.

He had never proposed a project that didn't get done until this point.

What did he run into?

He ran into Jane Jacobs.

This is a picture of Jane from later in her life.

This was in the 2000s,so this is a good 40,50 years after their battle.

But let's see what took place.

The setup was that Moses wanted to take Fifth Avenue through the park.

So Fifth Avenue comes down from the north and ends when it hits the famous arc there in Washington Square Park.

Moses wanted to run it through the park,wanted to divide the park,and it would have dramatically changed not only the park,but the neighborhood by increasing the traffic through that area.

This is a highly congested recreational area,and there was a lot of opposition from those who lived in the area against this.

So Jane Jacobs lived in the area,and she was not the first to form this coalition,but she was early on into the coalition,and she proved to be critical to it.

So ask yourself,if you were living in Washington Square Park in the 50s and Moses wanted to build this avenue through your neighborhood,it was four lane,big four lane,busy street,what would you have done about it?

You're facing the most influential guy in New York.

How could you stop him?

How would you have gone about stopping him?

So think about how you would hopefully form a coalition.

So one of the reasons we believe in coalitions is that when you don't have power,when you're in these relatively uninfluential positions,it's one of the best resources you have.

So what are you going to do?

So one of the places you might think about,well,let's get my neighbors,of course,form a petition,get some signatures.

And this,of course,is what they started with.

And then that may or may not be sufficient,depending on how strong the weight is behind the proposal.

It turns out it wasn't sufficient.

So what do you do next?

They started trying to bring media in,and they did it in creative ways.

So,for example,they had protests and being wise to the ways of the media,they trotted kids out,and they really emphasized the impact on children.

And eventually people started writing about this.

This was the dawn of the Village Voice,by the way.

The Village Voice,the first alternative weekly newspaper in the U.S.,started in New York,started at this era,and of course they loved this cause.

They recruited those who wrote architecture columns for some of the bigger newspapers,the dailies,to write on behalf of their cause as well.

So they pulled the media in here.

What else are they going to do?

They start working with young politicians.

The big established politicians don't want to take on Moses,but maybe some of the younger guys would.

So Ed Koch,for example,eventually the mayor of New York,got involved because he needed kind of a cause to get his name out there.

They started thinking about celebrities.

It turns out that one of the most famous women in the country at the time,Eleanor Roosevelt,lived in Greenwich Village,and she was very happy to throw her celebrity behind the cause.

And so with each of these steps,each of these additions to their coalitions,it added to their power.

Eventually,and this was after years,eventually they had a strong enough coalition and enough attention that they were able to go to probably the only politician in the area who could actually stop Moses,and that was Secretary of State Di Sapio.

Di Sapio was able to exert enough influence.

He saw what these guys wanted and the power they had mustered over years and was able to stop Moses from actually extending Fifth Avenue down through the park.

So at the height of the battle,Moses,in a final desperate and unsuccessful attempt to keep the Board of Estimate from closing the park to the traffic,said,there is nobody against this,nobody,nobody,nobody,but a bunch of mothers.

Well,it turns out mothers,if they're able to form a coalition,can be very influential.

They had gone beyond mothers and children to politicians like Koch,to Eleanor Roosevelt,and eventually to Secretary of State Di Sapio.

Jane Jacobs,by the way,went on to much greater fame.

She has a book called The Death and Life of Great American Cities.

She wasn't even trained in urban policy,urban development,but she wrote the book that public policy schools all over the country have used to teach in their schools.

What do we learn from this?Some thoughts from Jacobs.

One reason her coalition was so effective is that it played at multiple levels.

She had street-level protests with individuals.

She had newspaper coverage and editorials,not just one newspaper,multiple papers.

She had political pressure from multiple offices and candidates,and she had celebrity endorsements.

You see how many different levels there are to that.

The best coalitions do play at multiple levels.

Moses was,of course,trying to do the same thing.

Moses had all kinds of levers,and he would say one thing in press,and he'd have quiet meetings behind the scenes also.

So he was up against a lot.

They were up against a lot.

It took that kind of sophisticated coalition to get it done.

It was also an extremely strategic coalition.

She was intentional.

They were intentional on how they built this thing.

They earned each new layer of support.

They had to build it at one level before they could expand it to the next level.

One of the big ideas behind coalitions is that you often can't go directly at your target.

You have to go circuitously,indirectly.

These guys couldn't have gone straight to Di Sapio.

Had they just knocked on Di Sapio's door on day one,he wouldn't have listened to them.

He wouldn't have cared.

But they built enough support until he kind of needed to listen to them.

So some closing thoughts on coalitions.

The first and maybe the main lesson here is that you should look broadly for potential coalitions.

They are the key resource for the weak and they are the key threat to the strong.

You will find yourself in weak bargaining positions.

Sometimes the number one lever in those situations will be a coalition.

On the other side,you will sometimes be in these strong positions.

What is the greatest risk?

The greatest risk is a coalition against you.

So we all need to be on the lookout from both sides for these coalitions.

And finally,failures of implementation are almost invariably failures to build successful coalitions.

It's a critical tool in your influence toolbox.

3-03-01.01_模块介绍：策略与战术

欢迎回到《影响力》课程。

我们即将进入第三周的学习，本周我们将深入探讨一些更具体的影响力策略。

这部分内容我们将分为两个部分。首先，我们将讨论说服力。

说服力是影响力领域中被探讨和研究了数千年的话题之一。

因此，让我们先来了解一下那些行之有效的理论框架。

然后，在第二部分，我们将更广泛地讨论影响力风格。

在这里，我们反对那种认为特质、身体、生理禀赋在影响力中很重要的观念，而是强调行为和策略的重要性。

为此，我们将与您分享我们在过去十年中做的一些实证研究工作，希望能充实您的工具箱，也就是您的影响力策略工具箱。

敬请享用。

英文原文

Welcome back to Influence.

We are heading into week three here,and in this week,we're going to drop down into a little more detail on some influence tactics.

We're going to do it in two parts.First,we're going to talk about persuasion.

Persuasion is one of these influence areas that's been talked about and researched for literally millennia.

So,let's understand the frameworks that are useful there.

And then,in the second half,we'll talk about influence styles more generally.

Here,we're pushing against the notion of traits,physical,physiological dispositions being important in influence,and rather emphasizing behaviors and tactics.

To do that,we're going to share with you some empirical work that we've done over the last 10 years to hopefully fill out your toolbox,your influence tactic toolbox.

Enjoy.

3-03-01.02_说服力简介

我们将从讨论说服力开始本模块的内容。

为此，我们首先会分享一段我最近与两位同事尤里·西蒙森和乔·西蒙斯的访谈，讨论他们近期所做的一些研究。

他们发表了一篇题为《虚假的积极心理学：数据收集与分析中未披露的灵活性可使任何结果显得显著》的论文。

标题很长，主题看似有些晦涩，然而这篇论文却产生了巨大的影响。

自2011年发表以来，它已被引用两千次。

它可以说是心理学领域所谓的“可重复性危机”中最有影响力的论文。

这就引出了一个问题：说服力在这篇论文产生的影响中发挥了作用吗？

你可能会认为，学术研究是一个说服力不应起作用的领域。

事实上，这正是我想与尤里和乔交谈的原因，因为你可能会认为在这个领域，唯一重要的是想法本身。

但事实证明，这些人在修辞和说服力上投入了大量思考。

所以我们最近和他们坐下来，想了解这一切是如何发生的。

今天下午我们在这里，要与沃顿商学院运营信息与决策组的两位教授尤里·西蒙森和乔·西蒙斯聊聊他们过去，嗯，大概六七年里一直在做的研究？

其实可以追溯到更早一点。六年了。

这六年他们主要研究最初称为“虚假积极心理学”的课题。

人们普遍认为，这篇论文在很大程度上引发了心理学界关于可重复性的讨论，也就是有些人所说的“可重复性危机”。

当然，其他人也在其中发出了声音。

但这篇论文、这项研究以及后续的持续工作，确实产生了深远影响。

我们今天要讨论的是说服力，以及说服力和修辞在这个过程中所起的作用。

这么做的动机是，我们经常在其他领域谈论说服力。

我们在市场营销、公司内部政治中谈论它，但我们通常不会想到像科学这样的领域也会涉及说服力和修辞。

根据我在这段时间参与你们这个项目的观察，我觉得说服力一直是其中很重要的一部分。

所以我认为，我们稍微聊聊这个话题，听听你们内部是如何思考的，以及你们在这个领域对说服力和修辞的体会，会是件好事，也很有启发。

这是一篇我们真的非常需要人们去阅读和关注的论文。

否则，做这件事就完全没意义了。

我们试图改变整个领域做研究的方式。

我们当时确实绞尽脑汁地想，到底要怎样才能。

意思是，当你进行一项研究时，你会收集很多测量指标。

We're going to begin this module talking about persuasion.

And to do that,we'll start with an interview that I did recently with a couple of colleagues of mine,Yuri Simonson and Joe Simmons,about some research they've done recently.

They published an article called False Positive Psychology:Undisclosed Flexibility in Data Collection and Analysis Allows Presenting Anything as Significant.

Long title on a subject that seems a little arcane,and yet this paper has been wildly influential.

It's been cited 2000 times since it was published in 2011.

It's arguably the most influential paper in what has been called the reproducibility crisis in psychology.

And it raises a question:did persuasion have any role to play in the impact this paper is having?

You might think academic research is a place where persuasion shouldn't matter.

In fact,that's why I wanted to talk to Yuri and Joe,because you think this is a place where the only thing that matters is ideas.

But it turns out these guys put a lot of thought into rhetoric and persuasion.

So we sat down with them recently to find out how it went down.

So we're here this afternoon to talk to Yuri Simonson and Joe Simmons,both professors here at Wharton in the Operations Information and Decisions Group,about research that they've been doing for the last,what,fella,six or seven years now?

It goes back a little bit.Six years.

Six years on what they initially called false positive psychology.

And they published a paper in 2011,which,as of last count,has something like 2000 citations in less than six years,and more papers behind that.

And people generally give it considerable credit for the conversation in psychology around reproducibility,what some people will call the reproducibility crisis.

And others have had voice in this,obviously.

But the paper and the research and the ongoing program has been influential.

We're here to talk today about persuasion,the role of persuasion and rhetoric in that effort.

And the motivation is that we talk about persuasion all the time in other domains.

We talk about it in marketing or politics inside a firm,but we don't usually think that something like science would involve persuasion and rhetoric.

My sense of having been around you guys in this project for most of that time is that persuasion has been an important part of it.

And so I thought it'd be good and instructive for us to talk a little bit about it and hear kind of from the inside how you've thought about that and what your experience with persuasion and rhetoric has been in this domain.

This was a paper that we really needed people to read and pay attention to.

Otherwise,there's no point at all in doing it.

We were trying to change how the field as a whole did research.

And so for the first time in my life,I was involved in sort of a big persuasion attempt.

And so we really did think hard about how on earth.

To get people to read this paper.

Most people don't read papers that are read.

Even academics.Even academics,for sure.

Most papers do not get read,right?

So we're going to talk in a lot of detail about this research.

It might be useful to explain in a very short fashion what the enterprise was.

So what exactly were you trying to persuade people to do?

I know that's a ridiculous question,but it's concise.

Well,so basically change how people conduct and report the research.

So the idea is people have,when you conduct a study,you collect many measures.

For example,you may ask people how they feel about something.

You may ask them how much they'll be,how hard they would work to obtain it.

You may ask them multiple ways.

But then,so if you collect all those measures and you get to choose from them,the results you report are going to be biased towards the one that works.

So imagine you try a drug and you give it to 100 patients and you see if it helps with weight or with their heart condition or with their skin.

And then if you try enough of those things,one of them will work.

And then you report your results and you only talk about the one that actually worked.

Readers will be misled into thinking that it's very persuasive,very compelling evidence,when in fact it's just chance.

So this is an important feature here that this is basically a methodology paper.

So it's not just persuasion and rhetoric in a scientific endeavor,but it's scientific methods.

And so we're really getting into what I think most people would think is a pretty dry technical area,not much room for persuasion.

So how did you position this paper?

How did you argue in this paper in a way that was different from other attempts,other academic attempts?

I mean,we were writing a methods paper,and most methods papers are written for methods people.

And we didn't want to write a paper for methods people.

We wanted to write a paper for normal people,normal academics at least.And we had the advantage of being normal academics.

So a lot of methods,people writing methods papers are methods people,but we are not a methods people.

So we sort of understood like what would it take for us to read a methods paper?

And so we tried to build a methods paper that we ourselves would want to read.

So we started out by putting simulations in our paper because that sort of showed how big the problem was.

But I think the big insight was that a paper that just contains simulations is not a paper that many people are going to read.

And so we thought long and hard,many,many conversations around what is a good example or demonstration of the problem.

And we tried to come up with a demonstration that was interesting,kind of cute,maybe people would talk about it,you know,that sort of thing.

I think that's sufficiently cute.

You should tell us real quickly just to describe it at a high level.

So we basically wanted to show that scientists could find statistically significant evidence for any hypothesis,no matter how absurd.

And so we came up with a hypothesis that was demonstrably absurd,which is that listening to a particular song can change how old you are.

And no one on earth believes that's possible.

And so we ran a study using the norms of the day that basically showed that that effect was true.

We were like,look,if you do things the way that they are currently being done,you can find evidence for this crazy hypothesis.

And you can write it up in such a way that people will be,scientists would be persuaded by it.

And so we thought that piece was,I think,absolutely critical.

If we hadn't done that,I'm not sure we would have gotten published,but even if we had gotten published,it would have probably been ignored.

That was one aspect of it,at least.So in terms of the persuasion and thinking about it,we would picture our at least methodologically oriented friend and ask,what would get this guy to tell about this paper to his friends?

I think,at least introspecting,that's what I think of you.

Yeah,absolutely.

Wow.
