The next idea I want to think about is detecting deception.

The broad idea that I want you to take away is that detecting deception is hard.

We're more likely to be suspicious or feel like,hey,something isn't quite right.

As I mentioned before,we're often overconfident in our ability to detect deception.

And what I'd like to do is diminish your confidence and say,look,if you're feeling like something isn't quite right,that's the cue to go dig deeper and push further.

Now,here's what we can do.

The first thing we do is gather information.

So as we prepare,gather information from as many sources as we can.

Again,that's a key pillar of negotiations.

The second is to build relationships.

So we know that people are far less likely to deceive friends than strangers.

And so if we build rapport,even a little bit,we're less likely to be targets of deception.

People are less likely to deceive you if you seem prepared,if you seem like you're a friend,and you seem like you're serious about what you're trying to do.

Whereas if people feel like this is a stranger I'll never see again,this person is unprepared,they're not serious,they might feel entitled to teaching you a lesson,and you'd like not to be the object of that lesson.

Here's what to focus on.

So when you are exchanging information with someone,you want to focus on the content of the message.

So first,is what they're saying making sense?

Is it consistent with things they've said before?

And recall that I mentioned this idea about taking notes during a negotiation.

If you're taking notes,you can look back to see if the stories changed in some way.

And next,is there something unusual or odd that they said?

Did they add in extra information that isn't really relevant,perhaps as they're biding time to think about what to say?

So we can think about the content.

So is the content strange or off in some way?

Second,how is the message being delivered?

How are they saying things?

And is there a match between the content and the delivery?

So are people describing something that should make them very upset,but they're not seeming upset at all?

Or are they saying one thing that is negative,but they're nodding as if they're agreeing?

We're looking for some mismatch,which again is a cue.

that something isn't quite right and then we should probe further,we should seek information and try to dig deeper perhaps from other sources to figure out what's right.

When people tell lies there are two things that change.

The first thing is emotions.

So people who tell lies might feel bad,they might feel guilty or fearful or anxious as they're telling a lie.

And we know this when people feel really anxious about telling lies,they're eager to get out of that situation.

They want to switch topics,they want to create distance between you and them,they're eager for the meeting to end.

We also know that emotions leak out.

So they're micro expressions,and these expressions are very fast,less than a 20th of a second.

We might not even recognize them as they're happening,but we might non-consciously realize,hey,something's not quite right.

They smile like they're really happy that I asked the question,but something didn't feel quite right.

That could be a micro expression that you're picking up.

Now,if you're recording a meeting,you could go back and frame by frame,you might actually see micro expressions where somebody might,when you ask a tough question,give you one expression before they change the expression.

But we typically miss it in natural communication.

Another is that we'll get incomplete expressions.

So smiling,for example,when I say,oh,I'm really happy to build this partnership with you,they might smile,but if you look at authentic versus inauthentic smiles,they're called Duchesne smiles,these authentic smiles have the crow's feet in the eyes as well as the mouth.

When we're incompletely smiling,like the smile is probably in a lot of your photographs when you smiled for the camera,those smiles have the mouth movement,but it's difficult to fake the crow's feet around the eyes.

So that's emotions.The second thing that changes when people lie is the cognitive load.

And by cognitive load,I mean we just have more in our minds.

We've got to keep two stories straight.

So there's the lie that I'm telling,and there's the reality,and I've got to keep those two straight.

It's just more on my mind.

I've got to monitor my behavior.

So I might normally be gesticulating,or I might be shaking my head no when I mean no.

But now if I'm saying yes,oh,we're happy to do that,or that's going to be no problem,or the car is in great condition,I have to control my body in ways that are different than would be natural and authentic.

The next thing I've got to do is monitor the other person.

I've got to watch if they're believing me and monitoring what I should say next if I have to build more color to my story or if I've got to dial it back.

So altogether,there's just more that a deceiver has to do.

And that cognitive load means that we're likely to make mistakes.

So when people are lying,they're cognitively loaded.

So they're going to do things like say no but not yes.

Or they'll catch and correct themselves midway.

They'll say,yeah,I mean,no,that never happened.

So that's the catch incorrect.

Or there's delayed timing.

Like,oh,I never did that.

And there's a pause,and then they'll shake their head no.Or they'll delay reporting something.

So we'll see odd timing as well.

Now,when we're cognitively loaded,we have more in our minds,we're more likely to use pause fillers like ums and ahs.

We're more likely to take time before we answer a question,or we'll add some irrelevant information as we're building up time to figure out what to say.

People are more likely to stutter,their gesticulation gets shut down,our pupil sizes increase,though that's very difficult to tell in face-to-face communication.

A lot of these things we now know because we've videotaped thousands of people lying and we can analyze those tapes.

In natural communication,it's very hard,but again,you may find yourself detecting something that doesn't seem quite right,and there you should push further.

Another cue is people overdoing it,where people who are anxious pretend to be very comfortable,perhaps too comfortable.

So they yawn excessively or they spread out on a couch.

Sometimes even people self-medicate themselves when they really want to play it cool.

They might add statements like,oh,I'd never lie to you,or to tell you the truth,or to be honest,or I was always brought up to tell the truth.

They're adding things to try to create the impression that they're really honest,trying to compensate for being dishonest.

Now,some people just use these phrases naturally,but when these phrases get overused,that's a cue that people are likely to be deceiving you.

So here's the idea.

Detective deception is quite hard.

There are cues.

A lot of those cues are likely to make you uncomfortable,and we should be sensitive to that.

And negotiations is really this hotbed for...

Deception because it's so tempting for people to try to deceive you.

4-03-01.04_降低被骗的可能性

识破欺骗非常困难。

接下来我想思考的是，我们可以做些什么来降低成为欺骗目标的可能性。

那么，我们能做些什么来降低某人欺骗我们的可能性呢？

第一件事是建立人际关系。

正如我之前提到的，人们欺骗朋友的可能性小于欺骗陌生人。

因此，我们要建立人际关系，并传递出对诚实的承诺。

当我们展现出对诚实的承诺，保持透明时，人们就不太会觉得欺骗我们是合理的。

接下来，我们可以监控对话。

所以在某些情况下，我们可能会进行录音。

我们要将关键事项落实为书面形式。

我们要做笔记，以便确保如果故事发生变化，我们可以轻松追踪到。

我们可能还需要让其他人参与进来。

比如让其他人旁观，或者我们将情况汇报给其他人，以此明确声誉至关重要。

另一件我们可以做的事是面对面会面。

当我们面对面会面时，会增加对方的认知负荷。

人们会感到更亲密，也更在意人际关系。

这也让我们有更多机会获取非语言线索。

比如某人是否在向后倾身，时间节奏或手势是否不对劲？

人们的表达方式与其言语之间是否存在不匹配？

我们还希望通过收集大量信息来做好准备。

有时，我们可以就一些我们已经知道答案的事情提问。

这样我们就可以检查人们是如何回答那些我们已知的问题，以及那些我们未知的问题的。

另一个关键思路是对其他领域的行为保持敏感。

所以如果有人告诉你他们刚刚在税务上作弊，或者如何在另一个合作伙伴身上耍了花招，你要非常警惕。

也就是说，思路是如果他们愿意亏待别人，你就应该担心他们也可能欺骗你。

所以核心思路是，我们要谨慎并对那些可能引导我们更加小心的信号保持敏感。

但建立人际关系、获取这些信息以及传递对高道德标准的承诺，确实是至关重要的步骤。

接下来我想思考的思路是，假设你认为某人可能在对你撒谎。

以下是一些应对说谎者的思路。

首先，对质是有风险的。

权力动态至关重要。

所以如果你处于高权力位置，你是经理，风险就很低。

如果你处于低权力位置，风险就相当高。

如果你需要这段关系，你要非常谨慎。

指责某人对你撒谎，即使他们确实撒了谎，也可能导致对方丢面子。

我曾有一位前学生描述过他们在韩国的经历，那个人非常明显地对他们撒了谎。

他们收集了证据，并向那人出示，但他们是在公共场合这样做的。

这位韩国经理丢了极大的面子，尽管他们撒谎有错在先，但这引发了强烈的反弹，导致对方再也不想与这个人打交道。

同样，他们彻底断绝了整段关系。

所以在这里，仅仅试图澄清事实却导致了关系的破裂。

所以对质是有风险的，但如果你处于高权力位置，并希望改变那种关系的性质，直接指出问题可以是一种纠正现状的方式，但你应该认识到其中存在一定风险。

那么你还能做什么呢？

有一些更柔和的方法，比如搭建一座让人们可以走下来的桥梁。

也就是提供一种方式让人们退一步，比如说：嘿，也许这里有个误会。

或者关于这件事，你还有什么想补充的吗？

或者我感觉这个故事背后可能还有更多内容。

你能为我详细讲讲这一点吗？

所以你是在给人们一个台阶下，你没有让丢面子的程度那么大，但你给了他们一种方式来分享更多关于局势的信息。

所以这个搭建桥梁的思路，可能比直接揭穿某人要柔和。

所以这里的思路是。

直接揭穿某人可能是正确的做法。

只是要认识到这会导致丢面子，而在其他人面前这样做会加剧这种丢面子的程度。

有时，如果关系真的非常重要，而我们仍想给人们某种出路，我们可能希望采取更柔和的方法。

而且当我们并不完全确定已识破欺骗时，这也可能是合适的做法。

我们可能只想核实一下情况，并给人们一个机会，让他们分享比之前更多的信息。

英文原文

Detecting deception is difficult.

And what I want to think about next is things we could do to decrease the likelihood of being a target of deception.

So what can we do to decrease the likelihood that someone's going to deceive us?

The first thing is to build relationships.

As I mentioned before,people are less likely to lie to friends than strangers.

And so we want to build relationships and signal a commitment to honesty.

When we demonstrate a commitment to honesty,we're transparent,then people are less likely to feel justified in deceiving us.

Next,we can monitor the conversation.

So in some cases,we might record things.

We want to get key things in writing.

We want to take notes so we can make sure that if the story changes,it's easy for us to track that.

And we may want to involve other people.

So somebody else watching this or we're reporting this out to somebody else,so it's clear that reputations matter.

Another thing we can do is meet in person.

When we're meeting in person,it increases the cognitive load.

People feel more intimate and more concerned about the relationship.

And it also gives us more access to nonverbal cues.

So is somebody leaning away,is the timing,the gesticulation off?

Are there mismatches between how people are expressing something and what they're saying?

We also want to prepare by gathering a lot of information.

And sometimes we can ask questions about things that we know the answer to.

So we can check to see how people are answering questions that we already know as well as questions we don't know.

Another key idea is to be sensitive to behavior in other domains.

So if somebody tells you how they just cheated on their taxes or how they pulled a fast one over on another partner,you want to be very concerned.

That is,the idea is that if they're willing to shortchange somebody else,you should be concerned that they might be cheating you as well.

So the idea is we want to be careful and sensitive to cues that might guide us to be more careful.

But building relationships,gaining this information,and signaling a commitment to high ethics are really important steps.

The next idea I want to think about is suppose you think somebody may be lying to you.

Here are some ideas for confronting a liar.

First,confrontations are risky.

The power dynamic matters a lot.

So if you're in a high power position,you're the manager,the risks are low.

If you're low power,the risks are quite high.

If you need this relationship,you want to be very concerned.

Accusing somebody of lying to you,even if they have,can lead to a loss of face.

I had one former student describe how they were in Korea,this person had lied to them very clearly.

They documented,they presented it to the person,but they did it in a public space.

This Korean manager lost so much face,even though they were in the wrong having lied to them,there was a backlash and they never wanted to deal with this person.

Again,they severed the whole relationship.

So here,just trying to clear the air caused a rupture in the relationship.

So confrontations are risky,but if you're in a high power position,you want to shift the nature of that relationship,calling it out can be a way to course correct what's happening,but you should recognize that there's some risk involved in that.

So what else could you do?

There are softer approaches,like building a bridge that people could walk across.

So offering a way for people to take a step back by saying something like,hey,perhaps there's a mistake here.

Or is there something more you wanted to say about this?

Or I had the feeling there might be more to this story.

Could you expand on this for me?

So you're giving people a lifeline where you're not making the loss of face so big,but you're giving them a way to share more about a situation.

So this idea about building a bridge that might be softer than just calling somebody out.

So here's the idea.

Calling somebody out may be the right thing to do.

Just to recognize that there's a loss of face,doing it in front of other people will increase that loss of face.

And sometimes we may want to take a softer approach if the relationship really matters and we still want to give people sort of a way out.

And that may also be right when we're just not positive that we've caught the deception.

We may want to just check things and give people an opportunity to share more than what we got before.

4-03-01.05_信任

我想思考谈判中的信任问题。

信任让每一次互动都变得更加轻松。

当我们信任某人所说的话，信任他们将要采取的行动时。

当他们信任我们时，一切互动都会更加顺畅。

这就像是一种顺势而为，因为我们知道，如果拥有信任，我们就愿意原谅某些事情，愿意对他人展现脆弱。

我想思考我们对个人、对组织以及对机构的信任。

所以你可能信任另一个人。

我们会共度时光，一起外出用餐，一起观看体育赛事，一起旅行，我们一起做各种能够建立对个人信任的事情。

我们也可以做一些建立对组织信任的事情。

比如我信任这家公司，我信任国际商业机器公司会做正确的事。

或者我们可以信任像法院系统这样的机构。

其中一些是可以相互替代的。

所以也许我不太了解这个人，但我信任他们所属的公司。

或者也许我不太信任这个人，但我们签署了一份具有约束力的文件，而我信任法院系统会执行它。

正因为我可以信任机构，这才促进并简化了整个互动过程。

所以我可以飞往达拉斯，签署一份文件，然后在第二天飞回，而无需花费大量精力去建立融洽关系和人际关系。

但你可以想象，在某些国家，如果法院系统积压严重或效率不高，那么信任个人、信任组织就可能变得极其重要。

而在那些地方，也许我们需要花费大量时间来建立那种关系。

所以我们要思考信任。关键思路是：有了信任，我们才能达成那些没有信任就根本无法达成的协议。

现在，谈判者更有可能向他们信任的人透露信息。这减少了摩擦。

它减少了对律师和完备合同的需求，并真正使我们更有可能达成协议。

所以在谈判中成为一个受信任的人有着巨大的好处。

而我想问的问题是：我们如何展现信任？

展现信任有三个关键思路。第一是展现我们的能力。

也就是我们是否有能力履行承诺？

我们能做到吗？

所以如果我们有资历，有经验，有推荐客户，如果我们能展示能力，我们就能展现出能力。

所以，高能力是展现信任的第一个关键思路。我们能做到吗？

第二是展现善意。

也就是我们是否善良、关怀、温暖？

而展现善意，即我真正关心你，我在意你的利益，真诚地展现这一点就是在展示善意。

第三个关键思路是正直。

我是那种遵守规则的人吗？

我诚实且有道德吗？

展现对道德的承诺是展现信任的第三大支柱。所以是能力、善意和正直。

所以，我们要弄清楚如何做到这些。

以下是一些展现善意的实际步骤。

我们要询问关于他人的问题。

我们要展现出对他人的关注。

我们要赞扬他人所取得的成就。

我们要留意他们。

我们要建立融洽关系。

当我们未能达到预期时，要迅速且真诚地道歉。

当事情进展不顺时，我们要表现出悔意。

我们要传递平等的信号。

所以在谈判桌旁，我们坐同样的椅子，或者我们准时到场，以此表明我珍视你的时间如同珍视我自己的时间一样。

所以，我们要传递出我们在意这种与他人建立的平等合作伙伴关系的信号。

我们也可以通过展现对家庭、对社区的关怀来传递善意，当人们谈论志愿服务、谈论他们的宠物时，我们就是在展现温暖。

关于建立信任的其他思路，这里有一个关键思路：那就是，当我们信任他人时，我们愿意展现脆弱，但这种脆弱是双向的。

当我们暴露一个弱点，当我们对他人展现脆弱时，我们很可能建立起信任。所以，我可能会透露一个秘密。

现在，这应该是非核心的，也就是说，不应该是关于我如何伤害他人的秘密，而是其他一些秘密，比如，哦，是的，我最喜欢的甜点是某种我吃得太多的东西。

但我们可以思考一个弱点，或者当人们一起喝酒时，当人们一起喝酒时，他们就是在让自己变得脆弱。

也就是说，我们放下了戒备，或者我们唱着走调的卡拉OK。

唱得越差越好。

在这里，我以某种安全的方式让自己难堪，从而展现脆弱，或者在谈判中，我们透露一些信息。

所以这些都是让我展现脆弱的实际步骤，同时也帮助我建立这种温暖、这种善意、这种关系。

一个思路是思考存在一份正式合同。

我们可以看到它，可以阅读它。

此外还有心理学家所称的心理契约。

也就是说，我们有一些未写明的期望。

所以在工作场所，合同里并没有规定我们不能把脚放在桌子上，或者走进来时不能对人吼叫。

那是心理契约的一部分。

那里存在着期望。

在我们所有的人际关系中，都存在一份心理契约。

问题在于它没有写下来，所以我们很可能会违背它。

也就是说，我们要仔细思考人们的期望是什么，如果我们不确定，可能会去询问或保持敏感，因为如果我们违背了人们的期望，我们就违背了心理契约，我们就会失去信任。

所以我们要展现关怀，我们要可靠，我们要确保我们的行动与言语一致。

如果我们说了什么，即使没有人要求我们兑现，我们也要展现出对贯彻到底的关切。

所以通过这些方式，我们可以建立信任，而信任是帮助我们建立关系并真正促进我们可能进行的每一笔交易的必要要素。

我们信任个人、信任组织、信任机构，而我们要思考我们向他人展现的能力、善意和正直。

英文原文

I want to think about trust in negotiations.

Trust makes every interaction easier.

When we trust what somebody says,we trust what they're going to do.

When they trust us,it smooths every interaction.

It's like easing into something where we know that if we have trust,we're willing to forgive things,we're willing to be vulnerable to other people.

And I want to think about the trust that we have in people,in organizations,and in institutions.

So you might trust another person.

So we spend time together,we go out for meals,we go to sporting events,we go on a trip together,we do things that are going to build trust in a person.

We can also do things where we have trust in organizations.

So I trust this company,I trust IBM to do the right thing.

Or we can trust institutions like the court system.

And some of these are substitutes.

So maybe I don't know this person very well,but I trust the company that they're coming from.

Or maybe I don't trust this person very well,but we've signed a binding document,and I trust the court system to enforce it.

And because I can trust institutions,it facilitates and eases the whole interaction.

So I can fly to Dallas,sign a document,and fly back that next day without doing a lot of rapport building and relationship building.

But you can imagine in some countries where the court system is backlogged or not as effective,there trusting the people,trusting the organizations could be extremely important.

And there,maybe we need to spend a lot of time building that relationship.

So we want to think about trust.And the key idea is that with trust,we can reach agreements that we just simply couldn't without it.

Now,negotiators are more likely to reveal information to people they trust.It reduces the friction.

It reduces the need for lawyers and complete contracts and really makes us more likely to reach an agreement.

So there are huge benefits to being a trusted person in a negotiation.

And the question I want to ask is,how can we project trust?

There are three key ideas for projecting trust.The first is projecting our ability.

So do we have the competence to fulfill something?

Can we do it?

So if we have credentials,if we have experience,if we have referent clients,If we can demonstrate competence,we're going to project ability.

So,high ability is the first key idea for projecting trust.Can we do it?

The second is projecting benevolence.

So,are we kind,caring,are we warm?

And projecting benevolence,that I really care about you,I'm concerned about your interests,demonstrating that authentically demonstrates benevolence.

The third key idea is integrity.

Am I the kind of person that follows the rules?

Am I honest and moral?

Demonstrating a commitment to morality is the third pillar that's going to project trust.So,ability,benevolence,and integrity.

So,we want to figure out how we can do that.

So,here's some practical steps for demonstrating benevolence.

So,we're asking questions about other people.

We're demonstrating a focus on other people.

We're praising others for what they've done.

We're noticing them.

We're building rapport.

We're apologizing quickly and sincerely when we fall short.

We're demonstrating remorse when things aren't going well.

We're signaling equality.

So,at the table,we sit on the same kinds of chairs,or we show up on time,demonstrating that I value your time as much as my time.

So,we want to signal that we care about this sort of equal partnership that we have with others.

And we can also signal benevolence by demonstrating concern for family,our community when people volunteer,they talk about their pets,we're demonstrating warmth.

Other ideas for building trust,and here is a key idea:that is,when we trust others,we're willing to be vulnerable,but there's a bi-directionality to this vulnerability.

When we reveal a weakness,when we're vulnerable to others,we're likely to build trust.So,I might reveal a secret.

Now,it should be non-core,that is,it shouldn't be a secret about how I harmed somebody else,but you know,some other secret like,oh,yeah,my favorite kind of dessert is something that I eat too much of.

But we can think about a weakness or when people go drinking together,when people go drinking together,they're making themselves vulnerable.

That is,we're letting our guard down,or we're singing off-key karaoke.

The worse,the better.

Here,I'm embarrassing myself in some safe way that makes me vulnerable,or in a negotiation,we reveal some information.

So here are all practical steps that make me vulnerable,but also help me build this warmth,this benevolence,this relationship.

One idea is to think about there's a formal contract.

We can see that,we can read it.

There's also what psychologists call a psychological contract.

That is,we have expectations that aren't written down.

So at work,It's not in our contract that we keep our feet off the table or we don't yell at people as we walk in.

That's part of the psychological contract.

There are expectations there.

And in all of our relationships,we have a psychological contract.

The problem is it's not written down,so we're likely to violate it.

That is,we want to think carefully about what people's expectations are,and we're not sure we might ask or be sensitive,because if we violate people's expectations,we violate the psychological contract,we can lose trust.

So we want to demonstrate concern,we want to be reliable,we want to make sure our deeds match our words.

If we say something,even if somebody isn't holding us to it,we demonstrate a concern for following through.

So in those ways,we can build trust,and trust is this essential ingredient for helping us build relationships and really facilitate every transaction that we might have.

We have trust in people,in organizations,in institutions,and we want to think about the ability,benevolence,and integrity that we project to others.

4-03-01.06_应该信任谁

你应该信任谁？

我们需要信任某些人，同时更仔细地监控另一些人。

那么，我们最应该信任谁呢？

部分来说，应该是那些与我们有过良好重复互动的人，但有时我们也需要信任那些我们不太了解的人。

现在，我们可以思考他们的能力、他们的善意以及他们的正直。

我们可以思考他们是如何与他人互动的。

我们可以寻找关于他们声誉的信息。

所有这些都非常好且重要。

我想思考另一个关键特征，事实证明它在可信度方面至关重要。

真正值得信赖的人往往也倾向于感到内疚。

而易感内疚是一种人格特质。

这并非指正在感受内疚。

而是指倾向于担忧让他人失望。

当人们倾向于对有害行为感到难受，即使这些有害行为发生在私下，这就是易感内疚。

而那些易感内疚的人，结果证明非常值得信赖。

所以如果你思考一下，存在一个易感内疚量表，问题比如：想象你在一个晚宴上，你把酒洒在了主人的地毯上，没人看见，你会有什么感受？

所以这是发生在私下的事情。

它是有害的。

你会为此感到内疚吗？

你会为此担忧吗？

而这里的思路是。

也就是说，有些人非常担忧有害后果，他们会远离地毯喝白葡萄酒，而不是在地毯上方喝红葡萄酒。

正是那种远离地毯喝白葡萄酒的人，那种担忧让他人失望的人，那种担忧伤害他人的人。

那些人就是易感内疚者。

他们会更加努力，以免让他人失望。

结果证明，这些易感内疚的人非常值得信赖。

在我们所做的研究中，我们发现高度易感内疚的人比低度易感内疚的人显著更值得信赖。

而我想说的是，评估易感内疚远比直接衡量或评估可信度要容易得多。

因此，我们可以将易感内疚作为一种方式，来判断这个人是否值得我们建立关系，是否值得信任，或者是否需要更仔细地监控他们的行为。

我们也需要注意短期关系，短期关系的好处在于，通过评价系统，我们可以将短期关系转化为长期关系。

所以，你可以想想爱彼迎或优步。

它们看似是一次性交易，但通过人际关系、通过声誉系统，转化为了长期关系。

但如果这真的是一次性交易，那就是我们需要最为小心的地方。

我们在所谓被审查的环境中也要小心。

所以，想象你只能看到人们在部分时间的行为。

比如，想象有一位经常出差的经理。

每当经理来上班时，员工都拼命工作，而每当经理离开办公室，他们就看不到员工在做什么了。

现在，如果员工知道老板何时在场，他们可能只在老板在场时拼命工作，其余时间则偷懒。

这对老板来说就是一个被审查的环境。

老板只看到了部分行为，而在那些被审查的环境中，老板可能会推断：嘿，这里的每个人都工作非常努力。

每次我在办公室看到他们，他们都工作非常努力。

但那是一个被审查的环境，他们可能未能领会当他们不在场时发生的事情。

如果我们作为老板，只看到部分行为，而人们知道他们在那些时刻正被观察，这就有点像从面试中推断过多信息。

我们正在面试某人，而他们在那一天或那一小时表现得很积极。

那是他们一贯的样子吗？还是那只是一个被审查的环境？

所以，我们要意识到被审查的环境。

然后，当然，那些在其他领域吹嘘自己作弊的人，正是我们要非常小心对待的人。

但以上就是关于我们应该信任谁的一些关键思路。

We can think about how they've interacted with other people.

We can look for information about their reputations.

All of that's very good and important.

I want to think about one other key feature that turns out to be really important in trustworthiness.

Really trustworthy people also happen to be guilt prone.

And guilt prone is a personality trait.

It's not about feeling guilt.

It's about being prone and worrying about letting other people down.

When people are prone to feeling badly about harmful behaviors,even when those harmful behaviors occur in private,that's guilt-proneness.

And people who are guilt-prone turn out to be very trustworthy.

So if you think about,and there's a guilt-prone scale,questions like,imagine you're at a dinner party,you spill wine on the host's carpet,nobody sees it,how would you feel?

So here's something that happened in private.

It's harmful.

Would you feel guilty about that?

Would you worry about that?

And here's the idea.

That is,some people are so worried about a harmful consequence,they're going to drink white wine away from the carpet,not red wine over the carpet.

And it's the kind of person that's drinking the white wine away from the carpet,that's worried about letting other people down,that is worried about harming other people.

Those people are guilt-prone.

They're going to work harder so they don't let other people down.

And it turns out these guilt-prone people are very trustworthy.

And in studies that we've done,we found that highly guilt-prone people are significantly more trustworthy than low-guilt-prone people.

And what I'm suggesting is that it's far easier to assess guilt proneness than it is to directly measure or assess trustworthiness.

And so we can think about guilt proneness as a way to figure out if this is somebody we should.Should be jumping into a relationship with if we should be trusting them or really monitoring what they're doing more carefully.

We also want to be aware of short-term relationships,where the good thing about short-term relationships is that with review systems,we can transform short-term relationships into long-term relationships.

So,you can think about Airbnb or Uber.

They're seemingly single-shot transactions that have been transformed through a relationship,through a reputation system,into a long-term relationship.

But if it really is a one-shot deal,that's where we want to be most careful.

We also want to be careful in what's termed censored environments.

So,imagine you only see what people do some of the time.

So,imagine there's a manager who travels a lot.

Every time the manager comes into work,the staff is working furiously hard,and every time the manager leaves the office,they can't see what the staff is doing.

Now,if the staff knows when the boss is around,they may work furiously hard just when the boss is around and goof off the rest of the time.

That's a censored environment for the boss.

The boss is only seeing some behavior,and in those censored environments,the boss may make the inference that,hey,everybody here works really hard.

Every time I've seen them in the office,they work really hard.

But that's a censored environment,and they may fail to appreciate what happens when they're not there.

We want to think about if we're the boss,if we're only seeing some of the behaviors,and people know that they're being observed in those moments,it's sort of like inferring a lot from an interview.

We're interviewing somebody and they're on for that day or that hour.

Is that how they always are,or is that a censored environment?

So,we want to be aware of censored environments.

And then,of course,people who brag about cheating in other domains,those are the people we want to be very careful about.

But those are some of the key ideas about in whom we should be placing our trust.

4-03-01.07_时间压力

许多谈判中的一个关键特征是时间压力。

往往存在时间压力。

我们考虑时间成本，假设发生争端，工人罢工，罢工工人因无法获得工资而承担成本。

公司也因无法生产产品而承担成本。

或者律师费，如果我们互相起诉，就会产生时间成本。

随着时间的推移，双方的费用都在上涨。

这些就是时间成本。

此外还有最后期限。

人们收到限时报价非常常见。

你知道，这是给你的录用通知。

你有两周时间做决定。

所以我想思考时间成本和最后期限，以及我们如何在谈判中应对这些问题。

首先，让我们考虑时间成本。

时间成本可能对双方产生不对称的影响。

所谓不对称，我的意思是一方可能承担非常高的成本，而另一方成本较低。

所以想象一下，你聘请了昂贵的律师，而对方有一位当律师的兄弟，因此随着案件拖延，你们双方的成本极不均衡。

所以核心思路是，我们要思考这些成本的不对称性。

或者你可以想象一场罢工。

也就是说，一方是否拥有非常庞大的罢工基金？

公司的成本是多少？

我们可以思考这些不对称的成本。

请记住，我们谈过耐心。

时间成本会影响我们的耐心程度。

如果我们属于成本较高的一方，我们会更快地做出让步。

我们会更关注我们的最佳替代方案，也就是我们的底线，而不是我们渴望得到的目标。

在某些情况下，这会促使我们急于寻找某种结果。

我们可能会依赖某些启发式方法，比如干脆平分差额，或者聚焦于一个大问题，或者如果我们有了初步协议，就干脆接受，因为我们正匆忙试图达成协议。

所以你要非常仔细地思考时间压力。

我们要意识到自己面临的时间压力，并思考他人面临的时间压力。

所以可能是，你知道，我在一个案例中提到过，我们请了昂贵的律师，但我们要思考，嘿，你知道，如果我们有家庭成员，比如我们有位当律师的姐妹。

而对方聘请了花费高昂的名牌律师，我们要认识到我们可以相对更有耐心，并在这种情况下提高我们的期望值。

这些就是时间成本。

下一个思路是最后期限。

所以最后期限能推动事情进展。

也就是说，当我们说：听着，你有两周时间接受或拒绝这个报价，这就会促使人们行动起来。

他们很可能会在两周内给你答复。

在某些情况下，人们会操纵最后期限。

我曾与一些高管合作。

他们前往中国进行了一场非常漫长的谈判。

第一周，他们参加了一些谈判会议，但也游览了长城。

他们外出用餐。

他们参加了宴会。

那段时光非常美好。

直到最后一天，当他们感到面临巨大时间压力，因为即将乘机离开时，他们才开始认真谈判。

下次他们再去那里时，实际上预订了两家酒店。

其中一家酒店预订了一周。

同样的情况发生了，但他们随后换了酒店，继续谈判，由于让自己变得更有耐心，他们感受到的时间压力也减轻了。

现在，另一个思路是，除了让自己更有耐心之外，还要考虑透露你的最后期限。

所以如果你要赶飞机，或者有其他即将过期的事项，你可以告诉你的对手：嘿，我今天在这里。

我只有三个小时。

这是我的最后期限。

我与你分享这些信息，是因为我希望你理解我们正面临时间压力，而我们正在共同承担这种时间压力。

所以与其让你成为唯一匆忙的人，不如共享这种时间压力，这样你们双方都可以竞相完成交易。

你不希望成为唯一关注时钟的人，而对方显然却不着急。

现在，你要思考具体情境。

有时这可能会让你处于更糟糕的境地。

但在许多情况下，共享那个最后期限，如果它变成了共同的最后期限，就会像你所感受到的那样，给对方施加压力。

当你给别人设定最后期限时，什么最重要？

最后期限必须可信。

这是第一件事。

那么它可信吗？

我将分享一个例子，这发生在二十世纪八十年代。

当罗纳德·里根刚刚成为美国总统时，一万三千名空中交通管制员举行了罢工。

他们要求更高的工资、更好的工时以及更好的福利。

而这些空中交通管制员负责所有机场的飞机降落和起飞指挥。

在全国范围内，随着数千名空中交通管制员罢工，航空旅行面临停飞的威胁。

当时，罗纳德·里根刚开启他的总统任期，他发布了这项公告。

他说，你知道，这些空中交通管制员违反了法律。

如果他们在四十八小时内不返岗工作，他们将失去工作并被解雇。

所以他威胁要解雇他们。

他给出了四十八小时的最后期限。

而令人惊叹的是。

他真的付诸行动，总共解雇了一万一千三百五十九名空中交通管制员。

所以他们没有返岗工作，而他解雇了，你知道，再次强调，超过一万一千名负责空中交通管制的人员。

令人惊叹的是，他最终取消了他们工会的认证资格。

那是他总统任期的开端，正如他的美国司法部长埃德温·米斯后来描述的那样，他说这是他总统任期的奠基之举。

这建立了他反复使用的可信度。

所以无论是在国内用于立法行动，还是在国外用于外交行动，人们都相信他，因为他发出了这个威胁，这个最后期限。

他贯彻了这一承诺。

正因为他贯彻了这一承诺，他才拥有了可信度。

所以我们要思考可信度。

人们会相信你吗？

在许多情况下，人们并不会。

事实上，在危机谈判中，一种常见策略是危机谈判专家在最后期限到来前一刻打电话，只是陪着劫持者熬过那个最后期限。

所以他们说：嘿，你知道，中午十二点之前会发生这样的事。

而在十一点五十五分，他们只是打电话，继续交谈，就这样度过了最后期限。

他们再也不提这件事。

他们绝不会说：哦，嘿，等等，你忘了那个最后期限。

他们只是交谈着度过它，并忽略它，仿佛它从未发生过。

所以我们要思考最后期限的可信度。

当我们发出最后期限时，它可信吗？

我们对此有可信度吗？

人们会相信我们吗？

而且贯彻承诺可能代价高昂。

这对罗纳德·里根来说代价高昂。

他不得不调入空军，同时招聘和培训替补人员，但这是一个代价高昂的举动。

而这随后为他建立了可信度。

但你也要确保，当别人对你发出最后期限时，它可信吗？

有没有办法只是陪着人们熬过它？

好的，以下是关键教训。

当你面临时间成本时，你有时需要在并不耐心的情况下假装耐心。

如果你的时间成本很高，你不希望透露它们。

当你确实有最后期限时，你要考虑透露它们，因为这可以为你和你的对手创造一个共同的最后期限。

最后期限有助于推动事情进展，但你要确保在发出最后期限之前建立可信度，因为如果你不贯彻承诺，可能会损害你的可信度。

英文原文

One key feature in a lot of negotiations is time pressure.

There's often time pressure.

We think about time costs where suppose it's a dispute,people are on strike,and the striking workers are incurring costs because they're not getting wages.

The company is encouraging costs because they're not getting products built.

Or lawyers'fees,if we're suing each other,there are time costs.

As time goes on,our fees on both sides are rising.

So those are time costs.

There are also deadlines.

It's very common for people to have an exploding offer.

You know,here's your job offer.

You have two weeks to make a decision.

So I want to think about time costs and deadlines and how we navigate these through a negotiation.

First,let's consider time costs.

Time costs can apply asymmetrically to the two sides.

By asymmetric,I mean that one side might have very expensive costs,the other side might have lower costs.

So imagine you have the very expensive lawyer,the other side has a brother that's a lawyer,and so the two of you have very uneven costs as the case drags on.

So the idea is we want to think about the asymmetry in these costs.

Or you can imagine a strike.

That is,does one party have a very large strike fund?

What are the costs to the company?

And we can think about these asymmetric costs.

And remember,we talked about patience.

Time costs are going to influence how patient we are.

If we're the ones with the higher costs,we're going to make faster concessions.

We're going to focus more on our BATNA,that is our bottom line,more than what we aspire to get.

And in some cases,it causes us to be really quick to try to find some outcome.

We're likely to rely on some heuristic like,let's just split the difference,let's focus on a big issue,or if we have some tentative deal,let's just go there,where we're rushing to try to reach a deal.

So you want to be thinking quite carefully about time pressure.

We want to be cognizant of the time pressure we have and think about the time pressure others have.

So it could be,you know,I mentioned in one case,we have the expensive lawyer,but we want to think about,hey,you know,if we have the family member,you know,we have the sister who's the lawyer.

And they have the fancy lawyer that's costing a lot to recognize that we can be relatively more patient and we can inflate our aspirations in that case.

So those are time costs.

The next idea is deadlines.

So deadlines get things moving.

So the idea that we say,look,you've got two weeks to accept or reject the offer,well,that's going to get people moving.

They're going to likely give you a decision in two weeks.

In some cases,people manipulate deadlines.

I was working with some executives.

They were traveling to China and they had a very long negotiation.

The first week,they had some negotiation meetings,but they got a tour of the Great Wall.

They went out to meals.

They had banquets.

It was a really great time.

And they started negotiating only very seriously in the last day when they felt like they were under a lot of time pressure because they're about to fly out.

The next time that they traveled out there,they'd actually booked two hotels.

There was one hotel for one week.

And the same thing had happened,but then they just switched hotels and then kept negotiating and they felt less time pressure because they made themselves more patient.

Now,another idea is,in addition to making yourself more patient,is to think about revealing your deadline.

So if you have a flight to catch,if you have something else that's going to expire,you might tell your counterpart that,hey,I'm here today.

I only have three hours.

That's my deadline.

And I'm sharing that information with you because I want you to understand that we're under time pressure here and we're sharing that time pressure.

So rather than being the only one that's in a hurry,you're sharing that time pressure so that both of you can sort of race to get the deal done.

You don't want to be the only one that's thinking about the clock while the other person is clearly unhurried.

Now,you want to think about the specific context.

Sometimes that might put you in a worse position.

But in many cases,sharing that deadline,if it's now a shared deadline,it's going to put pressure on the other side the same as you feel.

When you're giving somebody a deadline,what matters?

Deadlines have to be credible.

That's the first thing.

So is it credible?

And I'll share one example,and this happened back in the 1980s.

When Ronald Reagan first became president in the United States,13000 air traffic controllers went out on strike.

They wanted better wages and hours and better.

Benefits,and the air traffic controllers,they handle all the airports,landing planes,letting the planes take off.

And across the country,with these thousands of air traffic controllers on strike,it was threatened to ground air travel.

Now,Ronald Reagan had just started his presidency,and he issued this proclamation.

He said,you know,these air traffic controllers,they're in violation of the law.

If they do not report for work within 48 hours,they will have forfeited their jobs and be terminated.

So he threatened to fire them.

He gave them a deadline of 48 hours.

And here's what's amazing about it.

He actually went ahead and he fired a total of 11359 air traffic controllers.

So they didn't return to work and he fired,you know,again,over 11000 people that were in charge of air traffic control.

And what's amazing,he ended up decertifying their union.

It was at the start of his presidency,and as his U.S.attorney,Edwin Mies described later,he said,this was the foundational act of his presidency.

It built credibility that he would use over and over and over again.

So both here domestically for his legislative actions and internationally for his diplomatic actions,people believed him because he had issued this threat,this deadline.

He had followed through on it.

And because he followed through on it,he had credibility.

So we want to think about credibility.

Are people going to believe you?

And in many cases,people don't.

In fact,in crisis negotiations,one common tactic is for the crisis negotiator to call right before a deadline and just talk the hostage taker through the deadline.

So they say,hey,you know,here's what's going to happen by 12 noon.

And at 11.55,they just call and just keep talking through the deadline.

And they never bring it back up.

They never say,oh,hey,wait,you forgot about that deadline.

They just talk through it and ignore it as if it never happened.

So we want to think about the credibility of deadlines.

When we issue a deadline,is it credible?

Do we have credibility in it?

Are people going to believe us?

And it could be costly to follow through.

It was costly for Ronald Reagan.

He had to bring in the Air Force as they hired and trained replacements,but it was a costly act.

that then built credibility for him.

But you also want to make sure when people are issuing deadlines for you,is it credible?

Is there a way to just talk people through it?

Okay,here are the key lessons.

When you have time costs,you want to sometimes pretend to be patient when you're not.

You don't want to reveal your time costs if they're high.

When you do have deadlines,you want to consider revealing them because those can create a shared deadline for you and your counterpart.

Deadlines can help get things moving,but you want to make sure that you build credibility before you issue deadlines that could cost you credibility if you're not going to follow through with it.

4-03-01.08_威胁

我们谈到了最后期限和可信度。

接下来我想谈谈与此相关的内容，即权力和威胁。

权力是每一段人际关系的基础特征之一。

纵观历史，跨越各种文化，每个人类群体的特征都是存在等级制度。

在每个社会群体中，总有一些人比其他人拥有更多权力。

在工作中、在家里、与朋友相处时，始终存在权力动态。

在谈判中，权力至关重要。

权力塑造我们的行为方式，也塑造我们的思维方式。

如果人们处于低权力状态，我们要思考自己拥有哪些选项。

我们能采取他人的视角吗？

我们能让谈判过程透明化吗？

我们能建立人际关系吗？

我们要关注根本利益，并诉诸规范。

什么是公平的，因为每个人都希望公平，如果我们处于低权力状态，诉诸规范和标准可能是我们的最佳选择。

如果我们在某种情境下拥有高权力，我们要小心不要滥用它，因为人们可能会表现出抗拒心理。

他们不喜欢被强迫做事。

所以我们希望关注根本利益。

如果我们陷入僵局，可能会提及我们拥有的权力并说：听着，事情可能会这样发展，但我真正想要解决的是根本利益，并顺势转向那里。

这才是让我们双方都受益的做法。

所以我们要避免显得软弱，但我们要关注关键的潜在利益以及基于利益的协议，也就是那些解决我们利益的协议，让双方都觉得自己有发言权，并且是创造该协议努力的一部分，这样他们更有可能致力于履行该协议，而不是强迫某人接受某些东西。

所以即使我们拥有权力，也要倾听他人。

因此，如果我们处于低权力状态，我们要诉诸规范；如果我们处于高权力状态，我们要转向真正关注根本利益，并最终利用这一点达成协议。

现在，在这种动态中，如果事情进展不顺，我们可能会使用威胁，或者在谈判中经常成为威胁的目标。

现在，威胁总是对人际关系有害。

这不是你可以轻易做的事情。

人们不喜欢被胁迫。

如果他们感到受到威胁，可能会破坏关系并拂袖而去。

所以我们要非常谨慎。

威胁在争端中更为常见。

回想一下我们谈过的争端与机遇的区别。

在争端中，威胁出现的可能性大得多，因为情绪如此高涨。

而当我们的最佳替代方案相互关联时，比如糟糕的离婚，事情进展不顺，我们可能会聘请律师诉诸法庭，结果大家一起完蛋。

所以我们的最佳替代方案是一起恶化。

或者是罢工或诉讼，在这种情况下，我们可能会走上一条情绪高涨、沟通不畅的道路，最终形成一个循环，共同摧毁大量价值。

所以我们要对威胁非常谨慎，并找出方法来阻止这种循环，以免我们损失价值。

那么，何时应该使用威胁呢？

以下是一些思路。

如果对方拒绝谈判，或者如果你想发出信号表明你不会被人利用，或者如果你觉得事情已陷入僵局且别无他法，或者回想一下里根与空中交通管制员的例子，有时你想树立一个先例，回想一下，那是他总统任期的开端，这样做代价高昂，但为他赢得了日后可以兑现的可信度，所以在某些情况下这是有用的。

但你要非常谨慎，因为它对人际关系伤害极大。

所以这里有一个框架。

我们要思考，如果你发出威胁，它可信吗？

你愿意贯彻到底吗？

我们仍然要思考人们拥有的根本利益。

我们要思考如何保全面子。

如果人们在威胁后退缩，他们会丢面子吗？

有没有办法为他们搭建一座桥梁，让他们采取行动而不显得像是在投降？

所以有人可能会怒气冲冲地离开房间，而你可能会发出威胁。

嘿，如果你不回来，我们就让这笔交易泡汤。

或者你可以用一种保全面子的方式来做，说：听着，你何不回去好好想想？

当你准备好了，只需告诉我。

我很乐意继续这次对话。

如果你确实发出了威胁，你要非常精确地说明你在做什么。

所以这是一个如果怎样的陈述，比如，接下来会发生什么。

所以你可能会，你知道，像限时报价那样说：嘿，我们真的很希望你在这里，但填补这个职位对我们来说至关重要。

如果你在两周内没有回复，我们将不得不向其他人发出报价，以便推进我们的计划。

但我们真的很想要你，所以你何不考虑一下，并尽快回复我们？

如果有人威胁你，你要确保避免这种冲突螺旋，认识到这是在按动按钮。

这就是所谓的抗拒心理。

我们不喜欢被胁迫。

所以我们不想仅仅因为抗拒心理而生气并做出反应。

但我们确实要确保不会以强化某种霸道关系的方式进行让步。

所以我们不想被欺负，我们要确保自己保持谨慎。

要做的一件事是考虑忽略威胁。

所以我之前提到过，危机谈判专家会在最后期限到来前一刻打电话，并交谈着度过它。

而在关于威胁与谈判的研究中，大多数谈判者，在这项研究中有百分之七十的时间，他们发现如果仅仅忽略威胁，威胁就不会得到回应。

所以有时我们可以忽略威胁。

接下来，我们要思考根本担忧是什么。

人们只是感到沮丧吗？

他们是否有某种觉得被忽视的担忧？

是否有对他们来说很重要的事情，而他们发出这个威胁是因为觉得需要引起关注？

他们真的拥有良好的外部选项吗？

还是他们在虚张声势？

这可信吗？

所以你要仔细且系统地思考，以确定这是否是你真正需要处理的事情，或者如我之前所说，大多数时候，我们可能只需忽略它并继续前进。

现在，我们可以提出问题以增进理解。

我们可以表达关切，让人们感觉自己的声音被听到了。

如果存在关键担忧，我们会将其弄清楚。

当其他方法都失效时，如果你觉得自己被逼入绝境或关系平衡不太对劲，你可以发出反威胁以建立可信度。

但关键思路之一是思考你所处的权力动态。

如果你处于低权力位置，你的选项确实较少。

如果你处于高权力位置，那么反击就是一个更具吸引力且被推荐的行动方案。

We talked about deadlines and credibility.

I next want to talk about something related to that,which is power and threats.

Power is one of the foundational features of every human relationship.

Every human group throughout history across cultures is characterized by a hierarchy.

Some people have more power than others in every social group.

At work,at home,with our friends,there's always a power dynamic.

In negotiations,power is very important.

Power shapes how we act and it shapes how we think.

If people have low power,we want to think about what options you have.

Can we take somebody else's perspective?

Can we make the negotiation visible?

Can we build relationships?

We want to focus on underlying interests and we want to appeal to norms.

What's fair,because everybody wants to be fair,and if we have low power,appealing to norms and standards may be our best bet.

If we have high power in a situation,we want to be careful not to throw it around because people can exhibit reactance.

They don't like being forced into things.

So we'd like to focus on underlying interests.

If we get stuck,we might refer to the power that we have and say,look,here's how things could happen,but I really want to address and segue to the underlying interests.

Here's what would make us both better off.

So we want to avoid appearing weak,but we want to focus on the key underlying interests and interest-based deals,so deals that address our interests where both parties feel like they had the voice and they were part of the effort of creating the deal,they're more likely to be committed to that deal rather than forcing somebody to take something.

So we want to listen to people even if we have power.

So if we have low power,we want to appeal to norms.If we have high power,we want to shift to really focus on underlying interests and ultimately use that to reach a deal.

Now,within this dynamic,if things aren't working,we may use threats or we may often be the target of threats in a negotiation.

Now,threats are always hard on the relationship.

It's not the kind of thing you want to do lightly.

People don't like being coerced.

If they feel like they're threatened,they may rupture the relationship and walk away.

So we want to be very careful.

Threats are far more common in disputes.

Recall we talked about disputes versus opportunities.

In disputes,threats are far more likely because the motions are so high.

And when we have linked batnas,so like a bad divorce,things aren't going well,and we could lawyer up and go to court,we're all going down together.

So our batna is getting worse together.

Or strikes or lawsuits,where things we can go down a path with high emotion,poor communication,and we end up creating a cycle where we destroy a lot of value together.

So we want to be very careful about threats and figure out ways to stop that cycle so we don't lose value.

Now,when should you ever use threats?

Here are some ideas.

If the other party won't negotiate,or if you want to signal that you're not going to be taken advantage of,or if you feel like things have reached an impasse and there's no other way forward,or recall the Reagan example with the air traffic controllers,sometimes you want to set a precedent where,

recall,this is at the start of his presidency,It was costly to do,but it gave him credibility he cashed in on later,where sometimes there are cases where it's useful.

But you want to be very careful because it's so hard on the relationship.

So there's a framework.

We want to think about,you know,if you make a threat,is it credible?

Are you willing to follow through?

We still want to think about the underlying interests that people have.

We want to think about saving face.

If people back down following a threat,are they going to lose face?

Is there a way to build a bridge for them to do things so they don't look like they're capitulating?

So somebody might storm out of the room and you might issue a threat.

Hey,if you don't get back here,we're going to blow up this deal.

Or you could do it in a face-saving way,saying,look,why don't you go and think about it?

And when you're ready,just let me know.

I'd love to continue this conversation.

If you do issue a threat,you want to be very precise about what you're doing.

So it's this if-then statement,like,here's what's going to happen.

So you might,you know,like an exploding offer,say,hey,we really want you here,but it's so important for us to fill this position.

If you don't respond within two weeks,we're going to have to make another offer so that we can move forward with our plans.

But we really want you,so why don't you think about it and get back to us as soon as you can?

If somebody's threatening you,you want to make sure you avoid this conflict spiral,recognize that it's pushing a button.

That is this idea of reactance.

We don't like being coerced.

So we don't want to just get mad and react just following reactants.

But we do want to make sure that we're not conceding in a way that's going to reinforce some domineering relationship.

So we don't want to be bullied and we want to make sure that we're careful.

One thing to do is consider ignoring the threat.

So I mentioned before that crisis negotiators call right before a deadline and talk through it.

And most negotiators in studies of threats and negotiation,70%of the time in this one study,they found that the threats go unreciprocated when they just ignore them.

So sometimes we can ignore threats.

Next,we want to think about what's the underlying concern.

Are people just frustrated?

Do they have some concern that they feel has been overlooked?

Is there something that is important to them and they're issuing this threat because they feel like they need to get attention?

Do they really have a good outside option?

Or are they bluffing?

Is this credible?

And so you want to think about it carefully and systematically to figure out if this is something you really need to attend to,or as I mentioned before,most of the time,we might just ignore it and move forward.

Now,we could ask questions to inform understanding.

We could express concerns so people feel as if they're being heard.

And if there is a key concern,we're going to figure it out.

When all else fails,you might deliver a counter threat to establish credibility if you feel like you're being backed into a corner or the relationship in balance isn't quite right.

But one of the key ideas is to think about the power dynamic that you have.

If you are in a low power position,you do have fewer options.

If you're in a high power position,then pushing back is a far more attractive and recommended course of action.

4-03-01.09_团队

团队。我们一些最重要的谈判都是在团队中进行的。

我想稍微思考一下，团队谈判与我们独自谈判有何不同。

首先，存在一些流程上的差异。

团队被认为比单人谈判者更有权力。

所以你可以想象去与另一家公司谈判。

你可能会带上一些人，有时人们甚至会直接去邮件收发室随便拉人。

他们会说，看，我只希望你加入我的团队，坐在我旁边。

仅仅拥有更多人这一感知，就会让你显得更有权力，即使你来自一个较小、权力较弱的组织。

团队还能形成对对方更准确的认知，部分是因为团队中有些人并不专注于自己即将说什么，而只是监控、观察、倾听，从而能够更准确地感知对方的想法、行为和言语。

另一个区别是，团队拥有更多可用的策略，他们有更多选项去做单人谈判者无法做到的事情。

所以你可以把“红脸白脸”策略作为一个例子。

想象一下，你有一名谈判者表现得通情达理，另一名谈判者则自始至终都表现得不可理喻。

这种对比会让那位通情达理的谈判者成为受信任、受喜爱的人。

即使那位“好警察”很强硬，人们也会关注那个最终变得受人喜爱和尊敬的人。

这种动态，也就是某种对比效应，使得这个人对对方来说如此有价值，以至于他们感到一种如释重负，觉得可以和这种“红脸白脸”套路中的人打交道。

现在，团队拥有这样的策略。

他们可以一起召开内部会议。

他们可以利用社会认同，让团队成员四处宣扬，是的，这是个好主意。

哦，那个主意真棒。

哦，我喜欢那个主意。

现在你面对的是一群已经就某事达成共识的人。

这是团队拥有的另一种策略。

现在，我想复述一个故事。

我曾与一家律师事务所合作，其中一位高级合伙人描述了他如何与另一位合伙人合作，并使用了“红脸白脸”策略。

在整个谈判过程中，一直有“好警察”和“坏警察”。

而他扮演的是“坏警察”。

在最后，他进行了角色互换。

所以在最后，他进行了切换，当时……他的搭档自始至终都是“好警察”，他们只剩下最后一个问题，现在他的搭档带着极大的愤怒冲出了会议室。

他说这让对方感到震惊，因为他们看着这个自始至终都通情达理的人，突然之间失控了。

现在他们看着他，这个自始至终都是“坏警察”的人，他却说，天哪，我从未见过他这样。

这让对方感到困惑，而他们正试图榨取最后的让步。

现在，这是一个广泛的理念。

当你与团队打交道时，他们拥有更多可用的策略。

他们能做单人谈判者做不到的事情。

当你与一个长期合作的团队打交道时，你要格外小心。

所以如果一个团队合作了一段时间，他们已经建立了融洽的关系，并发展出可以共同执行的策略，这些策略可能非常流畅且令人有些困惑。

所以你可以想想，我之前提到过，走进汽车经销店，那些作为团队一起工作的人，你知道，他们懂得一些策略。

所以你正计划在停车场买车，当你正在与销售员谈判时，另一位销售员走过来说，哦，嘿，你能告诉我，外面那辆车还有吗？

我有客户感兴趣。

这可能只是一种策略，要注意到嘿，这里存在团队动态在起作用，并认识到团队与单人谈判者不同。

团队也更具竞争性。

所以在团队内部，没人愿意出头成为最温和妥协的人。

他们也在努力管理自己在团队中的印象。

因此，团队往往让步更慢，也更难对付。

结果，团队达成协议所需的时间更长。

他们最终能达成更好的交易。

而且因为他们对对方了解更多，这些交易往往更具整合性。

但团队也有很多劣势。

我们反应缓慢，我们以两种方式泄露更多信息。

一是你可以想象，团队中的某人做出了你本不打算做出的让步。

或者对方提出了一个报价，你说，哦不，我们不能接受。

但你团队中的另一个人已经在点头，好像那是个好报价。

所以你正在泄露信息。

作为团队，你还要非常小心，不要假设对方听不见你们说话。

你可能会和旁边的人私下交谈，但在很多情况下，人们在国外旅行甚至在美国境内，可能会录制谈判过程，所以他们可能会听到私下交谈的内容。

有一个例子我想分享。

是一些印度人前往日本，与他们的日本对手进行谈判，他们用印地语彼此交谈，正确地推断他们的日本对手不懂印地语。

现在，他们没有意识到的是，谈判正在被录音，所以他们的日本对手将这些谈判内容转录并翻译，因此他们确切地知道了这次谈判中发生的一切。

所以我想强调的观点是，你知道，作为团队，你需要与对手沟通，但要小心不要臆断别人听不见你。

我提到了这些相互矛盾的反应。

所以你在说，不，我们不能那样做，而你的团队成员却在点头，好像那是个好报价。

我们损害了信誉。

作为团队，我们投射出的信任度低于作为单人谈判者时。

我们思考如何管理团队动态。

所以存在群体内部动态，我提到过我们正在努力管理印象。

我们希望在团队其他成员面前表现良好。

当你与另一个团队打交道时，请注意他们所说的一些话可能是为了内部消费。

他们希望确保自己看起来不错。

他们在团队成员面前表现良好。

因此，达成协议可能会更难。

而且速度更慢。

这些观众效应意味着，有时最有效的做法是找到对方团队中的一个人，进行一对一交流。

卡特总统调解萨达特和贝京之间的经典谈判，他在那里进行了一对一的散步，他与每位领导人分别召开内部会议，也就是将人们从他们更大的群体中带离出来。

首先，他实际上将谈判地点选在了戴维营，远离媒体，远离更大的人群，然后将个人分开，这通常是瓦解团队以达成协议的一种非常有效的方法。

所以团队谈判是组织生活中的常见特征，但我们有时可以考虑拆分不同的组成部分以尝试达成协议。

现在，是什么让团队行之有效？

最好的谈判团队是连贯一致的。

他们用一个声音说话。

这可能意味着你指定一个人作为团队的发言人。

你不希望人们发送相互矛盾的信息。

同样，如果你们有共同工作的经验，就更有可能达成共识。

但你要展现出连贯性，用一个声音说话。

这种连贯性会影响你的信誉和信任。它还会让你显得更有权力。

现在，建立连贯性的另一件事，不仅是准备和经验，你还可以分配角色。

分配的角色可能非常重要，每个人都在扮演自己的角色。

并且存在层级结构。

你要找出作为团队进行沟通的方式，也许通过笔记本电脑或其他移动设备。

你要找出一种方法达成共识，共同解决问题。

也许你们有小组会议，在定期时间点整合你们的知识和理解。

所以，当你找出驾驭和管理团队动态的方法时，连贯性真的非常重要。

英文原文

Teams.Some of our most important negotiations occur in teams.

I want to think a little bit about what makes team negotiations different from negotiating on our own.

First,there's some process differences.

Teams are perceived to be more powerful than a solo negotiator.

So you can imagine going to negotiate with another company.

You might bring people along,and sometimes people actually go out to the mailroom or just grab people.

And they say,look,I just want you to be on my team and sit next to me.

And just the perception you have more people seems as if you're more powerful,even if you're from a smaller,less powerful organization.

Teams also develop more accurate perceptions of the other side,in part because they have people not focused on what they're about to say,but just monitoring,watching,listening,that are able to develop more accurate perceptions of what the other side's thinking,doing,and saying.

Another difference is that teams,they have more available tactics,they have more available options to do things that a solo negotiator cannot do.

So you can take the good cop-bad cop routine as an example.

So imagine you have one negotiator that's being reasonable,another negotiator that's being unreasonable the whole way through.

That contrast is going to make the reasonable negotiator the trusted,liked person.

And even if that good cop is tough,people are going to focus on that person that ends up being well-liked,well-respected.

And the dynamic,the sort of contrast effect,makes this person so valuable to the other side that they feel some sense of relief they can deal with somebody in this good cop-bad cop routine.

Now,teams have tactics like that.

They can caucus together.

They can use social proof where a team of people can go around saying,yeah,that's a good idea.

Oh,that idea is really brilliant.

Oh,I love that idea.

And now you're facing a group of people who have all reached consensus on something.

That's another tactic teams have.

Now,I want to recount a story.

I was working with a law firm and one of the senior partners described how he had worked with another partner and they did this good cop-bad cop routine.

And the whole way through the negotiation,there were good cop and bad cop.

And he was the bad cop.

And at the end,he switched.

So at the end,he would switch where...

His partner who had been the good cop the whole way through,they had one final issue,and now his partner stormed out of the meeting with great anger about this one issue.

And he said it's shocking to the other side because they're looking,here's the person who's been reasonable the whole way through,and now all of a sudden they've just lost it.

And now they're looking at him,who's been the bad cop the whole time,and he's like,oh man,I've never seen him like this before.

And it's disorienting to the other side as they're trying to extract that last concession.

Now,here's the broad idea.

When you're dealing with a team,they have more available tactics.

They can do things that solo negotiators cannot do.

You want to be especially careful when you're dealing with a team that's worked together for a long time.

So if a team's been together for a while,they'll have developed some rapport in a relationship and they'll develop tactics they can engage in together that may be very smooth and somewhat disorienting.

So you can think about,I mentioned before,going into a car dealership,people who've been working together as a team,you know,they know some tactics.

So you're planning to buy the car out on the lot and somebody else comes by and as you're negotiating with your salesperson,another salesperson says,oh,hey,can you tell me,is that car out there still available?

I've got somebody interested.

It could just be a tactic that is to notice that,hey,there's a team dynamic at play here and to recognize that teams are different from solo negotiators.

Teams are also more competitive.

So within a team,nobody wants to stick their neck out and be the most conciliatory person.

They're trying to manage their impressions with their team too.

And so teams tend to make concessions more slowly and to be more difficult.

So as a result,teams take longer to reach agreement.

They end up getting better deals.

And because they learn more about the other side,those deals tend to be more integrative.

But there are a lot of disadvantages to teams too.

We are slow,we reveal more information in two ways.

One is you can imagine somebody on your team makes a concession that you weren't about to make.

Or the other side makes an offer and you say,oh no,we can't do that.

But somebody else on your team is already nodding like that was a good offer.

So you're revealing information.

You also want to be very careful as a team not to assume the other side can't hear you.

You might sidebar with somebody next to you,but there are a lot of cases where people traveling abroad or even in the United States,people might be recording negotiations,so they might hear sidebar conversations.

There's one example that I want to share.

It was Indian people that traveled to Japan,and they were negotiating with their Japanese counterparts,and they were talking amongst themselves in Hindi,correctly inferring their Japanese counterparts didn't speak Hindi.

Now,what they didn't realize is that the negotiations were being recorded,and so their Japanese counterparts had those negotiations transcribed and translated,and so they knew exactly what had been happening through this negotiation.

And so the point I want to share is,you know,as a team,you need to communicate with your counterparts,but you want to be careful not to presume that people can't hear you.

And I mentioned these mixed reactions.

So you're saying,no,we can't do that,and your team members nodding like that was a good offer.

We harm credibility.

We project lower trust as a team than we do as a solo negotiator.

We think about managing team dynamics.

So there's the within group dynamic,and I mentioned we're trying to manage impressions.

We want to look good to other people on our team.

And when you're dealing with another team,notice that some of the things they say may be for internal consumption.

They want to make sure they look good.

They look good for their team members.

And so it could be harder to reach an agreement.

And it's slower.

And these audience effects mean that sometimes the most effective thing to do is to find one person on the other team and have a one-on-one.

And the classic negotiations that President Carter mediated between Sadat and Begin,there he went on one-on-one walks,he caucused separately with each leader,where you're taking people away from their broader group.

And the first thing is he actually took this to Camp David,away from the press,away from a larger group of people,and then separating the individuals,that's often a very effective way to break down a team to find an agreement.

So team negotiations are a common feature of organizational life,but we can sometimes think about breaking up different components to try to reach an agreement.

Now,what makes teams effective?

The best negotiation teams are coherent.

They speak with a single voice.

And what that might mean is that you designate one person to be the mouthpiece of your team.

You don't want people sending conflicting messages.

And again,if you have experience working together,it's more likely you're going to be on the same page.

But you want to demonstrate coherence speaking with a single voice.

The coherence impacts your credibility and your trust.It also makes you seem more powerful.

Now,another thing to build coherence,not just preparation and experience,but you could have assigned roles.

And the assigned roles can be really important where each person is playing their part.

And there's a hierarchy.

You figure out how to communicate as a team,maybe through your laptops or other mobile devices.

You figure out a way to be on the same page and tackle a problem together.

And maybe you have group meetings that sort of integrates your knowledge and understanding at regular points in time.

So coherence is really important as you figure out a way to navigate and manage a team dynamic.

4-04-01.01_情绪调节

我想转而思考谈判者的心态。

也就是我们在谈判过程中是如何思考、如何感受的？

我想探讨的第一组理念与情绪有关。

我想深入思考的一个理念是情绪调节。

让我从一个故事开始。

那是十多年前的事了。

这是费城飞人队的一名冰球运动员。

冰球是一项节奏快、令人兴奋的运动。

有时也充满暴力。

费城飞人队的一名球员伊恩·拉佩里埃，以好斗著称。

飞人队刚刚连输六场比赛。

在第七场比赛中，伊恩·拉佩里埃进行了他第五十二次冰球斗殴。

这创下了球队纪录。

他掉了七颗牙齿。

其中两颗是他以前从未掉过的。

他最终需要缝五十多针。

这就是伊恩·拉佩里埃。

接下来发生了这样的事。

在此之前，你知道，在连输六场之后，他走出去说，我带着怒火来到冰场。

希望大家都怒气冲冲。

我们需要这样，我们需要把这种情绪带上冰面，在那里激发出一些激情。

我想思考的是关于承载情绪或为某事给自己打气的理念。

现在，这是冰球，但我想指出，不仅仅是冰球，人们会改变自己的情绪。

他们经常在进入谈判前改变自己的情绪。

你可以想象，在球队上场之前更衣室里会发生什么。

而不是仅仅被动接受。

我们要做的第一件事是选择我们的情境。

我们做什么？

我们去健身房吗？

我们去拜访朋友吗？

有一些我们可以具体去做的事情，这将改变我们的感受。

因此，通常我们在选择情境方面拥有的控制权比想象中更多。

所以，我们可以去改变我们的情境。

这里的关键理念是认识到，我们需要意识到身处何地如何影响我们的感受。

我们需要弄清楚这种关系是什么。

第二是情境修正。

比如，如果阳光刺眼，让我们想办法改变坐的位置或拉上百叶窗。

如果房间太热或太冷，有什么办法可以修正那种情境吗？

所以，我们可以修正我们的情境。

这里的理念是，有时我们可以以有助于我们的方式修正情境。

第三个理念是，我们要将注意力引导到特定事物或其他事物上。

你可以想象乘坐飞机。

我们试图转移注意力。

第四件事是我们可以改变感知情境的方式。

认知改变的理念是，我们试图弄清楚发生了什么，并可以讲述一个不同的故事。

所以，如果我们想象在这架飞机上，如果有另一位顾客无礼，或者空乘人员对我们很简短，我们可以做一个归因说，嘿，他们就是粗鲁的人。

请记住，基本归因错误是我们过度进行了个人归因。

你知道，或者嘿，这对他们来说一定是一个非常重要的问题。

这就是他们表现如此的原因。

所以，我们可以改变我们讲述故事的方式，改变我们理解情境的方式，从而转变我们的反应方式或内化他们言语的方式。

现在，最后一个理念是反应调节。

所以，我们正在改变我们的反应。

因此，当有人在谈判桌上撞到我们或说些粗鲁的话时，我们可以非常刻意地应对。

所以，如果有人说了侮辱性的话，我们以一种出乎意料或更友善的方式回应，而不是按我们原本想的那样。

所以，这个理念是，你知道，我们可以选择情境，我们可以修正情境，我们可以引导注意力，我们可以重新评估我们对某事的反应，然后我们可以改变我们的回应。

所有这些都能使我们采取行动并改变我们实际的感受。

所以，想想在谈判中，理念往往是人们进入谈判并放大愤怒。

他们经常这样做是为了不感到焦虑。

当人们审视并预期谈判时，感受到的头号情绪是焦虑。

这是一种低控制感的情绪，人们可能想要转而放大愤怒。

所以，这与试图抑制愤怒相反。

也就是说，通常我们担心把工作上的愤怒带回家并试图减少愤怒。

在这里，人们经常想在对抗前放大愤怒。

所以，我们可以让人们放松下来。

我们可以让谈判显得不那么具有对抗性。

我们可以专注于协作，说，嘿，我们正在一起努力。

我们试图解决一个谜题。

我们可以坐在桌子的同一侧共同解决问题，使其显得不那么具有对抗性，也不太像其他人需要放大他们的愤怒。

如果你的对手很生气，对你作为谈判者来说是不利的，他们思考方式更自我关注，思考不够开阔，而你如果人们很生气，你就无法达成整合性的好交易。

所以，你要想办法为人们化解那种情绪。

4-04-01.02_焦虑

焦虑是与谈判相关的最常见情绪。

焦虑有许多触发因素。

一般来说，不确定的事物会引发焦虑，因为我们不知道会发生什么。

谈判中也是如此。

我不知道对方具体会说什么，也不知道他们会如何反应。

当事物具有新颖性时，比如我在谈判方面没有经验，我不常进行谈判。

或者我以前从未与这个人谈判过。

这种新颖性会引发焦虑。

当事物具有重大后果时，也就是发生的事情对我至关重要，这也会引发焦虑。

因此，谈判中的不确定性、新颖性和后果严重性更容易引发焦虑。

所以请注意，我们能收集越多信息以减少不确定性，能进行越多练习以减少新颖性，我们在应对焦虑时就会越有利。

时间压力也会增加焦虑。

所以我们讨论过的一个关键主题是：是否有办法安排谈判时机，找到一个空间让我们感觉更有耐心？

我们也会对他人情绪产生反应。

所以如果有人对我们表达愤怒，这会让我们感到焦虑，特别是当我们权力较低时。

比如一个有权势的人，想象一位正在吼叫的老板，这会让我们更加焦虑。

同样，我们不太确定自己会发生什么，而且这可能后果严重。

所以我们要思考在某些情况下化解他人愤怒的方法。

我们能否做些什么来转变人们的情绪，或者换个时间再来？

所以如果人们很生气，稍后在另一个时间点进行谈判可能会平息某人的愤怒，特别是如果他们生气的事情与你没有直接关系。

我们在谈判中感受到的焦虑，在许多新颖且后果严重的场景中都很常见。

你可以想象进入医疗场景，你要接受化验，你不知道发生了什么，或者有一位理财顾问可能使用术语并谈论市场崩盘，这会引发焦虑。

这些事情非常重要，因为焦虑会激发逃避反应。

所以当我们感到焦虑时，我们想要逃离那种情境。

这与愤怒相反，愤怒会促使我们走向某事。

这更像是一种战斗反应。

所以焦虑会触发这种逃避，促使我们试图在谈判中脱身。

这并不好，因为我们可能会做出让步，并试图更快地退出。

焦虑还会增加我们的认知负荷。

它让我们心里装了更多事情。

我们现在担心各种事情，比如嘿，我表现得得体吗？

我那样说对吗？

我会发生什么？

这种额外的认知负荷挤占了我们驾驭谈判所需的心理空间。

它会损害我们的自信心。

我们担心自己表现不佳。

而在谈判中，这种较低的自信心和自我效能感可能是有害的。

此外，它可能导致我们寻找更多信息。

我们在监控他人。

嘿，我表现得还好吗？

人们对此反应如何？

我们正在以可能富有成效也可能毫无成效的方式搜寻更多信息。

现在，在某些情况下，焦虑是富有成效的。

那么焦虑有什么好处呢？

嗯，提前发生时是有益的。

所以如果我对演讲感到焦虑，对谈判感到焦虑，我就会去准备。

因此，它所激发的准备工作可能非常有用。

焦虑还能让我们更加警惕。

所以我们更有可能监控局势。

我们在四处寻找信息。

我们在寻求信息。

这种增强的警惕性可能是有帮助的。

所以无论是在更加努力还是更加警惕方面，它都能引导我们为谈判做更充分的准备。

但所有这些发生在事前，而不是当下。

在当下，当我们感到焦虑时，这并不好。

所以我提到过，当我们感到焦虑时，我们渴望退出。

在我与艾莉森·伍德·布鲁克斯进行的研究中，我们发现焦虑的谈判者会得到更差的结果。

他们预期结果较低，提出的首次报价较低，回应更快因为他们很匆忙，并且渴望退出谈判。

所以出于所有这些原因，他们在谈判中的表现最终更差。

那么焦虑会做什么呢？

我想指出的是，焦虑激发逃避，而愤怒激发战斗，两者形成对比。

所谓逃避，我的意思是当人们感到焦虑时，他们想要退出。

他们想要摆脱这种情境。

当人们感到愤怒时，他们想要走向这种情境。

我想要去处理那件事。

这就是为什么人们在谈判前，如果感到焦虑，可能会想要放大他们的愤怒感。

所以他们会去找房东谈，找经理谈。

他们受那种愤怒驱使去接近某事。

焦虑导致我们想要试图退出。

并且在谈判当下感到焦虑时，通常是相当有害的。

它增加了认知负荷。

我们心里装了更多事情。

我们很担心，所以我们担心自己表现如何或会发生什么。

我们的自信心降低，这降低了我们在谈判中的自我效能感。

而这种自信心缺失导致我们提出较低的报价。

并且我们不断寻求安慰和更多信息。

我们在观察其他人。

嘿，我表现得还好吗？

我说得有道理吗？

发生了什么？

现在，如果焦虑提前发生，它可能会产生积极影响。

所以在谈判前，焦虑会导致我们做更多准备。

所以我们担心事情会如何发展，于是我去准备。

或者我更加警惕，我在监控环境，我感到焦虑，我在集中注意力。

所以这种准备和这种高度关注，是焦虑能产生的积极作用。

这就有点像准备考试。

如果我提前感到焦虑，我就会更努力地学习。

这是有功能的。

现在，在当下，焦虑总是有害的。

所以当我在进行谈判时，当我在参加考试时，感到焦虑会损害表现。

在我与艾莉森·伍德·布鲁克斯进行的研究中，我们研究了焦虑与谈判，发现焦虑的谈判者会得到更差的结果。

他们得到更差的结果，是因为他们渴望逃离情境，所以他们降低了自信心，他们预期表现会更差，他们提出更低的首次报价，他们对收到的报价回应得更快，而且他们如此渴望摆脱那种情境，以至于他们愿意接受更差的结果。

不是高兴，而是他们感到焦虑并渴望脱身，因此愿意做出那些妥协。

所以正是这种急于离开以及谈判中较低的自我效能感和较低的自信心，导致他们表现更差。

现在，在谈判中，如果人们向我们提供想法，焦虑也会使我们更愿意接受别人所说的话。

当我们感到焦虑时，你可以想象那个医疗场景或财务情境，如果有人让我们感到焦虑，我们更有可能寻求他们的建议，更愿意接受他们的建议。

并且我们也变得不太能分辨好坏。

所以在中立状态下，我们能比在感到焦虑时更好地判断收到的是坏建议还是好建议。

在那种情况下，我们的辨别力荡然无存，我们对所接收的信息非常来者不拒。

如果我们碰巧收到了极好的建议，比如医疗专业人员给了我们好建议，那很棒。

我们会采纳它。

如果在谈判中我们感到非常焦虑，而人们给了我们好建议，那是有帮助的。

但如果对方给我们建议，我们就不太可能注意到利益冲突。我们辨别力较差，所以在感到焦虑时，我们不太可能拒绝糟糕的建议。

我们最终可能会做出错误的决定。

自信心是这个故事的关键部分。

焦虑会损害我们的自信心，但如果我们拥有高自信心，如果我们经过练习，经过排练，对自己感到自信，我们最终的表现会好得多，并且能抵御焦虑。

也就是说，如果我们感到自信，我们就极不可能感到焦虑。

In general,things that are uncertain,we're not sure what's going to happen.

That's true in negotiation.

I don't know exactly what someone's going to say or how they'll react.

When things are novel,so I'm not experienced in negotiation,I don't negotiate a lot.

Well,I haven't negotiated with this person before.

That novelty can trigger anxiety.

When things are consequential,so what's going to happen really matters to me when it's consequential,that also triggers anxiety.

So this uncertainty,the novelty,the consequential characteristics of a negotiation are more likely to trigger anxiety.

So notice that the more information we can gather to make it less uncertain,the more we can practice to make it less novel,the better off we'll be in dealing with anxiety.

Time pressure can also add anxiety.

So one of the key themes we've talked about is:are there ways to time the negotiation,to find a space so we feel more patient?

And we also react to other people's emotions.

So if somebody's expressing anger toward us,that can make us anxious,particularly if we have low power.

So a high-power person,you think about a boss who's yelling,that's going to make us more anxious.

Again,we're not quite sure what's going to happen to us,and it could be consequential.

So we want to think about ways,in some cases,to diffuse other people's anger.

Are there things that we can do to shift people's emotions or come back at a different time?

So if people are angry,negotiating later at a different point in time could be something that mollifies somebody's anger,particularly if what they're angry about is not directly related to you.

The anxiety we feel in negotiation,it's common for many novel consequential settings.

You can think about going into a healthcare setting,you're getting lab tests,you're not sure what's going on,or there's a financial advisor who might be using terms and talking about a market crash that can trigger anxiety.

Those things are really important because anxiety motivates flight.

So when we feel anxious,we want to get out of that situation.

As opposed to anger,which causes us to go towards something.

It's more of a fight response.

So anxiety triggers this flight,causing us to try to get out in negotiations.

That's not good because we're likely to make concessions and try to get out more quickly.

Anxiety also gives us more cognitive load.

It puts more on our mind.

We're now worried about things and hey,am I coming across the right way?

Did I say that the right way?

What's going to happen to me?

That extra cognitive load is crowding out the mental space we need to navigate a negotiation.

It harms our self-confidence.

And that lower self-confidence,that self-efficacy in negotiation,can be harmful.

And then it might cause us to look for more information.

Hey,is my coming house okay?

How are people reacting to this?

We're searching for more information in ways that may or may not be very productive.

Now,in some cases,anxiety is productive.

So what is anxiety good for?

Well,ahead of time,it's good.

So if I'm anxious about a presentation,I'm anxious about a negotiation,I'm going to prepare.

And so that preparation that it triggers can be very useful.

Anxiety can also make us more vigilant.

So we're more likely to monitor a situation.

We're looking around for information.

We're seeking information.

That increased vigilance can be helpful.

So both in working harder and being more vigilant,it can guide us to be more prepared for negotiation.

But all that happens ahead of time,not in the moment.

In the moment,when we're feeling anxious,it's not good.

So I mentioned when we're feeling anxious,we're eager to exit.

In research that I've done with Allison Wood Brooks,we found that anxious negotiators get worse outcomes.

They expect lower outcomes,they make lower first offers,they respond more quickly because they're in a hurry,and they're eager to exit the negotiation.

So for all of these reasons,they end up performing worse in a negotiation.

So what does anxiety do?

And I want to suggest that anxiety motivates flight in contrast to anger that motivates fight.

So by flight,what I mean is when people feel anxious,they want to exit.

They want to get out of the situation.

When people feel anger,they want to go toward the situation.

I want to go deal with that.

So this is why people,prior to negotiation,if they feel anxious,they might want to upregulate their feeling of anger.

So they're going to go talk to the landlord,talk to the manager.

They're motivated by that anger to go approach something.

Anxiety causes us to want to try to exit.

and is generally quite harmful when we feel it in the moment of a negotiation.

It adds cognitive load.

We have more in our minds.

We're worried,so we're worried about how we're coming across or what's gonna happen.

We are less self-confident,it drops our self-efficacy in a negotiation.

And that self-confidence causes us to make lower offers.

And we're constantly looking for reassurance and more information.

We're looking at other people.

Hey,am I coming across okay?

Am I making sense?

What's happening?

Now,anxiety can have positive effects if it happens in advance.

So before a negotiation,anxiety can cause us to prepare more.

So we're worried about how things will go,so I prepare.

Or I'm more vigilant,I'm monitoring my environment,I'm anxious,and I'm paying attention.

So this preparation and this heightened attention,that's what anxiety can do that's positive.

So sort of like preparing for an exam.

If I'm anxious ahead of time,I'm going to study harder.

That's functional.

Now,in the moment,anxiety is always bad.

So while I'm performing a negotiation,while I'm taking a test,feeling anxious is going to harm performance.

And in research that I've done with Allison Wood Brooks,we studied anxiety negotiations,and anxious negotiators get worse outcomes.

They get worse outcomes because they're eager to exit the situation,so they and they drop their self-confidence,they expect to do worse,they make lower first offers,they respond more quickly to the offers that they get,and they are so eager to get out of that situation,

they're happy to get worse outcomes.

Not happy,but they're anxious and they're eager just to get out,and they're willing to make those compromises.

So it's this hurry to leave and this lower self-efficacy,lower self-confidence in the negotiation that causes them to do worse.

Now,in a negotiation,if people are giving us ideas,anxiety also makes us more receptive to what other people are saying.

When we feel anxious,and you can think about that healthcare setting or that financial situation,if somebody's caused us to feel anxious,we're more likely to seek their advice,we're more receptive to their advice.

and we also become less discerning between what's good and bad.

So in a neutral state,we can tell if we're getting bad advice or good advice far better than if we're feeling anxious.

Where our discrimination goes out the window,we're very receptive to what we're getting.

And if we happen to be getting great advice,so the medical professional is giving us good advice,that's great.

We're going to take it.

If in a negotiation we're feeling very anxious and people are giving us good advice,that's helpful.

But if the other side's giving us advice,we're less likely to notice a conflict of interest.We're less discerning,so we're less likely to reject terrible advice when we feel anxious.

We may end up making bad decisions.

Self-confidence is a key part of this story.

Anxiety harms our self-confidence,but if we have high self-confidence,if we've practiced,we've rehearsed,we feel confident in ourselves,we end up performing much better,and we're buffeted from anxiety.

That is,if we feel confident,we're far less likely to feel anxiety.

4-04-01.03_应对焦虑

焦虑在谈判中普遍存在。

我们对此能做些什么？

我们如何应对焦虑？

事实证明，这不仅仅局限于谈判。

当我向人群谈论焦虑时，如果我问有多少人每天都感到焦虑，结果令我震惊。

绝大多数人都会举起手来。

人们在任何情况下都时刻感到焦虑，无论是在工作中、社交互动中，甚至在家里。

我们能做些什么来应对焦虑？

现在，针对谈判，我想重点关注几个理念。

一是练习的理念。

我们之前谈过这一点。

也就是说，通过练习，我们将建立自我效能感和自信心。

这种自信心能缓冲我们，使我们不易感到焦虑。

我还提到了提前规划。

因此，我们做的准备越充分，就会感觉准备得越到位，感觉越自信，焦虑对我们的伤害也就越小。

耐心至关重要。

时间压力会让我们感到焦虑。

所以，如果我们能想办法在那一刻保持耐心，规划好谈判的时机，规划好谈判的地点，以便我们能够保持耐心，这将有助于减轻我们的焦虑感。

我想在本模块中谈谈两个关键策略：重评和仪式。

我将对这两者做更多说明。

首先是重评。

现在，我想思考一下情绪。

这里有一个情绪环形模型，或者说情绪地图。

想象我们要沿着两个维度来刻画情绪。

第一个是效价。

这种情绪是令人愉悦的还是令人不悦的？

所以快乐非常令人愉悦，愤怒则非常令人不悦。

但还有许多令人愉悦的情绪，如快乐、满足、兴奋。

也有许多令人不悦的情绪，如恐惧、愤怒、悲伤。

它们各不相同。

我们可以思考其他维度。

另一个关键维度是激活度。

也就是你的激活程度如何？

你的心跳有多快？

所以如果你很兴奋，心跳就很快；如果你很平静，心跳就很慢。

那么让我们思考四种情绪，它们在愉悦、不悦、高激活、低激活上有所不同。

在高激活情绪中，焦虑是高激活且负面的。

兴奋是高激活且正面的。

现在，在最底部，一种令人愉悦的低激活情绪是平静。

与之相对的是无聊。

所以希望我没有把你们置于这个低激活、令人不悦的无聊领域，但我怀疑我的许多学生花了很多时间在这个状态里。

所以我们有高激活且负面的焦虑，高激活且正面的兴奋。

我们有低激活且令人愉悦的平静，以及低激活且负面的无聊。

现在，让我们稍微思考一下这个。

如果你告诉朋友，嘿，我对这次演讲感到焦虑，我对这次谈判感到焦虑，你得到的常见建议是，嘿，只要冷静下来。

所以他们的意思是，你想从高激活、令人不悦，转向低激活、令人愉悦。

这在情绪环形模型上几乎是跨度最大的移动。

所以他们要求你进行一次非常遥远的旅程，只要冷静下来。

现在也许他们会再补充一条建议，比如，只要深呼吸。

而我想指出的是，那条建议毫无价值。

也就是说，不可能通过一次深呼吸就从焦虑转为平静。

这根本行不通。

事实上，遵循那条建议，你会想，哦，我深呼吸了。

但我仍然感到焦虑。

为什么不起作用？

这实际上可能会让一些人更加烦躁。

所以我们要思考一些略有不同的方法。

我想建议的是，嘿，想象我说，保持高心率，这没关系。

我们就让它保持在那里。

我想让你做的是将焦虑重评为兴奋。

所以两者都是高激活状态。

我想让你将正在发生的事情从威胁重构为机会。

所以你在谈判，你关注的是事情可能出错的方式，谈判可能会如何伤害你。

而嘿，我想让你转而关注，如果事情顺利，你将如何受益。

想象一下结果会有多美好。

这里面有所有这些机会。

关注机会而不是威胁。

变得兴奋而不是焦虑。

这里的理念是，从焦虑转向兴奋实际上出奇地容易。

也就是说，我们通过关注机会来重新评估局势。

在艾莉森·伍德·布鲁克斯进行的研究中，只是让人们在做某事之前说“我很兴奋”，就会触发这样的想法：嘿，这是一个令人兴奋的机会，从而开始改变人们的感受。

无论他们是被要求这样说，还是自发这样说，我们都做了这类研究，观察了一系列不同的事物。

比如歌唱表演、数学测试，人们改变了他们的感受，他们的自我效能感更高，表现也提升了。

我将向你们展示一个有点有趣的任务。

我们在演讲、公开演说、歌唱、数学测试中都做过这个，这对谈判也很重要。

我们用威卡拉OK机做了这个实验。

人们必须唱歌，机器会对他们唱歌的准确度和音高进行评分。

告诉人们在做一个引发焦虑的任务之前说“我很兴奋”，他们最终的得分显著更高。

好的，所以将事物从焦虑重评为兴奋是一个理念。

所以在考试前，变得兴奋。

在谈判前，变得兴奋。

第二个理念是仪式。

我想将仪式视为应对焦虑的一种方式。

我想指出，宗教仪式全都是关于这一点的。

当我们经历过渡期时，出生、死亡、婚姻，任何变化都伴随着一系列仪式。

我们与他人共同进行的仪式，在减轻焦虑方面可能非常强大。

在体育界，每位主要运动员都有他们执行的仪式。

这些仪式在某些行动前夕尤为强烈。

所以当比赛暂停，所有人的目光都集中在一名球员身上时，比如网球运动员在发球前，篮球运动员在罚篮前，他们会进行一种仪式，这赋予他们控制感，减轻焦虑，并提升表现。

对于那些焦虑且难以入睡的人，仪式能提高我们入睡的能力。

我想建议的是，谈判前的仪式会非常有帮助。

这是我与一些合著者进行的一项研究。

我们告诉人们，嘿，你要对着这台威卡拉OK机唱歌。

它会给你打分。

你要唱《别停止信念》。

我不会为你们唱，那我就省了。

但这首《别停止信念》。

是一首非常流行的歌曲。

许多人都知道它。

我们给人们歌词，然后把他们带进一个房间，他们要在这台威卡拉OK机前演唱。

在这项研究中，我将向你们展示心率和仪式会发生什么。

现在，请记住我之前说过降低心率很难，确实如此。

但仪式可以做到。

所以我们使用了脉搏血氧仪。

在人们刚走进来时，在我们告诉他们要唱歌之前，我们让他们闭上眼睛深呼吸。

所以这只是他们的基础心率。

我们记录了那个数据。

然后我们说，好了，这是实验。

你要唱歌，我们会给你打分。

接着我们最终做的是把人们带进房间，我们让他们首先要么什么都不做。

第二，我们说，嘿，冷静下来。

在唱歌前尽力冷静下来。

那是你朋友的建议。

然后在第三种条件下，我们让人们参与我们编造的一个仪式。

我们说，画一幅画表达你的感受，在画上撒盐。

我们准备了盐瓶。

在心里数到五，把纸揉皱，把纸扔进垃圾桶。

所以他们参与了那个仪式。

现在，这里真正酷的地方来了。

你可以看到人们走进来，他们的心率很低。

我们告诉他们要唱歌并接受评分。

每个人的心率都上升了。

然后我们要么说，试着冷静下来。

那没多大作用。

我们什么都不做。

那也没多大作用。

或者我们给他们一个仪式，那是唯一真正降低心率的干预措施。

所以我想指出，仪式通常是减轻焦虑的一种非常有效的方式。

我只是顺便展示一下，这在许多不同领域都是如此，但就歌唱表现而言，在仪式之后，人们实际上唱得更好了。

谈判也是如此，我想建议的是，当我们感到焦虑时，我们要提前规划。

我们要认识到自己的感受，以便重评那种情绪，认识到我们能做些什么来改变它。

我们要通过练习来增强自信。

我们要变得兴奋，关注机会，想象事情顺利进行以及那意味着什么。

我们要参与那些帮助我们应对焦虑的仪式。

4-04-01.04_愤怒

我想回到谈判中两个真正重要的核心概念。

我想谈谈愤怒和权力。

一个理念是，有权势的人在行事上拥有更宽的余地。

所以有权势的人，就像在手术室里可以扔器械的外科医生，而不是护工。

是可以在对人吼叫的律所合伙人，而不是律师助理。

有权势的人就是能做与其他人不同的事情。

这在表达愤怒方面尤为如此。

我们允许有权势的人比低权力者表达更多的愤怒。

另一个关键理念是，我们倾向于进行反向推断。

我们倾向于赋予表达愤怒的人更高的地位。

所以对于某个表达愤怒的人，我们会假设，哦，他们一定很有权势。

因此，表达愤怒对高权力者来说是一件风险较低的事情。

在不确定的情境中，表达某种愤怒的人会被认为更有权势。

在谈判中，人们经常会对表达愤怒的人做出让步，尽管他们真的很不喜欢这样。

所以愤怒在谈判中非常普遍，尤其是在争端中，而非合作机会中。

正如我已经提到的，人们希望带着愤怒进入谈判。

这给了他们一种控制感。

人们常常用愤怒来掩饰自己的情绪。

他们调节情绪以变得愤怒，而不是焦虑。

现在，当某人的目标受阻时，往往会导致愤怒。

他们觉得自己受到了不公平对待，觉得无法做自己想做的事情。

在这种情况下，人们更容易感到愤怒。

现在，当我们精力耗尽时，当我们感到疲惫不堪时，比如在长途旅行后，熬夜后，如果我们累了，没吃东西，人们就无法很好地调节情绪，较小的触发因素就会让他们感到愤怒。

我之前提到的一个关键理念是，如果你的对手感到愤怒，对你并没有好处。

那么，什么样的事情会激怒人们呢？

比如目标受阻、不承认他们所说的话、人身攻击、翻白眼、打断别人。

有许多无礼的行为，比如语言刺激物，我们可能会说，指出某人的错误，将问题个人化。

而不是关注更广泛的问题，告诉别人该做什么。

有许多触发因素会引发焦虑。

我们在沟通时要小心，尽量减少这些因素。

所以，如果你的谈判团队中有某人，你要确保他们关注的是问题，而不是攻击个人。

现在，当人们感到愤怒时，会损害信任。人们变得更具批判性。

他们不太愿意接受建议。

请记住，我说过当人们感到焦虑时，他们更愿意接受。

愤怒的人不太愿意接受别人所说的话。

当人们感到愤怒时，他们也更容易使用欺骗手段。

他们更关注自我，不太关心他人。

愤怒造成的另一个关键问题是损害换位思考。

所以如果我们感到愤怒，我们会将注意力收缩到自己身上。

我们就不太能很好地站在别人的角度思考。

现在，想象我说，你知道，这里有一张图片。

有个人面前有一个数字。

我说，那个人面前的数字是多少？

现在我们可以看着这个数字说，看，这个人面前的数字是数字一六。

或者我们可以说，嗯，我们是站在他们的角度，那是九一。

现在请记住，我之前提到过，换位思考对于优秀的谈判者至关重要。

高效的谈判者会站在对方的角度，弄清楚他们需要什么，他们愿意接受什么，而换位思考创造了达成协议的空间，这更有可能对你有利。

所以我想思考的是，换位思考如何使我们能够更有效、更高效地协作，但愤怒会抑制我们换位思考的能力。

所以这种需要努力的换位思考，在我们感到愤怒时会变得更加困难。

愤怒将我们的注意力收缩到自己身上，所以我们不太可能expansive地思考我们的对手，也不太可能思考他们的需求。

我与杰里米·伊普所做的研究，我们研究了不同的情绪和换位思考，我们一致发现，在我之前提到的这类试验中，比如这个人面前的数字是多少，在许多换位思考的情境中，当人们感到愤怒时，他们极不可能站在对方的角度思考。

他们极有可能从自己的视角看待世界，以一种利己的、自我关注的方式看待事物。

所以换位思考对于谈判极其重要。

愤怒是损害我们换位思考能力的关键因素之一。

权力也会损害换位思考，因为这需要付出努力，而有权势的人已经养成了不再思考他人的习惯。

所以我们需要在换位思考上更加努力，特别是如果我们感到有点不安。

或者如果我们觉得自己更有权势，或者感觉更自我关注，为了跨越鸿沟，为了找出谈判中的空间，我们必须在换位思考上付出额外的努力。

I'd like to return to two key constructs in negotiation that are really important.

It's the law partners that can scream at people,not the paralegals.

Powerful people can just do different things than other people.

And it's particularly true with respect to expressing anger.

We let powerful people express more anger than low-power people.

Another key idea is that we tend to make that reverse inference.

We tend to give greater status to people who express anger.

So somebody who's expressing anger,we assume,oh,they must be powerful.

So expressing anger for high-power people is a less risky thing for them to do.

And in uncertain situations,people who express some anger are perceived to be more powerful.

And in negotiations,people often make concessions to somebody who's expressing anger,though they really don't like it.

So anger is very common in negotiation,particularly disputes rather than opportunities.

And as I already mentioned,people want to come to negotiations angry.

It gives them a sense of control.

And people often paper over their emotions with anger.

They regulate to become angry rather than anxious.

Now,anger can often result when somebody's goals are blocked.

rather than about the broader problem,telling other people what to do.

There are many triggers that can trigger anxiety.

And we want to be careful as we're communicating that we minimize some of these things.

So there's somebody on your negotiating team,you want to make sure that they're focusing on the problem,not attacking the person.

Now,when people feel anger,it harms trust.People become more critical.

They're less receptive to advice.

Remember,I said when people feel anxious,they're more receptive.

Angry people are less receptive to what people are saying.

And when people feel angry,they're also more likely to use deception.

They're more self-focused and less concerned about others.

Another key thing anger does is it harms perspective taking.

We're taking other people's perspective less well.

So what I want to think about is how perspective taking enables us to collaborate more effectively and more efficiently,but anger can curb our ability to take perspective.

So this effortful thinking of perspective taking is harder when we feel anger.

And anger collapses our focus on ourselves,so we're less likely to think expansively about our counterpart and think about their needs.

studies that I've done with Jeremy Yip,we looked at different emotions and perspective taking,and we consistently find that in trials like the one that I mentioned before,like what numbers in front of this person,in many perspective taking contexts,when people feel angry,

they're far less likely to take the other side's perspective.
